Exact Baseline Geometry, Hydraulic Solution, Parts, Tools, Fabrication, Installation, Controls, and Validation


  

Prepared for Taylor Heller | Monsters Ink LLC | 30 July 2026
Status: engineering concept and prototype specification - not a certified pool structure or listed pump assembly
________________


1. Executive Design Decision
Selected architecture
Use a low-speed, flooded-suction Archimedes-screw pre-stage in series with a conventional listed variable-speed centrifugal pool pump. The screw handles coarse debris, air-tolerant bulk transport, and quiet low-head circulation; the centrifugal stage supplies the pressure required by the filter, heater, sanitizer, and return fittings. A bypass manifold lets either stage operate independently when the operating mode requires it.
	

This architecture resolves the central engineering conflict: an Archimedes screw is naturally suited to low-head, high-volume transfer, while pool filtration is a pressurized duty. The hybrid does not pretend that one mechanism is optimal for both. It separates the functions and couples them through measured flow, pressure, motor-current, and vibration feedback.
Design question
	Resolved solution
	Can the screw alone replace a modern pressure pump?
	No. Use the screw as a pre-stage or quiet bypass; retain a listed centrifugal booster for filtration pressure.
	How is clogging reduced?
	4.026 in tube ID, 3.750 in rotor OD, 0.138 in radial clearance, coarse basket upstream, removable inspection spool.
	How is priming handled?
	Install screw stage below normal waterline on flooded suction; slope its axis 3° upward to the outlet for air purge.
	How is energy controlled?
	Variable-speed drives; target 25-35 gpm; slow each stage to the minimum speed that satisfies flow and filter-pressure residuals.
	How is safety preserved?
	No single submerged suction; listed booster and controls; GFCI and bonding; pressure relief; interlocks for water level, current, vibration, and filter differential pressure.
	What is exact and what is provisional?
	Pool geometry and calculations are exact for the declared baseline. Pump curves, efficiencies, and fabrication tolerances are prototype targets requiring bench validation.
	1.1 Claim and evidence boundary
The design follows the corpus rule that claims remain inside the evidence interior. Geometric dimensions and arithmetic derived here are Tier I calculations. Hydraulic performance is a Tier II conditional model. Target curves and controller thresholds are Tier III simulation inputs until measured. Safe swimmer operation is Tier IV and requires pressure, leakage, electrical, sanitation, and endurance testing. Any claim of superior energy efficiency remains Tier V until tested against a modern variable-speed pool pump under identical head and water-quality conditions.
________________

9. Fabrication and Installation Instructions
  

Figure 7. High-level sequence. Detailed steps follow.
1. Survey and stake: Establish the exact center point. Mark a 9 ft radius pool wall line and a 9 ft 9 in minimum base-pad radius. Verify the site is free of overhead and underground hazards before excavation.
2. Prepare base: Remove sod and organic material. Cut high areas down rather than filling low areas with loose soil. Compact the subgrade, install geotextile if needed, and build a level 2 in sand/foam pad. Full-diameter level tolerance target: ±1/8 in.
3. Index supports: Mark 18 radial lines at 20° increments. Set each footing pad so the rail joint and upright center are on the 9 ft radius datum. Check opposite chord dimensions and circumference before wall erection.
4. Install pool structure: Assemble the 18 bottom rail sectors, erect the continuous wall, secure the seam, install cove and liner, fill only enough to seat the liner, then install uprights and top rail according to the structural-system instructions.
5. Cut hydraulic openings: After the liner is seated and water support is present as directed by the pool system, install the skimmer at 315° and return at 135°. Do not add a single submerged suction opening. Use approved fittings and gaskets.
6. Fabricate screw rotor: Machine or form a 3.750 in OD, 3.000 in pitch, four-turn rotor on a 1.000 in shaft. Deburr and radius all wetted edges. Verify pitch, runout, concentricity, and balance before housing insertion.
7. Build screw wet end: Install bushings/bearings, inlet cone, inspection spool, outlet diffuser, shaft-seal or magnetic coupling, and unions. Rotate by hand through 360° with no contact. Hydrostatic-test the isolated module.
8. Install equipment pad: Set the screw module and listed booster on a drained, level pad with service clearance. Keep the screw inlet below the normal pool waterline and set its axis 3° upward toward the outlet.
9. Plumb the hybrid loop: Use 2 in PVC, full-port valves, unions, check valves, coarse basket, bypasses, filter, sanitizer/heater interfaces, and return. Support pipe independently so no nozzle carries pipe weight.
10. Install sensors and controls: Install flow, differential pressure, water-level, vibration, leak, current, and temperature inputs. Wire emergency stop and mode interlocks. Electrical and bonding work must be completed by qualified personnel.
11. Leak and pressure test: With drives locked out, fill and vent the loop. Test each section within its rated pressure. Correct every leak before energizing. Never pressure-test with people in the line of fire.
12. Commission screw stage: Run screw alone at 250 rpm with low-head bypass open. Confirm direction, air purge, current, vibration, bearing temperature, and predicted flow. Increase in 25-50 rpm increments.
13. Commission booster stage: Bypass the screw and commission the listed pool pump according to its manufacturer. Record clean-filter pressure and flow.
14. Commission series mode: Open the series path, start screw first, then ramp the booster. Tune speeds to 30 gpm while maintaining stable suction and filter differential pressure.
15. Set return jet: Aim the primary return 20° tangentially clockwise and 15° downward. Use dye or floating markers to verify a coherent circular sweep without a stagnant zone behind the skimmer.
16. Document baseline: Record water level, flow, screw rpm/current, booster speed/current, filter ΔP, vibration, noise, temperature, and valve positions. This becomes the clean-system reference ledger.

	Vibration, current, temperature

	Leak-cavity sensor / drip tray

	11.1 Safety constraints
* Use the custom screw wet end only as a prototype until pressure, endurance, materials, electrical, and sanitation validation are complete.
* Keep every electrical component, receptacle, bonding connection, and disconnect compliant with the locally adopted code and the listed equipment instructions.
* Never work on the system while pressurized or energized. Isolate, lock out, verify zero energy, open the relief path, and confirm zero pressure.
* Do not allow swimmers in the pool during prototype commissioning or fault testing.
* Do not use unverified transparent plastics, 3D-printed pressure housings, or improvised flanges in a pressurized loop.
* Do not represent target curves, theoretical displacement, or simulated efficiency as measured performance.

1. Executive Design Decision
Selected architecture​

Use a low-speed, flooded-suction Archimedes-screw pre-stage in series with a conventional listed variable-speed
centrifugal pool pump. The screw handles coarse debris, air-tolerant bulk transport, and quiet low-head circulation; the
centrifugal stage supplies the pressure required by the filter, heater, sanitizer, and return fittings. A bypass manifold lets
either stage operate independently when the operating mode requires it.

This architecture resolves the central engineering conflict: an Archimedes screw is naturally suited to low-head,
high-volume transfer, while pool filtration is a pressurized duty. The hybrid does not pretend that one mechanism is optimal
for both. It separates the functions and couples them through measured flow, pressure, motor-current, and vibration
feedback.

Design question

Resolved solution

Can the screw alone replace a modern pressure pump?

No. Use the screw as a pre-stage or quiet bypass; retain a listed
centrifugal booster for filtration pressure.

How is clogging reduced?

4.026 in tube ID, 3.750 in rotor OD, 0.138 in radial clearance,
coarse basket upstream, removable inspection spool.

How is priming handled?

Install screw stage below normal waterline on flooded suction;
slope its axis 3° upward to the outlet for air purge.

How is energy controlled?

Variable-speed drives; target 25-35 gpm; slow each stage to the
minimum speed that satisfies flow and filter-pressure residuals.

How is safety preserved?

No single submerged suction; listed booster and controls; GFCI
and bonding; pressure relief; interlocks for water level, current,
vibration, and filter differential pressure.

What is exact and what is provisional?

Pool geometry and calculations are exact for the declared
baseline. Pump curves, efficiencies, and fabrication tolerances
are prototype targets requiring bench validation.

1.1 Claim and evidence boundary

The design follows the corpus rule that claims remain inside the evidence interior. Geometric dimensions and arithmetic
derived here are Tier I calculations. Hydraulic performance is a Tier II conditional model. Target curves and controller
thresholds are Tier III simulation inputs until measured. Safe swimmer operation is Tier IV and requires pressure, leakage,
electrical, sanitation, and endurance testing. Any claim of superior energy efficiency remains Tier V until tested against a
modern variable-speed pool pump under identical head and water-quality conditions.

9. Fabrication and Installation Instructions

Figure 7. High-level sequence. Detailed steps follow.

1. Survey and stake: Establish the exact center point. Mark a 9 ft radius pool wall line and a 9 ft 9 in minimum base-pad
radius. Verify the site is free of overhead and underground hazards before excavation.

2. Prepare base: Remove sod and organic material. Cut high areas down rather than filling low areas with loose soil.

Compact the subgrade, install geotextile if needed, and build a level 2 in sand/foam pad. Full-diameter level tolerance
target: ±1/8 in.

3. Index supports: Mark 18 radial lines at 20° increments. Set each footing pad so the rail joint and upright center are on the
9 ft radius datum. Check opposite chord dimensions and circumference before wall erection.

4. Install pool structure: Assemble the 18 bottom rail sectors, erect the continuous wall, secure the seam, install cove and
liner, fill only enough to seat the liner, then install uprights and top rail according to the structural-system instructions.

5. Cut hydraulic openings: After the liner is seated and water support is present as directed by the pool system, install the
skimmer at 315° and return at 135°. Do not add a single submerged suction opening. Use approved fittings and gaskets.

6. Fabricate screw rotor: Machine or form a 3.750 in OD, 3.000 in pitch, four-turn rotor on a 1.000 in shaft. Deburr and

sanitizer/heater interfaces, and return. Support pipe independently so no nozzle carries pipe weight.

inputs. Wire emergency stop and mode interlocks. Electrical and bonding work must be completed by qualified personnel.

The Phase Locking Distance Index and
Dual Breach Principle: A
Multi-Dimensional Framework for
Synchronized Crisis Risk and Policy
Evaluation in Advanced Economies, with
Detailed Application to Australia and
Canada
Lai, Yehong

13 May 2026

Online at https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/129145/
MPRA Paper No. 129145, posted 05 Jun 2026 15:03 UTC

 The Phase Locking Distance Index and Dual Breach Principle: A MultiDimensional Framework for Synchronized Crisis Risk and Policy Evaluation in
Advanced Economies, with Detailed Application to Australia and Canada
Yehong Lai Independent Researcher, Brisbane, Australia
The author publishes under the working pseudonym “Talon” within this analytical line of research. The
Talon Threshold concept defined in §3.2 retains the pseudonym as its standard reference name, following
the precedent of Student’s t-distribution (Gosset, writing as “Student”, 1908). All formal authorship,
intellectual ownership, and academic responsibility rest with Yehong Lai.
[Working Paper Version 0.4 draft, May 2026]
This paper has evolved through multiple revisions addressing internal consistency, empirical extension,
formula correction, positioning, authorship attribution, and formal Lean 4 machine verification of the
aggregation function’s mathematical properties. Detailed version history is maintained separately in
paper_changelog.md (available on request) and is summarized in the SSRN revision log upon upload.
The SSRN-archived reference versions (abstract ID 6742863): initial v0.3.3 deposit 2026-05-10; current
v0.12-canada-extended revision approved 2026-05-12. The present text is the v0.10.16 post-revision
working draft incorporating additional defensive prior-art engagement (§2.2 / §2.3 / §2.5.5 / §3.2 / §4.4).

Abstract
This paper introduces a multi-dimensional framework for measuring synchronized macroeconomic
crisis risk in advanced economies, with detailed first application to Australia. We define the Phase
Locking Distance Index (PLDI) as the geometric mean distance between four key economic dimensions
— inflation (A, two-sided to capture both high-inflation and deflation breach), unemployment (B),
federal fiscal sustainability (C), and household debt (H) — and their crisis thresholds.
The framework integrates four capabilities that no single EWS indicator provides: (a) multi-dimensional
risk monitoring across A/B/C/H; (b) ex-ante policy evaluation via the Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE; §3.5, §11); (c) counterfactual policy comparison (Sequenced Demolition, §10); (d) crossfrequency mechanism validation (§8.7, §13.3 b). Empirical validation comprises three complementary
tests on the D3b cross-country panel (33 advanced and emerging economies, 1980-2025 quarterly,
merged with Laeven-Valencia 1970-2017 banking-crisis dating and Jordà -Schularick-Taylor 1870-2020
long-history macrohistory): (i) joint out-of-sample validation with the Borio-Drehmann credit gap —
the EWS literature’s dominant incumbent indicator (Drehmann, Borio, Tsatsaronis 2011) — establishes
PLDI_pr and the credit gap as complementary, non-redundant signals: in the multi-predictor logit specification on the 10-country common-credit-gap sample (n = 2,148 country-quarters, 73 forward-24-month
banking crisis events), PLDI_pr’s coefficient magnitude increases in absolute value when controlling
for credit gap (univariate M1 −3.74 → joint M3 −5.32, p < 0.0001 under country-clustered robust
standard errors), with likelihood-ratio tests rejecting either single-predictor specification at p < 0.0001
in both directions — a complementary-signal pattern rather than substitution. The joint specification
achieves in-sample country-clustered AUC = 0.853 on the same sample, with leave-one-country-out
cross-validation AUC in the 0.798-0.816 range across four annual aggregations and rolling-window
pseudo-real-time AUC = 0.84-0.85 on 1,888 OOS predictions covering 62 forward-24-month banking crisis events on a broader 33-country panel; the +0.05-0.07 AUC margin above credit gap alone

1

 captures the three credit-gap-blind dimensions (A inflation / B unemployment / C fiscal) that the Hchannel credit aggregate is structurally insensitive to (§8.7, §13.5, §A.4, §13.9, §14.5); (ii) direct causal
identification via a Jordà (2005) local projections analysis on a 17-country panel of high-frequency
monetary policy shocks (Jarocinski-Karadi 2020, Braun-Miranda-Agrippino-Saha 2025, Altavilla et
al. 2019, Hambur-Haque 2023, Bolhuis-Das-Yao 2024) — n = 553-1,190 country-quarters across 14
entities under country-clustered standard errors — showing monetary tightening lowers pseudo-realtime PLDI at the credit-cycle horizon h = 13 quarters with peak t-statistic in the −2.7 to −3.7 range (β =
−0.0029, p = 0.002), confirming the framework’s central credit-cycle mechanism (§6.5a, §A.6.7); (iii)
cross-frequency mechanism validation, where the framework’s Cox proportional-hazards specification
on dual-breach episodes reproduces a significantly negative coefficient on PLDI-at-formation at both
quarterly (1980-2025 D3b panel, z = −3.32, p = 0.0009) and annual (1948-2020 JST panel, z = −4.09, p
= 4.4 × 10⁻⁵) frequencies, supporting the framework’s mechanism scope as cross-frequency robust on
independent data (§8.7, §13.3 b). Credit gap remains the single-best indicator for the H dimension; the
framework’s contribution is the integrated capability set — simultaneous A/B/C diagnosis, ex-ante
PPLE policy evaluation, and counterfactual analysis (§10) that single-indicator approaches cannot
deliver.
Drawing on Minsky’s financial instability hypothesis, Reinhart-Rogoff’s documentation of synchronized
historical crises, and Kuramoto’s phase synchronization framework from physics, we propose the
Dual Breach Principle as the framework’s central empirical regularity: when any two of the four
dimensions simultaneously breach their crisis thresholds in an episode that subsequently escalates to a
systemic banking crisis, the remaining two dimensions converge to crisis (warning zone) within 6-24
months in 28 of 30 historical cases (93.3%, 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [78.0%, 99.2%]; n = 30 across
20+ countries, 1929-2024, sample drawn from Laeven-Valencia and Reinhart-Rogoff databases). This
93.3% rate is conditional on the dual breach episode subsequently escalating to a Laeven-Valencia
or Reinhart-Rogoff-classified systemic banking crisis; the unconditional convergence rate on the 33country pseudo-real-time quarterly panel without crisis-occurrence conditioning is 21.4% (95% CI
[10.3%, 36.8%], §13.3 b panel audit). The principle is therefore most precisely characterised as a
feature of crisis-conditional dual breach episodes, with the 4× crisis-conditional vs unconditional gap
quantifying the selection-on-dependent-variable premium of the 30-case sample. The empirical case
for the principle in this paper rests jointly on the conditional regularity, the panel-audit unconditional
4.16× crisis-lift on the panel, and the Cox-PH cross-frequency validation reported above.
We introduce the Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE) as a tool to evaluate whether individual policies
push the system toward or away from dual breach, and a 15-case ex-post validation track record (14/15
= 93.3% ≥ 2/3-criterion hit rate, spanning 8 countries) comprising 10/10 = 100% on the §11.4-§11.12
reference set (Truss UK 2022, Volcker Fed 1979-82, Keating Australia 1988-91, Rudd Australia 2009
GFC stimulus, Greek austerity 2010-12, Abenomics Japan 2013, Biden American Rescue Plan 2021,
Trump TCJA 2017, Erdogan Turkey 2021-23, Milei Argentina 2023-25; 29/30 = 96.7% total points)
and 4/5 = 80% on the §11.13a-e Canada Phase 3 extension (BoC 2022-23 tightening, BoC 2017-18
tightening, housing-cooling 7-policy portfolio, Trudeau COVID fiscal, BoC 2020 emergency easing), with
political-symmetry verified across left-wing fiscal expansion (N=3 within-coalition cross-validated),
right-wing fiscal expansion, monetary tightening, monetary expansion, austerity, and shock therapy,
and counterfactual-methodology robust under Abadie-Diamond-Hainmueller 2010 synthetic control
(13/15 sign-agreement with peer-mean verdicts; §11.16). The framework is designed for general
application across advanced economies; we present Australia 2026 as the first detailed empirical
application. Applied to Australia’s 2025-2026 policy portfolio of fourteen identified instruments, we
find an aggregate PPLE central estimate of approximately −0.35 (90% CI [−0.55, −0.15]), indicating
policy that is more likely synchronizing than de-synchronizing. Australia’s current PLDI of 1.16 is
2

 0.36 units from the Talon Threshold — defined as the universal cutoff PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 applied to the
pseudo-real-time PLDI scale (§3.2 / §5.3), functionally country-specific in deployment via the pseudoreal-time σ-normalisation. The threshold’s univariate empirical deployment validity is established
on the D3b 31-country panel at a 21.35× crisis lift (single-predictor logit AUC 0.6407; §A.4), with the
joint specification with credit gap above documenting the framework’s multi-dimensional incremental
contribution.
We argue that mainstream “soft landing” narratives systematically underweight this risk by evaluating
the four dimensions as approximately independent. The paper presents a counterfactual policy path
inspired by Volcker (1979-82) and Keating (1989-91), engages the Modern Monetary Theory critique,
and concludes with falsifiability conditions, generalizability discussion (extension to Canada, New
Zealand, United Kingdom, Korea, and other advanced economies), and implications for central banks,
treasuries, prudential supervisors, and academic discourse.
Keywords: macro-financial crisis, phase synchronization, household debt, fiscal sustainability, inflation
expectations, monetary policy, Australia, Dual Breach Principle
JEL Classification: E32, E44, E52, E62, G01

1. Introduction
1.1 The puzzle of single-variable monitoring in advanced economies
Advanced economies are increasingly exposed to coupled multi-dimensional macroeconomic stress.
The financial history of the past century—from the United States in 1929 and 2008, to Greece, Ireland,
Spain, and Portugal in 2010-2012, to Japan in 1990, to Argentina, Turkey, and Venezuela in recent
decades—reveals a consistent pattern: variables presumed independent (inflation, unemployment,
fiscal balance, household leverage) become tightly coupled near crisis thresholds and synchronize
their failures. Yet standard macroeconomic monitoring frameworks—including the DSGE models
employed by central banks and treasuries across advanced economies—continue to evaluate these
dimensions as approximately independent variables. Each dimension receives separate attention,
separate forecasting models, and separate policy responses. The implicit assumption is that even if one
or two dimensions deteriorate, the others provide stabilizing buffers, and that policy can sequentially
address each dimension as it approaches concern.
This assumption holds in normal times. It fails systematically at critical thresholds.
This paper introduces a quantitative framework for measuring this multi-dimensional synchronization risk and a corresponding tool for policy evaluation. We illustrate the framework with detailed
application to Australia 2026, which we argue exhibits a configuration that mainstream “soft landing”
narratives systematically underweight. By each conventional Australian macroeconomic metric, the
economy looks resilient. Inflation, while elevated at 4.6% headline (3.3% trimmed mean), remains
within historical experience. Unemployment at 4.3% sits comfortably above the RBA’s revised NAIRU
estimate of approximately 4.5%. Federal net debt at 34.4% of GDP is below the OECD average of 112%.
Household debt at 113.7% of GDP is high but mortgage arrears remain low at approximately 0.6%.
Major institutional forecasts—the IMF Article IV consultation (February 2026), the OECD Economic
Survey of Australia (January 2026), the Reserve Bank’s May 2026 Statement on Monetary Policy, and
projections from the four major Australian banks—describe a “soft landing” trajectory with GDP growth
between 2.0% and 2.4% for 2026. The framework introduced in this paper, applied with Australian

3

 data and threshold calibration, gives a different reading: a four-dimensional configuration approaching
synchronization, with two dimensions (inflation and household debt) within one normalized standard
deviation of crisis thresholds and active fiscal policy systematically eroding the buffers in the other two.
Beneath these reassuring single-variable Australian readings, the paper identifies a measurement
gap that applies broadly across advanced economies. Australia is the first detailed application; the
framework is designed for direct extension to Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Korea, and
other comparable economies (§14.5).
The financial history of advanced economies—from the United States in 1929 and 2008, to Greece,
Ireland, Spain, and Portugal in 2010-2012, to Japan in 1990, to Argentina, Turkey, and Venezuela in
recent decades—reveals that variables presumed independent become tightly coupled near crisis
thresholds. They synchronize. They cross thresholds together rather than sequentially. The household
sector, fiscal balance, monetary stance, and labour market enter what physicists studying coupled
oscillator systems term “phase locking.” The single-variable buffers that appeared to provide insurance
dissolve simultaneously.
What is missing for Australia is a systematic measurement tool that captures this synchronization
risk. The RBA’s Financial Stability Review measures financial sector pressure but not coupled realeconomy risk. Treasury’s Intergenerational Report projects long-term sustainability but does not model
dimensional coupling. International tools such as the IMF Macro-Financial Conditions Index and the
US Office of Financial Research Financial Stress Index measure related concepts but lack a specifically
Australian calibration and do not explicitly address the “dual breach to full synchronization” empirical
regularity this paper documents.
1.2 Contributions
This paper makes five contributions.
First, we introduce the Phase Locking Distance Index (PLDI): a quantitative measure of how close an
advanced economy is to a four-dimensional simultaneous crisis. The PLDI applies a geometric mean
of normalized distances from current values of inflation, unemployment, federal fiscal position, and
household debt to their respective crisis thresholds. Values below the Talon Threshold (PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80
on the pseudo-real-time PLDI scale; §3.2) indicate the historically validated zone in which synchronized
crisis probability has been elevated.
Second, we provide a four-capability framework with three-test empirical validation on the D3b crosscountry panel (33 advanced and emerging economies, 1980-2025 quarterly, merged with LaevenValencia 1970-2017 and Jordà -Schularick-Taylor 1870-2020 long-history sources). The framework
simultaneously delivers what single-indicator EWS approaches cannot: (a) multi-dimensional crisis
monitoring across A/B/C/H — diagnosing which dimensions carry the active stress; (b) ex-ante policy
evaluation via PPLE (contribution 4 below) — single-indicator approaches cannot evaluate policy
direction; (c) counterfactual policy comparison (Sequenced Demolition, §10) — quantifying PLDI
trajectory under alternative policy mixes; (d) cross-frequency mechanism validation — the framework’s
Cox proportional-hazards specification on dual-breach episodes reproduces a significantly negative
coefficient on PLDI-at-formation at both quarterly (z = −3.32, p = 0.0009 on 1980-2025 D3b panel) and
annual (z = −4.09, p = 4.4 × 10⁻⁵ on 1948-2020 JST 18-country panel) frequencies on independent data
(§8.7, §13.3 b).
The framework’s empirical case rests on three complementary tests: (i) Joint out-of-sample validation
with the Borio-Drehmann credit gap as the EWS literature’s dominant incumbent indicator (Drehmann,
4

Third, we propose the Dual Breach Principle: an empirical regularity conditional on the dual breach

4× crisis-conditional vs unconditional gap quantifies the selection-on-dependent-variable premium

Fourth, we introduce Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE) as a tool to evaluate whether individual

The framework is designed for general application across advanced economies. Australia 2026 is the
first detailed empirical application because of the unusually informative current configuration (two

elasticities, structural buffers that imply slow rather than fast crisis transition). Direct extension to

requires only country-specific threshold calibration (§5.3) and re-estimation of policy elasticities; the

classification structure transfer without modification.

1.3 Roadmap
The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literatures: multi-dimensional crisis
theory (Minsky, Fisher, Reinhart-Rogoff, Schularick-Taylor), phase synchronization in physics and
complex systems (Kuramoto), existing financial stress indices, and Australian-specific debates (Keen,
Murray, Eslake, Mallick, the RBA-Treasury mainstream). Section 3 develops the theoretical framework:
the ABCH coupling system, the PLDI definition, the Dual Breach Principle, the Policy-Induced Phase
Locking mechanism, and the PPLE concept. Section 4 details the methodology for constructing the
PLDI: variable selection, threshold calibration, sigma normalization, and aggregation function choice.
Sections 5-6 present the methodology for empirically testing the Dual Breach Principle and constructing
the PPLE. Section 7 provides the empirical setting for Australia 1959-2026. Section 8 presents the
quantitative results. Section 9 compares Australia to historical analogues. Section 10 develops a
counterfactual policy path. Section 12 addresses the political economy of policy inaction. Section
13 confronts robustness concerns and counterarguments. Section 14 concludes with falsifiability
conditions and policy implications.

2. Literature Review
2.1 Multi-dimensional crisis theory
The recognition that macroeconomic crises involve multiple coupled variables rather than singlevariable failures dates at least to Fisher (1933), whose debt-deflation theory traces a sequential chain
6

 in which falling asset prices, distressed selling, declining nominal values, falling business profits, output
contraction, unemployment, and shaken confidence reinforce one another. Fisher explicitly identifies
nine interlocking mechanisms that operate simultaneously in deep depressions, anticipating modern
coupling concepts.
Minsky (1986) developed this into the financial instability hypothesis: a sequential progression from
“hedge finance” through “speculative finance” to “Ponzi finance,” culminating in a “Minsky Moment”
when overleveraged borrowers cannot meet obligations and the entire system reprices simultaneously.
The Minsky framework explicitly contemplates synchronized failure across credit markets, asset prices,
real economy, and policy capacity—precisely the four-dimensional coupling this paper formalizes.
Reinhart and Rogoff’s (2009) systematic empirical analysis across 800 years and 66 countries documents five common features of major financial crises that consistently appear together: real estate
price collapse, equity price decline, banking crisis, sovereign debt distress, and output contraction.
Their subsequent work on public debt overhangs (Reinhart, Reinhart, and Rogoff 2012) documents
that elevated public debt is associated with significantly lower growth in 26 high-debt episodes since
1800, with a median duration of 23 years. The duration finding is particularly relevant: debt overhangs
are not resolved through brief sharp adjustments but through extended periods of macroeconomic
underperformance, suggesting that the synchronized state, once entered, is persistent.
Schularick and Taylor (2012), examining 14 advanced economies from 1870 to 2008, find that credit
growth is the single most reliable predictor of financial crises, more reliable than current account imbalances, fiscal positions, or monetary aggregates. Critically, they document that credit-driven crises are
followed by deeper and longer recessions than other downturns—consistent with the synchronization
hypothesis that financial stress propagates simultaneously across multiple economic dimensions.
Mian and Sufi (2014), in their analysis of the 2008 US crisis, document that household leverage was
the proximate cause of the recession, and that the synchronized collapse of housing prices, household
consumption, employment, and government finances followed a coupled rather than sequential pattern
across US counties. The county-level variation they exploit allows clean identification of the householddebt channel and provides the cleanest empirical demonstration that synchronized multi-dimensional
crisis is a real phenomenon, not merely a metaphor.
Diamond and Dybvig (1983) provide a theoretical foundation for sudden coordinated failure in banking systems through their multi-equilibria framework. While focused on bank runs specifically, the
underlying logic—that systems with positive feedback can shift discontinuously between stable equilibria—generalizes to the broader coupling phenomenon this paper studies.
Kindleberger (1978) provides the canonical narrative framework: financial crises proceed through
identifiable stages of mania, distress, and revulsion, with the transition from one stage to the next
typically discontinuous rather than smooth. The stage transitions Kindleberger documents map closely
to the dual breach pattern this paper formalizes.
2.2 Phase synchronization in physics and complex systems
The concept of phase locking originates in the physics of coupled oscillator systems. Kuramoto (1975,
1984) developed the canonical mathematical framework: a population of coupled oscillators, each
with its own natural frequency, undergoes a phase transition at a critical coupling strength below
which oscillators rotate at independent frequencies and above which they synchronize their phases.
The Kuramoto model has been extensively applied in neuroscience (synchronization of neural firing),
biology (firefly synchronization, circadian rhythms), and engineering (power grid stability).
7

 The mathematical structure of the Kuramoto framework—a critical coupling threshold separating
asynchronous from synchronous regimes—provides direct theoretical justification for the Dual Breach
Principle. The principle is consistent with Kuramoto-type behavior in which the macroeconomy, normally exhibiting weakly coupled fluctuations across variables, undergoes a phase transition near critical
thresholds beyond which variables synchronize their trajectories.
A subtle but important clarification central to the framework’s naming convention comes from Strogatz’s
(2000) canonical review: the Kuramoto synchronization transition is itself a continuous bifurcation
of the mean-field order parameter 𝑟 at critical coupling 𝐾𝑐 = 2/(𝜋𝑔(0)), with 𝑟 ∝ (𝐾 − 𝐾𝑐 )1/2 in
the vicinity of 𝐾𝑐 — not a Hopf bifurcation of literal oscillator phases. The four-dimensional ABCH
coupled system analysed in §A.7 exhibits a structurally analogous order-parameter bifurcation at critical
coupling intensity 𝜅𝑐 , specifically a transcritical / saddle-node configuration under the §3.3-derived
coupling matrix (§A.7.3); §A.7.7 separately demonstrates that a Hopf bifurcation is mathematically
achievable within the same 4-D linear framework under engineered anti-symmetric coupling, confirming that the saddle-node finding is a substantive empirical claim about the natural §3.3-derived
coupling rather than a structural artefact. This alignment with canonical Kuramoto phenomenology —
continuous bifurcation of a coupling-threshold order parameter — defends adoption of “Phase Locking”
as the framework’s naming convention even though the four ABCH dimensions do not possess literal
oscillator phases in the dynamical-systems sense (§3.3 metaphor disclosure).
Mandelbrot’s work on fractal market dynamics (1963, 1997, 2004) provides complementary theoretical
support. Mandelbrot demonstrated that financial returns exhibit “wild” rather than “mild” randomness:
returns have power-law tails rather than Gaussian tails, and large movements cluster in time. The
implication for macro-financial coupling is that periods of synchronized stress are not anomalies relative
to a Gaussian baseline but are intrinsic features of complex adaptive systems.
The application of phase synchronization concepts to economics has been limited but suggestive.
Lucas (1977) and subsequent business cycle literature documented co-movement of macroeconomic
variables, but typically modeled this through common shocks rather than coupling per se. Recent work
on financial network analysis (Acemoglu, Ozdaglar, and Tahbaz-Salehi 2015; Diebold and Yilmaz 2009)
has begun to formalize coupling concepts but has not, to our knowledge, applied phase synchronization
specifically to multi-dimensional crisis measurement.
Contemporaneous work by Kathiravelu (2026, SSRN abstract 6378278) develops an explicit Kuramoto
phase-oscillator application to algorithmic-trading-flow crowding: a capital-weighted endogenous
coupling function 𝐾(𝑟) = 𝐾0 (1 + 𝛾𝑟2𝛿 )(𝛽−1)/2 is estimated from a microstructural liquidity-elasticity
parameter 𝛽 across 1,543 instruments (43 CME futures plus 1,500 US equities at daily and minute
frequency), with the order parameter 𝑟 > 0.85 specified as a calibrated activation threshold for the
synchronisation feedback loop. Critically, Kathiravelu reports that the aggregate order parameter
peaked at only 𝑟 = 0.14 during the March 2020 COVID crash — far below the 0.85 activation threshold
— confirming that the microstructural-Kuramoto synchronisation mechanism does not activate during
macro-banking stress episodes. The contrast with PLDI’s intended operating domain is sharp and
instructive: Kathiravelu operates on daily-to-minute frequency at individual-security level (algorithmictrading microstructure), while PLDI operates on quarterly frequency at country level (macro-structural
balance sheets across the four ABCH dimensions specified in §3.1). The two frameworks are mathematically distinct (Kathiravelu has literal oscillator phases, an endogenous coupling equation, and a
population-coherence order parameter; PLDI is a static cross-sectional geometric mean of standardised
macroeconomic distances with no dynamical phase variable) and target orthogonal stress regimes. We
engage Kathiravelu (2026) specifically to clarify that PLDI’s “phase locking” terminology is metaphorical
in the Strogatz (2000) canonical-Kuramoto sense (order-parameter approach-to-criticality across cou8

 pled dimensions), not a claim that PLDI is itself a Kuramoto-style dynamical-systems model; the explicit
Kuramoto application in finance is Kathiravelu’s, mathematically disjoint from PLDI’s macro-structural
construction (see §3.2 metaphor disclaimer and the phase-locking-value footnote therein).
2.3 Existing financial stress indices
Several institutions maintain quantitative indices of financial system stress that share elements with
the PLDI but differ in important respects.
The Office of Financial Research Financial Stress Index (OFR FSI), maintained by the US Treasury,
aggregates 33 financial market variables across credit, equity valuation, funding, safe asset, and volatility
categories. The OFR FSI is purely financial-sector focused and does not include real-economy variables
such as unemployment or household debt.
The IMF Macro-Financial Conditions Index integrates broader variables but is calibrated for crosscountry comparison rather than country-specific crisis prediction. The IMF index is published quarterly
with significant lag and is not widely used in policy decision-making.
The European Central Bank Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS; Holló , Kremer, and Lo Duca
2012, ECB Working Paper No. 1426) is the closest large-scale antecedent in the family of composite financial-stress indices. CISS aggregates fifteen raw stress measures into five market-segment
subindices (money market, bond market, equity market, financial intermediaries, FX market), normalising each via recursive empirical-CDF transformation to the unit interval and combining subindices
via a portfolio-theory variance form with time-varying EWMA cross-correlations. CISS is coincident by
design: it monitors realised stress in market prices and volatilities at weekly frequency, with thresholds
calibrated inside a threshold-VAR against industrial-production transmission rather than ex-ante crisis
prediction. PLDI is the structural counterpart, not a substitute: it operates at quarterly frequency on
real-economy and balance-sheet macro variables (headline CPI inflation A, unemployment B, federal net
debt-to-GDP C, household debt-to-GDP H per §3.1), aims for 1-3 year lead time, and asks whether the
four orthogonal ABCH vulnerability axes are simultaneously near breach rather than whether market
stress is co-moving contemporaneously. The two indices are complements: a CISS-style coincident
monitor and a PLDI-style structural early-warning index can be operated jointly without redundancy,
much as Borio-Drehmann’s credit-to-GDP gap (a stock measure) and contemporaneous Financial Stress
Index variants (flow measures) coexist in operational macroprudential frameworks.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Financial Stress Index and the Cleveland Financial Stress Index
are similar single-country US indicators.
What distinguishes the PLDI from these existing measures:
1. The PLDI focuses on real-economy coupling (inflation, unemployment, fiscal, household), not
financial market indicators
2. The PLDI is specifically constructed to measure dual breach risk, not generalized stress
3. The PLDI uses a geometric mean aggregation that gives appropriate weight to the most-stressed
dimension
4. The PLDI is paired with the Dual Breach Principle, an explicit empirical regularity, rather than
presented as an indicator without theoretical grounding
5. The PLDI is specifically calibrated to Australian institutional and historical conditions
Mahalanobis distance (Mahalanobis 1936), used in financial crisis prediction by Kritzman and Li
(2010) and others, provides an alternative aggregation method that explicitly accounts for variable

9

 correlations. Section 4 discusses why we adopt geometric mean as the baseline aggregation while
presenting Mahalanobis distance as a robustness check.
2.4 Australian-specific literature
Australian macroeconomic discourse divides broadly into mainstream and heterodox traditions, both
of which inform this paper.
The mainstream tradition, represented by RBA staff research, Treasury working papers, and major
bank economists, employs DSGE-style modeling with single-variable Taylor Rule monetary policy and
standard fiscal multiplier analysis. Key references include the RBA’s quarterly Statement on Monetary
Policy and the Treasury Intergenerational Report. Mallick (2024), in the Australian Economic Review,
provides the most recent comprehensive analysis of Australian Phillips curve dynamics in the inflation
targeting era. Bishop and Greenland (2021), in RBA Research Discussion Paper 2021-09, examine
regional variation in Phillips curve slopes. Ruberl, Ball, Lucas, and Williamson (2021) provide the
current Treasury NAIRU estimation framework. These studies are technically sophisticated but treat
each variable largely independently.
The heterodox tradition has produced sustained warnings about Australian household leverage. Steve
Keen’s work, beginning with his 1995 PhD thesis and extending through Debunking Economics (2011)
and Can We Avoid Another Financial Crisis? (2017), argues that private debt accumulation generates
endogenous financial instability not captured by neoclassical models. Keen’s specific predictions for
Australia—particularly regarding mortgage debt and house prices—have been contested in their precise
timing but his framework’s identification of the household-debt channel as central to Australian crisis
risk informs this paper’s selection of H as one of four critical dimensions.
Cameron Murray, in Game of Mates (2017) and Rigged (2022), documents the political economy of
Australian housing and tax policy as a system of cross-subsidies favoring property owners, financial
intermediaries, and government revenue at the expense of younger and lower-income Australians.
Murray’s framework provides direct support for this paper’s identification of cross-subsidy policies as
fuses raising synchronized crisis risk.
Saul Eslake, in continuous public commentary including his February 2026 report to the ACT Legislative
Assembly Select Committee on Fiscal Sustainability, has consistently emphasized the structural rather
than cyclical nature of Australian fiscal pressures. Eslake’s identification of the 2018 GST distribution
arrangement as “the worst public policy decision of the 21st century thus far” highlights the institutional
complexity of Australian fiscal-state coordination that this paper’s PPLE framework attempts to make
legible.
The Grattan Institute and e61 Institute represent independent policy research voices that have documented specific aspects of Australian fiscal sustainability concerns. Grattan’s work on NDIS reform,
housing affordability, and intergenerational equity, and e61’s February 2026 report (with McKinnon)
declaring Australian government spending “unsustainable,” provide empirical foundations for the policy
assessments in Section 8.
The MMT tradition, represented in Australia primarily by William Mitchell (Newcastle), provides the
most rigorous theoretical challenge to this paper’s framework. The MMT position—that currencyissuing sovereign governments face no financial constraint and that fiscal sustainability concerns
conflate household and government finance—would imply that the C dimension cannot meaningfully
breach in the way the PLDI assumes. Section 13 addresses this challenge directly.

10

 2.4b Canadian-specific literature
Canadian macroeconomic discourse divides, like its Australian counterpart, into mainstream and
heterodox traditions, both of which inform this paper’s adaptation of the PLDI/PPLE framework to the
Canada P3 case. Two transparent structural features of the Canadian academic landscape distinguish
it from Australia and warrant explicit acknowledgement before the literature is reviewed: (i) Canada
has no single tenured academic figure who combines Minsky-style financial-instability theory with a
bestseller bubble-prediction record in the way that Steve Keen does for Australia, so the Keen-equivalent
role is functionally split between an industry-side popular-press warner (Hilliard MacBeth) and an
academic post-Keynesian theorist (Louis-Philippe Rochon); and (ii) Canada has no MMT-proper scholar
of William Mitchell’s stature, so the closest heterodox challenge to the framework’s C-dimension
specification comes from the post-Keynesian stock-flow consistent (SFC) tradition primarily associated
with Marc Lavoie and the late Mario Seccareccia at the University of Ottawa. Both lacunae are real
features of the Canadian heterodox-economics ecosystem rather than gaps in our literature search; we
flag them as strength signals of transparent literature-mapping.
The Canadian mainstream tradition is represented principally by the Bank of Canada’s research department, Finance Canada / Department of Finance budget-projection work, and the Parliamentary Budget
Officer’s independent fiscal-sustainability analysis. The Bank of Canada has produced an unusually rich
set of recent staff papers directly relevant to the PLDI framework’s four dimensions: Bank of Canada
Staff Discussion Paper 2024-7 (output-inflation trade-off; the Canadian Phillips-curve analog to Mallick
2024 Australian Economic Review), Staff Analytical Note 2024-8 (labour-market health and the Canadian
NAIRU analog to Ruberl-Ball-Lucas-Williamson 2021), Staff Working Paper 2024-20 (markups and
the New Keynesian Phillips Curve slope; the Canadian counterpart to Bishop-Greenland 2021 RBA
RDP 2021-09 regional-slope analysis), and the Champagne-Poulin-Boucher / Champagne et al. Staff
Analytical Note series 2023-6 / 2024-11 / 2025-14 on potential-output estimation. Together these
provide the operational A-channel and B-channel calibration anchors used in the Canada Cal B threshold
derivation (per §C.3 / §11 / §7’.2 calibration discussion). Finance Canada’s annual Update of Long-Term
Economic and Fiscal Projections (most recently 2024) and the Parliamentary Budget Officer’s Fiscal
Sustainability Report 2024 (PBO RP-2425-014-S, July 2024) provide the C-channel mainstream baseline.
Like their Australian counterparts, these studies are technically sophisticated but treat each dimension
largely independently and do not aggregate dimensions into a coupled phase-locking measure.
The Canadian heterodox tradition has produced sustained warnings about Canadian household leverage
and the post-2008 mortgage-debt accumulation that the H dimension of PLDI is designed to capture, but
the warnings come from two distinct sources rather than a single tenured-academic-plus-popular-press
figure. Hilliard MacBeth, an Edmonton-based portfolio manager and author, published When the Bubble
Bursts: Surviving the Canadian Real Estate Crash (Dundurn Press 2015; expanded second edition 2018),
which argued that the post-2008 Canadian housing market had reached bubble territory through a
combination of large mortgage-debt accumulation, demographic-driven demand exhaustion, and raterise vulnerability. MacBeth’s specific predictions about timing have been contested in the same way that
Keen’s Australian predictions have been contested — the call has been “right but early” relative to the
eventual realised stress — but the framework’s identification of household debt as the central Canadian
crisis risk is materially aligned with this paper’s selection of H as one of four critical dimensions.
MacBeth is read as the Canadian popular-press analog of Keen’s Debunking Economics market reach,
without holding equivalent tenured-academic status. Louis-Philippe Rochon (Laurentian University;
Editor-in-Chief of Review of Political Economy until 2024) has provided the closest Canadian academicside equivalent to the Minskyan endogenous-money critique of mainstream DSGE that Keen advances
theoretically. Rochon’s co-edited The Encyclopedia of Central Banking (Edward Elgar, 2015) and his
11

 extensive post-Keynesian endogenous-money corpus argue, paralleling Keen, that endogenous credit
creation by the banking sector cannot be reduced to a loanable-funds money multiplier and that the
resulting balance-sheet dynamics generate the kind of phase-locking risk this paper attempts to measure
quantitatively. Rochon’s work informs the theoretical motivation for treating H as endogenously coupled
to A and C, not as a residual reflection of household optimisation under exogenous prices.
Transparent caveat on the Keen-equivalent role. Canada has no single academic figure
who combines (i) tenured heterodox status, (ii) a Minsky-financial-instability theoretical

rows. These works supply the empirical basis for the §11.13 Canada Phase 3 housing-cooling ex-post
cases, and several are direct sources for the §6.2 elasticity calibration table rows added in v0.10.7-9.
The Australian §2.4 MMT-proper challenge to the framework’s C-dimension specification is voiced by
William Mitchell (University of Newcastle, NSW), whose Modern Monetary Theory work argues that
currency-issuing sovereign governments face no operational financial constraint and that conventional
fiscal-sustainability concerns conflate household and government finance. The direct Canadian analog
is not MMT-proper but rather post-Keynesian stock-flow consistent (SFC) macroeconomics, principally
through two University of Ottawa scholars. Marc Lavoie (University of Ottawa, emeritus) is co-author
with the late Wynne Godley of Monetary Economics: An Integrated Approach to Credit, Money, Income,
Production and Wealth (Palgrave Macmillan, first edition 2007; second edition 2012), the foundational
stock-flow consistent macroeconomic textbook. Lavoie’s Post-Keynesian Economics: New Foundations
(Edward Elgar, 2014; second edition 2022) provides the canonical contemporary post-Keynesian
methodological reference. Mario Seccareccia (University of Ottawa, deceased 2023), together with
Rochon and Lavoie, anchored the Canadian post-Keynesian endogenous-money tradition through the
Centre for the Study of Economic Liberalism (2013-2020) and an extensive corpus on monetary-fiscal
coordination.
Transparent caveat on the Mitchell/MMT-equivalent role. Canada does not have an MMTproper scholar of William Mitchell’s stature. The closest Canadian heterodox framework is
post-Keynesian stock-flow consistent macroeconomics, primarily through Marc Lavoie and
Mario Seccareccia at the University of Ottawa. This is conceptually adjacent to MMT but
methodologically distinct: where MMT emphasises currency-issuing sovereignty as making
fiscal-constraint claims invalid, post-Keynesian SFC emphasises real-resource constraints
captured through Godley sectoral balances (households, firms, government, rest-of-world).
Section 13’.1 engages this Lavoie post-Keynesian critique as the closest Canadian heterodox
challenge to the framework’s C-dimension specification. The substantive bite of the critique
is similar (the C-dimension fiscal-stress reading depends on framing assumptions a postKeynesian would contest); the methodological route to it differs.

 2.5 Deep engagement with closest theoretical precedents
Sections 2.1–2.4 cover the broad literature. This sub-section deliberately engages in greater depth
with four works most closely related to the PLDI/PPLE framework, identifying explicit conceptual and
methodological relationships, points of agreement, and points where this paper extends or differs from
each precedent.
2.5.1 · Schularick and Taylor (2012, AER) Schularick and Taylor’s Credit Booms Gone Bust exploits
the Jordà -Schularick-Taylor (JST) macrohistory database—14 advanced economies, 1870-2008 in
the original 2012 publication; the dataset (now JST R6) has since expanded to 18 countries through
2020—to estimate logit predictions of financial crisis as a function of lagged credit growth. They
establish that real bank credit growth is the most reliable single-variable predictor of subsequent
financial crisis, more so than current account imbalances, fiscal positions, or monetary aggregates, and
that credit-driven crises produce systematically deeper and longer recessions than other downturns.
Where the frameworks converge: Both ST and the present paper center on the proposition that crisis
dynamics emerge from levered economic systems, that the relevant time scale spans multiple business
cycles, and that single-variable monitoring is insufficient. The H dimension (household debt to GDP)
directly inherits the ST credit-cycle intuition; the 30 historical cases in our sample include the bulk of
episodes ST identifies as systemic banking crises through Laeven-Valencia overlap.
Where this paper extends: ST is single-dimensional (credit) and reduced-form (logit on lagged predictors). PLDI generalizes to four coupled dimensions with explicit cross-dimensional dependence via the
geometric mean aggregation, captures the configuration of stress (not just its presence), and pairs with
PPLE to evaluate individual policies—a tool absent from the ST framework.
Where this paper differs: ST has ~2,000 country-year observations; our 30-case sample, while drawn
from the same canonical crisis databases (Laeven-Valencia, Reinhart-Rogoff), is much smaller. ST
therefore supports rigorous panel inference; our paper offers more granular configuration measurement
at the cost of weaker statistical power. The two frameworks are best understood as complementary: ST
establishes that credit cycles matter; we establish how credit cycles couple with other dimensions and
how policy choices modify the coupling.
Future integration: Extension of PLDI computation to the full JST sample is identified as priority future
research (§14.5).
2.5.2 · Mian and Sufi (2014, House of Debt; 2018 Journal of Economic Perspectives) Mian and Sufi
use county-level US data spanning the 2008 crisis to establish that pre-crisis household leverage was
a quantitative predictor of subsequent regional consumption collapse and recession severity. Their
cross-region variation (high-leverage versus low-leverage counties within the same monetary and fiscal
jurisdictions) provides clean identification of the household-debt-to-recession channel, far cleaner than
time-series identification typically achievable in macroeconomic research.
Where the frameworks converge: The H dimension of PLDI is essentially the Mian-Sufi household debt
variable, with the same theoretical motivation: levered households cut consumption sharply when their
balance sheet positions deteriorate, transmitting financial stress into the real economy. The paper’s
identification of H as a central PLDI dimension is a direct inheritance of the M-S framework.
Where this paper extends: M-S focus is on real-economy transmission (consumption, employment)
via the household-debt channel. PLDI generalizes to the multi-dimensional configuration of which
H is one component, allowing measurement of how H combines with concurrent fiscal stress (C),
14

 inflation/deflation pressure (A), and labor market dynamics (B) to produce or avoid synchronized
crisis. The Dual Breach Principle, in particular, is not derivable from the M-S framework.
Where this paper differs: M-S exploits cross-region variation within a single country (US); PLDI is crosscountry and uses time-series cross-section dynamics. The identification strength is correspondingly
weaker; the geographic and institutional scope is correspondingly broader.
Honest acknowledgment: The Mian-Sufi framework provides the cleanest causal evidence in the
literature on the H dimension’s importance. PLDI presupposes this evidence rather than re-establishing
it; readers skeptical of the household-debt channel should engage the M-S work directly.
2.5.3 · Brunnermeier and Sannikov (2014, AER) Brunnermeier and Sannikov’s A Macroeconomic Model
with a Financial Sector presents a continuous-time stochastic equilibrium model with financial intermediaries facing balance-sheet constraints, generating endogenous amplification and phase-transition
dynamics. The model exhibits three distinct regimes (normal, intermediate, crisis), with discontinuous
transitions and amplification effects that produce non-linear responses to apparently small shocks.
Their phase-space methodology and explicit treatment of macro-financial phase transitions are the
closest theoretical analog in the literature to the phase-locking metaphor employed in this paper.
Where the frameworks converge: Both contemplate the macroeconomy as a non-linear dynamical
system capable of distinct regimes, with discontinuous transitions between them. The Talon Threshold
(universal cutoff PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 on the pseudo-real-time PLDI scale; §3.2) is conceptually analogous to
the threshold in the Brunnermeier-Sannikov phase diagram beyond which the system enters the crisis
regime. Both frameworks reject the implicit assumption in much applied macroeconomics that the
economy operates in a perpetual neighborhood of a unique, well-behaved equilibrium.
Where this paper extends: Brunnermeier-Sannikov is theoretical—the phase transitions are properties
of the model, not directly observed. PLDI provides an empirical, observable measure that approximates
the phase-transition concept in a quantifiable way, and pairs it with the Dual Breach Principle, an
empirical regularity claim that the model does not predict.
Where this paper differs: Brunnermeier-Sannikov models the intermediary balance sheet explicitly as
the source of amplification. PLDI does not model intermediaries at all; rather, it captures intermediaryadjacent stress indirectly through household debt (H, which is on intermediary balance sheets) and
federal debt (C, which intermediaries hold). The choice not to model intermediaries directly reflects
data limitations and the focus on aggregate measurement, not a denial of intermediary importance.
Honest acknowledgment: A more complete framework would integrate the Brunnermeier-Sannikov
amplification mechanism with the PLDI multi-dimensional measurement. Such integration—deriving
the Talon Threshold from explicit model dynamics—is identified as the most ambitious future research
direction (§14.5). The present paper proposes PLDI as a tractable empirical interpretation of phasetransition concepts, not as a derivation from first principles.
2.5.4 · Borio and BIS Financial Cycle Indicator (2014, 2018) Borio’s work at the Bank for International
Settlements, especially the BIS Financial Cycle Indicator (FCI), develops the related concept of a multiyear financial cycle distinct from the conventional business cycle. The BIS FCI combines credit and
property price measures over long windows (15-20 years) and argues that macroprudential and
monetary policy should respond to financial cycle position rather than business-cycle position alone.
Borio (2014) explicitly proposes financial cycle peaks as crisis predictors, with empirical support across
advanced economies.

15

 Where the frameworks converge: Borio’s lens is macroprudential—measuring system-wide vulnerability rather than individual-bank stress—which is exactly the framing of PLDI. Both papers argue
that single-variable monitoring (interest rates, inflation) misses systemic risk that becomes apparent
only when multiple dimensions are jointly elevated. The Talon Threshold is conceptually parallel to the
“credit gap” benchmarks Borio and colleagues identify as macroprudential intervention triggers.
Where this paper extends: Borio’s FCI is two-dimensional (credit + property prices); PLDI is fourdimensional (adding inflation pressure A and unemployment B). The expansion is motivated by the
observation that crises differ in their stress configurations: 1929-style debt-deflation requires A on the
downside, 1970s-style stagflation requires A on the upside, sovereign crises require C centrally, all of
which the two-dimensional FCI does not separately capture.
Where this paper differs: Borio frames the financial cycle as a cycle—a multi-year recurring pattern—while PLDI frames the system state as a distance—a measure of proximity to multi-dimensional
breach. These framings can be reconciled: the financial cycle is approximately a rotation through
different PLDI states, and a PLDI peak is approximately a financial cycle peak. But the methodologies
and emphases differ.
Honest acknowledgment: PLDI’s four-dimensional generalization of Borio’s framework introduces
estimation cost (four normalizations and one aggregation rather than two) without yet demonstrating
that the additional dimensions provide non-redundant predictive power. Empirical comparison of PLDI
with the BIS FCI on the same historical sample is identified as priority future research; the Index Horse
Race section in §14.5 explicitly notes this as a Tier 1 robustness check.
2.5.5 · Aikman, Kiley, Lee, Palumbo & Warusawitharana (2017, Journal of Banking & Finance); Lee,
Posenau & Stebunovs (2017, Federal Reserve IFDP 1191) Within the US Federal Reserve tradition,
Aikman, Kiley, Lee, Palumbo and Warusawitharana (2017) developed the closest balance-sheet-oriented
antecedent to PLDI. Their “heat map” framework aggregates 46 indicators of financial-system vulnerability across three pillars — valuation pressures, nonfinancial borrowing, and financial-sector health —
and demonstrates predictive lead time over the credit-to-GDP gap of approximately one year. The 2017
Journal of Banking & Finance publication (vol. 81, pp. 36-64) consolidates a series of Federal Reserve
FEDS Notes and working papers initiated in 2015. Lee, Posenau and Stebunovs (2017, Federal Reserve
International Finance Discussion Papers 1191) extend the framework to a 27-country advanced-andemerging panel and map the empirical sequence in which vulnerabilities materialise — pressures in
asset valuations first, followed by the build-up of imbalances in external, financial and nonfinancial
sectors.
Where the frameworks converge: Both the Aikman-Lee tradition and PLDI seek to summarise balancesheet vulnerability accumulation across multiple structural dimensions and to flag systemically risky
configurations 1-3 years before crisis realisation. The Lee-Posenau-Stebunovs 27-country panel and
PLDI’s D3b 33-country panel cover substantially overlapping sample spaces, and both empirically
demonstrate predictive content above the Borio-Drehmann credit-to-GDP gap baseline.
Where this paper extends: PLDI differs along three axes that we believe make it a complement rather
than a substitute. First, dimensionality and derivation: PLDI is restricted to four pre-committed axes
(headline CPI inflation A, unemployment B, federal net debt-to-GDP C, household debt-to-GDP H)
derived from first principles in §3.1.2 and Appendix B, whereas the Aikman-et-al. heat map aggregates
dozens of indicators under data-driven weighting without an axiomatic restriction on the dimension
count. The trade-off is explicit: PLDI sacrifices breadth-of-coverage for axiomatic interpretability and
parsimony. Second, aggregation semantics: PLDI uses a geometric mean that imposes a multiplicative
16

 penalty when distances co-approach zero (the formal Dual Breach Principle motivation) — a property
the heat-map’s arithmetic averaging does not produce. Third, the Dual Breach Principle (§3.3) and the
decision-theoretic Talon Threshold (§3.2) have no analogue in the Aikman-Lee tradition: neither paper
reports a breach-counting empirical regularity with the conditional crisis rate the Dual Breach Principle
documents, nor a threshold derived from explicit false-negative / false-positive cost asymmetry rather
than Youden’s-J or AUC-optimal selection.
Where this paper differs: The Aikman-Lee heat map is operational rather than axiomatic — its 46indicator construction is justified by empirical performance and Federal Reserve macroprudentialmonitoring practice. PLDI is axiomatic-first: the four-dimensional ABCH structure is derived from three
independent theoretical traditions (§3.1.2 / Appendix B) before empirical validation. Readers who
prioritise comprehensive coverage of the financial vulnerability landscape may prefer the Aikman-Lee
approach; readers who prioritise parsimonious interpretation and explicit theoretical derivation may
prefer PLDI. Empirical comparison of PLDI joint multi-predictor performance against Aikman-Lee-style
indicator aggregations on the same historical sample is identified as priority future research alongside
the BIS FCI comparison (§14.5), and we report joint multi-predictor logit performance against the
Borio-Drehmann credit-to-GDP gap baseline in §A.4.
Honest acknowledgment: The Aikman-Lee tradition is the empirical antecedent against which PLDI’s
additional dimensions (A inflation, B unemployment) need to demonstrate marginal predictive contribution; the Lee-Posenau-Stebunovs 27-country panel is the cross-country empirical benchmark closest
in spirit to PLDI’s D3b 33-country panel. As with the BIS FCI comparison, the marginal predictive
contribution of PLDI’s parsimonious four-dimensional structure over the Aikman-Lee 46-indicator
heat map remains an open empirical question, identified as Tier 1 robustness work in §14.5.
2.6 Gap identification
The literature reviewed above contains all the conceptual elements required for understanding multidimensional Australian crisis risk: theoretical foundations (Minsky, Fisher, Kuramoto, BrunnermeierSannikov), empirical patterns (Reinhart-Rogoff, Schularick-Taylor, Mian-Sufi), macroprudential frameworks (Borio, BIS Financial Cycle), institutional knowledge (Mallick, Keen, Murray, Eslake), and political
economy (Murray, Grattan, e61). What no existing work provides is integration: a single framework
that
1. quantitatively measures multi-dimensional crisis distance at a single point in time (the PLDI
integrates dimensions in a way that single-variable indicators and the two-dimensional BIS FCI
do not);
2. couples this measurement to an empirically-validated principle about the dynamics of multidimensional breach (the Dual Breach Principle is novel to this paper);
3. provides a tool for evaluating individual policies’ marginal contribution to or mitigation of synchronized risk (the PPLE framework, with its Fuse/Defuser typology, has no direct precedent in
the literature).
This paper attempts that integration. The framework does not displace the precedents reviewed
above—Schularick-Taylor remains the canonical reference for credit-cycle empirics; Mian-Sufi remains
the canonical reference for the household-debt channel; Brunnermeier-Sannikov remains the canonical
reference for theoretical phase-transition macro-finance; Borio remains the canonical reference for
macroprudential cycle analysis—but rather extends them by providing the integration none of them
individually offers.

 3. Theoretical Framework
3.1 The ABCH coupling system: formal definition
We define the macroeconomic state at time t as a four-dimensional vector:
X(t) = (A(t), B(t), C(t), H(t))
where: - A(t) = headline CPI inflation, year-over-year percent change - B(t) = unemployment rate,
seasonally adjusted percent - C(t) = federal net debt as percent of GDP - H(t) = household debt as
percent of GDP
The choice of these four dimensions reflects three considerations. First, each dimension captures a
distinct macroeconomic stress channel: A measures real purchasing power, B measures labour market
slack, C measures sovereign fiscal capacity, H measures private sector financial fragility. Second, the four
dimensions span both nominal (A) and real (B), and both public (C) and private (H), domains—providing
comprehensive coverage of the macroeconomy without redundancy. Third, all four dimensions are
publicly measured at quarterly or higher frequency by official statistical agencies (ABS, RBA, Treasury,
BIS), enabling real-time monitoring.
For each dimension i ∈ {B, C, H} we specify a single crisis threshold τᵢ and a normalization volatility σᵢ.
For dimension A (inflation), we specify a two-sided structure capturing both high-inflation and deflation
crisis risk: an upper threshold τ_A_upper with sigma σ_A_upper, and a lower threshold τ_A_lower with
sigma σ_A_lower. The rationale for treating A as two-sided while B, C, and H are one-sided is given in

For dimensions i ∈ {B, C, H}, we define the distance to threshold:
dᵢ(t) = max(0.01, (τᵢ − Xᵢ(t)) / σᵢ)
For dimension A (inflation), we define two distances and aggregate by minimum:
d_A_high(t) = max(0.01, (τ_A_upper − A(t)) / σ_A_upper) d_A_low(t) = max(0.01, (A(t) − τ_A_lower) /
σ_A_lower) d_A(t) = min(d_A_high(t), d_A_low(t))
This formulation has the following properties: 1. When Xᵢ(t) is below threshold (in the safe direction,
for B/C/H), dᵢ(t) is positive, increasing as Xᵢ(t) moves further from threshold 2. For A, d_A is maximized
when A is in the optimal range near 2-3% (RBA target band), and decreases as A approaches either
6% (high inflation breach) or 0% (deflation breach) 3. The min aggregation for A produces a singlepeak piecewise linear (tent-shape, ∧) function rather than a smooth U-shape: A breach can occur
from either direction, and the binding constraint is whichever side is closer. The peak at A* (the
intersection of d_A_high and d_A_low) is non-differentiable, reflecting the discrete nature of crossing
distinct crisis thresholds. While a smooth quadratic alternative is mathematically possible, we adopt
the piecewise linear form for three reasons: (i) the threshold endpoints (τ_A_upper, τ_A_lower) directly
correspond to the breach boundary at d_A = ε, requiring no additional calibration; (ii) the asymmetric
slopes (σ_A_upper ≠ σ_A_lower) capture the fact that high-inflation and deflation distributions have
empirically different volatilities; (iii) piecewise linear formulations are common in macroeconomic
threshold models (Hansen 1996, Hamilton regime-switching, kink-utility specifications) 4. When any
Xᵢ(t) crosses its threshold (in the breach direction), the floor of 0.01 prevents the geometric mean
aggregation from collapsing to zero, while still signaling severe stress 5. The normalization by σᵢ makes
distances comparable across dimensions with different units and historical volatilities
3.1.1 Why A is two-sided while B, C, H are one-sided
This asymmetric treatment requires explicit justification.
A (inflation) is intrinsically two-sided. The central bank consensus across all advanced economies (Fed,
RBA, ECB, BoE, BoJ) is that the optimal inflation rate is positive but moderate—typically a 2% target.
Both too high and too low inflation generate distinct crisis transmission channels:

19

 • High inflation channel: erodes real purchasing power, triggers monetary tightening, raises debt
service costs (→ pressures C), depresses real wages (→ pressures B), and is associated with the
1970s stagflation, GIIPS 2010-12, and emerging-market crises (Argentina 2018, Turkey 2021).
• Deflation channel: triggers Fisher (1933) debt-deflation dynamics (real debt rises → pressures
H), depresses consumption via deferred spending (→ pressures B), invalidates monetary policy
at the zero lower bound (→ pressures C indirectly via output collapse), and is associated with US
1929-32, Japan 1990s-2010s, Ireland 2009-10, Spain 2009, and Greece 2013.
Both channels are documented in this paper’s empirical sample (Appendix D). Treating A as onesided would mathematically classify the deflation cases as “safe” on dimension A, contradicting the
framework’s own historical record.
B, C, H are one-sided in the directions relevant to crisis:
• B (unemployment): Very low unemployment (e.g., 1.5%) may indicate labor market overheating
but does not directly produce crisis. Crisis-level B stress is exclusively elevated unemployment.
(Some literature treats sub-NAIRU unemployment as a stability concern, but its direct crisis
transmission is via A, which is captured.)
• C (federal net debt %GDP): Very low public debt is not a crisis source. Crisis-level C stress is
exclusively elevated debt.
• H (household debt %GDP): Very low household debt is not a crisis source. Crisis-level H stress is
exclusively elevated debt.
Hence the asymmetric treatment is not arbitrary but reflects the underlying economic theory: among
the four dimensions, only A has two distinct crisis channels operating through opposite directions of
the variable. This asymmetry is consistent with monetary economics consensus and does not weaken
the framework’s parsimony.
3.1.2 First-principle derivation: why 4-dim ABCH is the minimum sufficient dimensionality
A natural reviewer question is why the framework specifies four dimensions ABCH rather than a different number (e.g., 5-dim including corporate non-financial debt; 6-dim including currency crash
and domestic default; or 2-dim per Brunnermeier-Sannikov asset-price-leverage formulation). The
§3.1 empirical-pragmatic justification (stress-channel coverage, nominal-real and public-private spans,
official-statistics measurability) is sufficient for operational deployment but does not address the
theoretical-foundation question of dimensional necessity. We therefore derive 4-dim ABCH as theoretically necessary from three independent theoretical traditions, converging on the same dimensional
choice. The full derivation chain is presented in Appendix B (Theoretical derivation of 4-dim
ABCH); this sub-section reports the condensed summary.
Three independent derivations of ABCH 4-dim necessity:
1. Brunnermeier-Sannikov 2014 macro-finance extension (Appendix B §1): the canonical 2-dim
coupling (asset price × leverage) of Brunnermeier and Sannikov (2014, AER 104(2): 379-421)
extends to 4-dim ABCH under (i) leverage decomposition: the macro-financial leverage state
η decomposes naturally into household leverage H and sovereign leverage C, both of which
carry independent first-order information about crisis vulnerability; (ii) asset price as derivative:
the BS asset price q is a derivative of household-balance-sheet wealth (H) and sovereign-fiscalcapacity (C), not an independent dimension; (iii) coupled macro-state: BS 2014’s stable-macroand-fixed-labor simplification is a tractability assumption, not a substantive uncoupling claim

3.2 The Phase Locking Distance Index
The Phase Locking Distance Index (PLDI) at time t is defined as the geometric mean of the four dimensional distances:
PLDI(t) = (d_A(t) · d_B(t) · d_C(t) · d_H(t))^(1/4)
The geometric mean has three desirable properties for our purposes.
First, it is sensitive to the minimum: a single small distance significantly reduces the overall index,
capturing the intuition that a near-breach in any single dimension is a meaningful stress signal.
Second, it rewards dispersion: holding the arithmetic mean constant, the geometric mean is higher
when distances are more equal. This captures the Dual Breach intuition that synchronized approach to
thresholds is more concerning than a single dimension being close while others are far.
Third, it is dimensionless and invariant to multiplicative rescaling of any dimension’s sigma, making
cross-country and cross-period comparisons more meaningful.
We define the Talon Threshold as the universal cutoff PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 applied on the pseudo-real-time
PLDI scale (the deployment-quality variant specified in §5.3, with country-specific σ-normalisation
against each country’s prior-data window). Because the pseudo-real-time normalisation absorbs
cross-country baseline heterogeneity into the country-specific σ, a single universal cutoff on this
normalised scale is functionally country-specific in deployment: each country’s own historical volatilityadjusted distance-to-threshold determines when that country’s PLDI𝑝𝑟 crosses the Talon Threshold.
The threshold value 0.80 is empirically validated below (§A.4: 21.35× crisis lift; single-predictor logit
AUC = 0.6407 on the 31-country D3b pseudo-real-time panel of 3,120 country-quarters with 107
forward-24-month banking-crisis events).
For the Australian narrative scale (full-sample PLDI in level units, §8.1), the same threshold value 0.80
also obtains as a special case of the country-baseline-relative formula 𝑇𝑐 = 𝜌 ⋅ PLDI∗𝑐 (§5.3a; 𝜌 ≈ 0.83,
PLDI∗AUS = 1.066, 𝑇AUS = 0.885, 95% CI [0.549, 1.042] covers 0.80). However, the level-scale countryspecific 𝑇𝑐 formulation is not the deployment instrument: empirical validation on the D3b panel shows
that level-scale country-specific cutoffs 𝑇𝑐 produce a 0.80× crisis lift (anti-predictive, AUC 0.4437)
because the PLDI∗𝑐 stable baseline for structurally-stressed countries (e.g., Spain, Italy, Japan, Greece) is
calibrated too low and misses crisis episodes that occur above the country baseline. The level-scale 𝑇𝑐
formula is retained in §5.3a as a narrative tool for describing cross-country PLDI baseline heterogeneity,
not as a recommended deployment threshold (§A.4 reports the head-to-head validation).
