A terminological disambiguation. The label “Phase Locking” in PLDI is metaphorical, evoking the
cross-sectional regularity that the four ABCH distances simultaneously approach zero rather than a
literal coupled-oscillator dynamics. PLDI is not a Kuramoto-style dynamical-systems model: there
are no oscillator phases, no endogenous coupling equation, and no order parameter computed from
instantaneous phase coherence. The contemporaneous Kuramoto application to finance by Kathiravelu (2026), engaged in §2.2, is mathematically distinct and operates on entirely different objects
(microstructural liquidity elasticities and population order parameters) at entirely different frequencies
(daily / minute on individual securities). The terminological borrowing here follows Strogatz (2000)’s
canonical-Kuramoto sense in which the order-parameter bifurcation captures the macroeconomic
analogue of population-coherence approach-to-criticality across coupled dimensions (§2.2 + §A.7); the
underlying mathematics are entirely distinct from the Kuramoto oscillator-population model.
A separate disambiguation is warranted because of an unfortunate abbreviation collision: the phaselocking value (PLV) of signal-processing and neuroscience (Lachaux, Rodriguez, Martinerie, and Varela
1999, Human Brain Mapping 8: 194-208) quantifies the consistency of instantaneous phase differences
between two oscillating time series across trials and is the canonical inter-channel phase-coherence
statistic in cognitive neuroscience EEG / MEG analysis. PLDI is not a PLV: it contains no Hilbert-transform
phase extraction, no across-trial averaging, and no two-signal phase comparison. The convergence of
the abbreviations (PLDI vs PLV) is coincidental; the underlying constructions are entirely orthogonal in
both methodology and application domain.
3.3 The Dual Breach Principle
Beyond the static measurement provided by the PLDI, this paper proposes a dynamic empirical regularity. Define a breach at time t in dimension i as occurring when dᵢ(t) ≤ 0.01. For dimensions B, C, H, this
is equivalent to Xᵢ(t) > τᵢ. For dimension A, breach occurs when either A(t) > τ_A_upper (high-inflation
breach) or A(t) < τ_A_lower (deflation breach). Define a dual breach at time t as the simultaneous
breach of any two dimensions, where dimension A may breach in either direction.
The Dual Breach Principle states:
24

 Following a dual breach at time t in an episode that subsequently escalates to a systemic
banking crisis, the remaining two dimensions converge to their crisis thresholds (warning
zone, dⱼ < 1.0) within 6-24 months in over 90% of such historical cases (n=30 across 20+
countries, 1929-2024; observed support 28/30 = 93.3%; 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [78.0%,
99.2%]; sample drawn from Laeven-Valencia and Reinhart-Rogoff crisis databases).
The italicised conditioning clause (“in an episode that subsequently escalates to a systemic banking
crisis”) makes explicit the sample-selection mechanism of the 30-case evidence base: the sample is
restricted to historical episodes already classified as systemic banking crises by Laeven-Valencia (2018,
2020) or Reinhart-Rogoff (2009, 2014) databases. The unconditional rate of 4-dimensional warningzone convergence among all dual breach episodes (whether or not followed by crisis) is materially
lower; on the D3b pseudo-real-time quarterly panel (33 countries, 1980-2025), the unconditional rate
is 21.4% (95% CP CI [10.3%, 36.8%]; see §13.3 b for the panel audit). The principle is therefore most
precisely understood as a characteristic feature of dual breach episodes that escalate to crisis, rather
than as a universal regularity of dual breach occurrence. The crisis-conditional and unconditional rates
differ by roughly 3-4×, with the gap quantifying the selection-on-dependent-variable premium of the
30-case evidence.
The principle is empirical rather than derived from first principles, but several theoretical mechanisms
support its plausibility.
Mechanism 1: Fiscal endogeneity. A breach in B (unemployment) triggers automatic stabilizers (transfer
payments rise, tax receipts fall), pushing C (fiscal) toward breach. A breach in A (inflation) typically
triggers monetary tightening, raising debt service costs and pushing C toward breach. Either or both
contribute to dual breach in (B,C) or (A,C) configurations.
Mechanism 2: Monetary endogeneity. A breach in A typically triggers central bank tightening, which
pressures H (households via mortgage costs) and B (employment via reduced demand). A breach in H
may trigger central bank loosening, but this loosening is constrained if A is already elevated.
Mechanism 3: Confidence endogeneity. A breach in C (fiscal) tends to trigger credit rating concerns
and risk premium increases, which propagate to H (household borrowing costs), B (investment-driven
employment), and potentially A (currency depreciation and import inflation).
Mechanism 4: Asset price endogeneity. A breach in H (household debt servicing) typically involves
house price decline, which through wealth effects depresses consumption and B, and through bank
balance sheet effects pressures C (via potential financial sector support requirements).
These mechanisms imply pairwise coupling of all four dimensions. The Dual Breach Principle asserts
the empirical claim that this coupling is sufficient to drive convergence within 6-24 months once two
dimensions have breached. Section 5 provides the methodology for testing this claim, and Section
8 reports the empirical results. A numerical bifurcation analysis of a 4-dimensional linearised ODE
model with coupling matrix specified (not estimated) from the four mechanisms above is provided
in §A.7 as illustrative conceptual exposition; the analysis identifies a transcritical (saddle-node) bifurcation at a critical coupling intensity κ_c under one calibration consistent with §3.3 magnitudes.
Because the parameters in §A.7 are not econometrically estimated and the noise amplitude is selected
to match the post-1990 Australian empirical PLDI moment, §A.7 is best read as conceptual demonstration of the bifurcation structure rather than as structural identification of the Talon Threshold; the
empirical case for the 0.80 calibration rests on the panel evidence in §A.4 (joint OOS AUC 0.84–0.85,
single-predictor lift 21.35×), the panel-wide converse test in §13.3 (b) (breach_count dose-response
0%/2.9%/6.8%/9.4%/23.5%), and the §6.5a 17-country panel local-projections analysis, not on §A.7.
25

 Note on the “Phase Locking” terminology: The framework’s name derives metaphorically from the
Kuramoto (1975, 1984) synchronization literature in physics and complex systems (§2.2). The metaphor
is analogical rather than literal — the four-dimensional ABCH state vector does not have intrinsic
oscillator phases in the dynamical-systems sense, and the §A.7 numerical bifurcation analysis confirms
that the realised dynamical structure under the §3.3-derived coupling matrix is a transcritical (saddlenode) bifurcation rather than a Hopf bifurcation of oscillator phases. This is consistent with Kuramoto’s
own original mean-field synchronization bifurcation, which is also transcritical in the order parameter
(Strogatz 2000 review). Readers seeking dynamical-systems literal interpretation should treat “Phase
Locking” as the metaphorical naming convention adopted at framework design time; the substantive
content of the framework is captured by the PLDI distance index (§3.2), the Dual Breach Principle
(§3.3), the PPLE policy elasticity (§3.5), and the bifurcation structure (§A.7).
3.4 Policy-Induced Phase Locking
The Dual Breach Principle has direct implications for policy design. Consider a policymaker observing
pressure on dimension A. Conventional analysis suggests the appropriate response is to intervene in A:
monetary tightening to reduce inflation, or fiscal expansion to subsidize inflation-affected households
(e.g., energy rebates, fuel excise relief).
The PLDI framework reveals a complication. Fiscal subsidies that suppress A simultaneously increase
pressure on C: the government balance sheet absorbs what would otherwise have been household pain.
The marginal effect on the PLDI depends on whether the reduction in A-stress more than offsets the
increase in C-stress. In the geometric mean framework, the answer depends on which dimension was
more stressed before the intervention.
Policy-Induced Phase Locking describes the systematic tendency of policy interventions of this type—using a less-stressed dimension’s buffer to absorb pressure on a more-stressed dimension—to reduce
the PLDI rather than increase it. Mathematically, when starting from an asymmetric distribution of
distances, transferring stress from a small distance to a large distance reduces the geometric mean
(because the geometric mean is maximized for equal distances).
The implication is profound. Cross-subsidy policies that appear to address single-dimension pressures
actively raise synchronized crisis risk by accelerating dual breach. The C buffer that policy is consuming
was the single most important defense against the dual breach scenarios documented in Section 5. Each
dollar of fiscal cross-subsidy is a dollar removed from this defense.
This paper’s identification of Policy-Induced Phase Locking is the central political-economy contribution.
It is not that policymakers are ignorant of the costs of fiscal expansion—they are well-informed about
budget impacts. It is that they lack a framework for evaluating fiscal expansion’s contribution to
synchronization risk, as distinct from fiscal sustainability concerns considered in isolation.
3.5 Policy Phase Locking Elasticity
To make Policy-Induced Phase Locking operationally measurable, we define the Policy Phase Locking
Elasticity (PPLE) of a policy p:
PPLE_p = (PLDI_with_p − PLDI_baseline) / cost_p
where: - PLDI_with_p is the projected PLDI assuming policy p is implemented - PLDI_baseline is the
projected PLDI assuming policy p is not implemented - cost_p is the policy’s expected cost as a percentage
of GDP
26

 PPLE is a measure of marginal effectiveness in PLDI units per unit of fiscal cost. The sign indicates
direction:
• PPLE > 0: Policy raises PLDI → de-synchronizing → Defuser ✅
• PPLE < 0: Policy lowers PLDI → synchronizing → Fuse ❌

4. Methodology: PLDI Construction
4.1 Variable selection rationale
The choice of A, B, C, H as the four PLDI dimensions reflects three criteria: (1) coverage of distinct
macroeconomic stress channels, (2) data availability at appropriate frequency, (3) policy actionability.
A (inflation) captures the nominal anchor of the macroeconomy. We use headline CPI year-over-year
change rather than core or trimmed-mean measures because headline inflation is the variable to
which household expectations and political pressure respond, and because the empirical literature
(e.g., Mallick 2024) suggests headline measures contain information about wage-price dynamics not
captured by core measures alone. Robustness checks using trimmed mean inflation are provided in
Section 13.
B (unemployment) captures real-economy labour market slack. We use the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate from the ABS Monthly Labour Force Survey rather than broader underutilization
measures, because the unemployment rate is the headline variable affecting household behavior and
political response. Robustness using the underutilization rate is provided in Section 13.
C (federal fiscal) captures sovereign fiscal capacity. We use general government net debt as a percentage
of GDP rather than gross debt, because net debt better reflects the actual claim against future taxpayers
(gross debt overstates the burden by ignoring offsetting assets). We focus on federal rather than
combined federal-state debt because the federal level holds primary monetary-coordination capacity.
Robustness using gross debt and combined federal-state measures is provided in Section 13.

27

 H (household debt) captures private sector financial fragility. We use total household debt to GDP
from the BIS Total Credit Statistics database, which provides internationally comparable measures.
Alternative measures (household debt to disposable income, debt service ratio) are discussed in Section
13 as robustness.
We considered and rejected several alternative dimensions for inclusion:
• External position (current account, net foreign liabilities): omitted because Australian debt is
overwhelmingly AUD-denominated and the floating exchange rate provides automatic adjustment
• Asset prices (equity, real estate): omitted because asset prices are partially captured indirectly
through H (mortgage debt mirrors house prices) and inclusion would create double-counting risk
• Business debt: omitted because Australian business debt is below international norms and the
household sector is the dominant Australian credit-cycle driver
• State government debt: omitted because monetary-coordination capacity sits at the federal level;
state debt is captured indirectly through C
4.2 Threshold calibration
Each dimension’s threshold τᵢ embeds judgment. We propose three calibration approaches and report
results for each:
Calibration A: Theoretical thresholds (baseline approach) - A_upper: 6.0% (twice the RBA upper target
band) - A_lower: 0.0% (CPI ≤ 0% triggers Fisher debt-deflation; central bank effective lower bound
concern) - B: 7.0% (50% above current RBA NAIRU estimate) - C: 60% (OECD warning threshold for
advanced economies) - H: 130% (slightly below Switzerland’s current level; well above Australia’s
historical peak of 124%)
Calibration B: Historical P95/P5 thresholds (data-driven) - A_upper: 6.5% (P95 of Australian quarterly
CPI YoY, 1948-2025) - A_lower: −0.5% (approximate P5 of Australian quarterly CPI YoY, 1948-2025;
rare but observed during 1962, 1997, 2020) - B: 9.0% (P95 of Australian quarterly unemployment,
1978-2025) - C: 35% (P95 of Australian net debt %GDP, 1980-2025) - H: 122% (P95 of Australian
household debt %GDP, 1990-2025)
Calibration C: International crisis thresholds (comparative) - A_upper: 8.0% (median CPI at GIIPS crisis
onset) - A_lower: −1.0% (median CPI at deflation crisis episodes: Ireland 2010, Spain 2009, Greece
2013, Japan recurring) - B: 12% (median unemployment at GIIPS crisis peak) - C: 80% (median net
debt at GIIPS crisis onset) - H: 100% (median household debt at GIIPS crisis onset)
The baseline analysis uses Calibration A, which is intermediate between the more conservative B
(Australian-specific historical experience) and the more lenient C (international crisis experience).
Section 13 reports robustness across all three. The choice of τ_A_lower deserves particular attention:
0.0% is a conservative descriptive threshold (any negative CPI reading triggers Fisher dynamics), while
−1.0% allows a buffer for transitory mild disinflation. The qualitative finding that Australia 2026-Q1
PLDI is in the warning zone is robust across all three τ_A_lower choices.
4.3 Sigma normalization
The normalization volatility σᵢ converts each dimension to comparable units. We use the standard
deviation of the dimension over its full available historical sample, rounded to a stable value:
• σ_A_upper = 2.0 (high-inflation side; corresponds to historical CPI volatility of ~2.1%)

28

 • σ_A_lower = 1.5 (deflation side; smaller than σ_A_upper because the negative-CPI distribution
is empirically narrower in advanced economies—negative readings are bounded by the Fisher
dynamic floor and rarely fall below −10% outside Great Depression conditions)
• σ_B = 1.5 (corresponds to historical unemployment volatility of ~1.5%)
• σ_C = 15 (corresponds to historical net debt volatility, accounting for trend growth)
• σ_H = 20 (corresponds to historical household debt volatility, accounting for trend)
These sigmas determine how rapidly the distances fall as values approach thresholds. For dimension
A, the two-sided structure means d_A is maximized in the optimal range. With σ_A_upper = 2.0 and
τ_A_upper = 6.0%: A = 4.0% gives d_A_high = 1.0. With σ_A_lower = 1.5 and τ_A_lower = 0.0%: A = 1.5%
gives d_A_low = 1.0. The minimum aggregation d_A = min(d_A_high, d_A_low) means whichever side is
closer to its threshold is the binding constraint. The asymmetry (σ_A_upper > σ_A_lower) implies that
for equal numerical proximity to threshold, the deflation side produces a smaller (more concerning) d_A
— reflecting that deflation in advanced economies is typically more persistent and harder to reverse
than high-inflation episodes.
4.3a Reality check on alternative aggregation and normalization choices
A quantitative reality-check series (scripts 70–75 in d3b_data/scripts/) systematically tested four
alternative aggregation or normalization choices on the 33-country D3b panel. The series confirmed
that the calibration A specification above with geometric-mean aggregation (§4.4) is empirically the
strongest variant available within the four-dimensional ABCH framework. We summarise findings for
transparency and to disclose recognised residual weaknesses that future research may address.
Empirical inspection of normalized-distance scale balance. On the 33-country D3b panel, the calibration
A specification yields cross-dimension mean normalized distances of (d_A, d_B, d_C, d_H) ≈ (0.84, 0.84,
1.79, 3.76). The d_H mean is approximately 5 × the d_A mean, indicating that the geometric-mean
PLDI is less sensitive to H-dimension stress than to A-dimension stress in marginal terms (∂PLDI/∂d_i
∝ 1/d_i). The imbalance reflects the underlying measurement convention — A and B are flow-rate
variables (typically 0–10% range), while C and H are stock-ratio variables (typically 20–130% range)
— and is preserved despite the σ_i normalization above. This is a recognised feature of the framework
rather than a defect, as the empirical tests below confirm that alternative scale-balancing approaches
do not yield predictive or empirical improvement.
(a) Covariance correction (Mahalanobis distance). Replacing the geometric mean with Mahalanobis
distance from the safe corner produced AUC = 0.39 on the forward-24-month banking crisis prediction
task (33-country panel, n = 4,183, 228 crisis events), versus 0.73 for the geometric-mean PLDI on the
same sample. The four normalized distances exhibit only modest pairwise correlation (maximum |r| =
0.27; first principal component explains 38.6% of variance, second 24.7%, with the remaining variance
distributed across the third and fourth components). Mian-Sufi-style “double-counting” or dimensional
redundancy concerns are not empirically supported. Covariance correction is therefore degradation,
not improvement (script 70 Diagnostic 2).
(b) Sigma rebalancing. Adjusting σ_i values to balance normalized distance scales across dimensions
(σ_H from 20 → 28, σ_A from 2.0 → 1.5) reduced cross-dimension imbalance from 0.66 to 0.49 but
degraded predictive AUC (Δ −0.003), AUS empirical baseline alignment (mean PLDI 1.10 → 1.00, worsening fit to PLDI* = 1.5 target), and Talon Threshold lift (1.02× → 0.97×). Net verdict: cosmetic rebalancing
without substantive empirical gain (script 71).
(c) Three-dimensional reframing (C × H composite). Combining fiscal (C) and private (H) leverage

(+0.1308 for PLDI(ABCG)).

noting that variants which include G (credit_gap distance) inside the PLDI geometric mean (BCHG /
ABCHG / ACHG / ABCG) gain single-index predictive power by absorbing the credit-cycle signal into
the composite, but lose joint complementarity with raw credit_gap because the credit-cycle signal
31

macroeconomic stress dimensions (inflation, unemployment, fiscal debt level, household debt level),
which are statistically orthogonal to the credit-cycle dimension that raw credit_gap measures. This
orthogonality is the source of the +0.217 complementarity gain and the +0.10 joint margin.
Operational criterion. The framework’s empirical validation in §14.5 (33-country joint logit) and §A.4
establishes that the deployment-quality use of PLDI is joint with credit_gap, reaching AUC = 0.853
in-sample and 0.84–0.85 out-of-sample under rolling-window pseudo-real-time validation on the
33-country panel. Under this operationally-relevant criterion, the existing ABCH dimensional basis

choice is empirically the right basis for the operational PLDI-plus-credit_gap deployment framework.

4.4 Aggregation function: justification of geometric mean
We adopt the unweighted geometric mean as the baseline aggregation function:
PLDI(𝑑𝐴 , 𝑑𝐵 , 𝑑𝐶 , 𝑑𝐻 ) = (𝑑𝐴 ⋅ 𝑑𝐵 ⋅ 𝑑𝐶 ⋅ 𝑑𝐻 )1/4 .
The choice is grounded in four formal properties of the unweighted geometric mean of four nonnegative reals, with complete proofs in Appendix A.2. Supplementary machine-verification of the proofs
is available; see §A.2.5 for replication details.
Property P1 (Conservative lower bound): PLDI ≤ arithmetic mean of the same distances, with equality
if and only if all four distances coincide (Theorem A.2.1). This means PLDI is never less alarming than
arithmetic averaging at the same configuration, and strictly down-weights configurations exhibiting
dispersion across dimensions—formalizing the Dual Breach intuition that synchronized stress is more
dangerous than dispersed stress at the same average distance.
Property P2 (Constant unit elasticity): The elasticity of PLDI with respect to each dimension is exactly
1/4, the same for all four dimensions and independent of the current configuration (Theorem A.2.4). A
1% change in any single dimension produces a 0.25% change in PLDI. This formalizes the framework’s
claim that no dimension is privileged in the baseline specification; the unweighted form follows from
the structural decision that A, B, C, H are equally important contributors and need not be re-weighted
ex post.
Property P3 (Minimum-coordinate amplification): PLDI’s sensitivity to each dimension is given by the
formula 𝜕 PLDI/𝜕𝑑𝑖 = PLDI/(4𝑑𝑖 ), whereas AM’s sensitivity is the constant 1/4. The PLDI sensitivity
dominates AM’s sensitivity whenever PLDI ≥ 𝑑𝑖 , which always holds at the worst-stressed coordinate
32

 since PLDI ≥ min𝑗 𝑑𝑗 (Theorem A.2.3 with supporting Lemma A.2.3a). In the limit where one dimension
approaches breach (𝑑𝑖 → 0+ ), PLDI’s sensitivity to that dimension diverges to infinity while AM’s
remains bounded at 1/4. This is the formal expression of the framework’s central design principle: a
single dimension approaching breach should dominate the aggregate crisis-distance signal.
Property P4 (Diagonal boundary): When all four dimensions coincide at value 𝑑 ≥ 0, PLDI = AM = 𝑑
(Corollary A.2.2). The aggregator behaves as expected on the symmetric diagonal where dispersion is
absent.

A note on the aggregation choice in relation to portfolio-variance composite indicators. The geometricmean aggregation in PLDI may invite comparison with the more elaborate portfolio-theory variance
form pioneered by Holló , Kremer and Lo Duca (2012) for the ECB’s Composite Indicator of Systemic
Stress (CISS), in which subindices are combined as CISS𝑡 = (𝑤 ⊙ 𝑠𝑡 )⊤ 𝐶𝑡 (𝑤 ⊙ 𝑠𝑡 ) with 𝐶𝑡 an EWMAestimated time-varying cross-correlation matrix (see §2.3 for fuller engagement with CISS). We deliberately avoid the portfolio-variance form for two reasons. First, the cross-correlation structure of
the four ABCH macroeconomic dimensions at quarterly frequency is materially less informative than
the cross-correlation of market-stress flows at weekly frequency that CISS exploits: cross-correlations
across CPI inflation, unemployment, federal debt-to-GDP, and household debt-to-GDP are dominated
by slow co-movement driven by common business-cycle and credit-cycle factors rather than by the
abrupt co-stress this paper aims to detect, so the additional structural complexity of the variance form
purchases relatively little informational gain at quarterly frequency. Second, sub-sample robustness
across 33 heterogeneous economies under data-sparse historical conditions strongly favours simple
aggregation — a concern Holló et al. (2012) themselves raise in their footnote 9 in the cross-country

34

 context. The portfolio-variance form is the appropriate choice for CISS’s coincident weekly marketstress measurement; the unweighted geometric mean is the appropriate choice for PLDI’s quarterly
structural-vulnerability measurement. The two choices are not in competition; they reflect the differing
operating frequencies and dimensional natures of the two indices, as elaborated in §2.3.

5. Methodology: Empirical Test of the Dual Breach Principle
5.1 Hypothesis statement
The Dual Breach Principle states an empirical regularity rather than a theoretical theorem. To facilitate
falsification, we state the hypothesis in operational form:
H1 (Dual Breach Convergence): Conditional on a dual breach event at time t—defined as two of the
four dimensions (A, B, C, H) simultaneously satisfying the breach condition Xᵢ(t) > τᵢ—the remaining
two dimensions will satisfy dⱼ(t+k) < 1.0 for at least one k ∈ [1, 24] months in over 80% of cases.
The threshold of 80% (rather than 90%) is chosen as the formal hypothesis to avoid post-hoc rationalization of an observed regularity. We report the empirically observed support rate separately.
The convergence criterion dⱼ(t+k) < 1.0 corresponds to the remaining dimensions reaching the warning
zone (within one normalized standard deviation of breach) rather than full breach. This weaker
convergence criterion is chosen because: (1) the remaining dimensions in some cases may be prevented
from full breach by emergency policy intervention, even though they were on a convergent trajectory;
(2) the warning zone threshold provides a less arbitrary cutoff than full breach; (3) the principle’s
policy implication—that dual breach signals an economy approaching synchronized stress—holds
under the warning-zone criterion.
5.2 Case selection criteria
We construct a primary sample of 30 historical financial crisis episodes for testing H1, drawing from
established crisis databases:
35

 • Laeven and Valencia (2018, 2020) Systemic Banking Crises Database, which documents 151
systemic banking crisis episodes globally during 1970-2017 with consistent definitions and
dating
• Reinhart and Rogoff (2009, 2014) crisis database, providing extended historical coverage back to
the early 1900s for advanced economies
• For Australian cases, the RBA Financial Stability Review historical archives
Selection criteria:
1. Period: 1929-2024 (inclusive)
2. Crisis identification: Episode must be classified as systemic crisis by at least one of: (i) LaevenValencia systemic banking crisis criteria, (ii) Reinhart-Rogoff banking or sovereign debt crisis,
(iii) NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee severe recession (US-only), (iv) IMF Article IV Consultation acknowledgment of severe stress
3. Data availability: Quarterly or annual data must be available for at least three of the four dimensions (A, B, C, H) over a window from 24 months prior through 36 months after the candidate
dual breach event
4. Dual breach verification: Two of the four dimensions must satisfy the breach condition simultaneously using country-specific calibration (Section 5.3)
5. Sample independence: No two cases drawn from overlapping country-year windows
The 30 cases comprise the 12 cases from earlier analysis plus 18 additional cases identified through
systematic search of the Laeven-Valencia and Reinhart-Rogoff databases.
Original 12 cases: Australia 1990, US 1929, US 1973, US 2008, Greece 2009, Ireland 2008, Spain 2009,
Portugal 2010, Argentina 2018, Turkey 2021, South Korea 1997, Thailand 1997.
Extended 18 cases: Sweden 1991, Finland 1991, Norway 1988, Mexico 1994, Russia 1998, Brazil 1999,
Brazil 2015, Indonesia 1997, Malaysia 1997, UK 2008, Iceland 2008, Italy 2012, Cyprus 2012, Argentina
2001, Argentina 1989, Argentina 1981, Mexico 1982, Chile 1982.
This expanded 30-case sample improves on the 12-case sample in three respects: (1) broader geographic
and temporal coverage, (2) systematic rather than convenience-based case selection, (3) consistency
with the canonical crisis databases used in mainstream financial crisis research.
Important caveats remain: - 30 cases remains small relative to formal econometric standards - Selection on dependent variable (all are crises) persists - Dual breach detection in some cases requires
interpolation of annual data to quarterly - Country-specific threshold calibration introduces judgment
We characterize the expanded analysis as systematic suggestive evidence rather than definitive empirical
proof. Full panel data analysis using the complete Laeven-Valencia 151-case sample with rigorous
statistical inference is identified as a priority for subsequent research.
5.3 Breach detection methodology
For each case, we compute country-specific thresholds τᵢ and normalization volatilities σᵢ using:
• τᵢ = country-specific historical 95th percentile of the dimension over the 30 years preceding the
candidate breach
• σᵢ = country-specific historical standard deviation over the same window
This country-specific calibration controls for institutional differences that affect what constitutes
“crisis-level” stress in each economy.
36

 Quarterly data are used where available; annual data are interpolated to quarterly using cubic splines
for volatile variables (CPI) and linear interpolation for slow-moving variables (debt ratios). Section 13
reports robustness using only quarterly observations.
A breach is recorded in dimension i at quarter t when Xᵢ(t) > τᵢ. A dual breach is recorded when two
breaches occur in the same quarter.
Out-of-sample validation: To verify that the country-specific calibration produces an out-of-sampleinformative PLDI series (rather than capturing only in-sample fit), the calibration was applied pseudoreal-time to the full Laeven-Valencia 1970-2017 panel (43 countries × ~180 quarters; 3,142 countryquarter cells with sufficient prior history). At each (country, t) cell, σ_X(t) and τ_X(t) were computed
using only data available at time t−1. The resulting PLDI_pr(t) below the Talon Threshold (PLDI < 0.80)
was associated with a 21.5× higher rate of LV systemic banking crisis onset within the next 24 months
than PLDI_pr ≥ 0.80 (4.1% vs 0.2% conditional probability). Single-predictor logistic regression yielded
ROC AUC = 0.64. Replication code and full results are in d3b_data/scripts/.

5.4 Convergence measurement
For each dual breach event at time t, we examine the subsequent trajectory of the two non-breached
dimensions j over the window [t+1, t+24] months.
We record: - First convergence quarter k*: the smallest k such that dⱼ(t+k) < 1.0 for both non-breached
dimensions - Convergence outcome: binary indicator equal to 1 if k* ≤ 24, equal to 0 otherwise - Time
to full breach: the smallest k such that dⱼ(t+k) ≤ 0.01 for either non-breached dimension
The 24-month window is chosen for three reasons. First, financial crisis literature consistently identifies
18-30 months as the typical duration over which sequential dimensional stress propagates. Second, 24
months is policy-relevant: it spans the typical electoral cycle. Third, beyond 24 months, identification
of “convergence caused by initial dual breach” versus “convergence caused by subsequent independent
shocks” becomes increasingly tenuous.

not as the primary converse evidence. The Japan 1990 case illustrates a single-H-breach episode that
exhibited 30-year gradual deterioration without escalation to dual breach — consistent with the 75.8%
non-escalation rate documented in Spec 2 above. The Australia 2022 case illustrates a single-A-breach
episode that recovered without escalation. Switzerland and Sweden cases sit at breach_count = 0,
which has zero 24-month LV crisis rate on the panel.
Verdict on §5.5 selection-on-DV concern: The panel-wide converse test substantively addresses the
four-case anecdotal limitation. The Dual Breach Principle’s central empirical content survives the
converse test in two refined forms: (i) dual breach is 2.3-2.7× more informative than single breach
in raw cell-level crisis rate; (ii) breach_count is monotonically related to subsequent crisis rate in a
dose-response pattern across the panel. The principle’s earlier framing as “absent dual breach, the
system does not converge” is corrected: single breach is informative, but dual breach is substantially
more informative.
5.6 Statistical inference and limitations
With 30 cases, statistical inference is more meaningful than with the original 12-case sample but
remains subject to small-sample limitations relative to formal econometric standards. We report:
• The proportion of cases supporting H1 (binary outcome)
• 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals
• Sensitivity to definition choices (breach threshold, convergence criterion, window length)
The 30-case sample is best understood as systematic suggestive evidence motivating policy attention,
not as definitive empirical proof. The Reinhart-Rogoff (2009) database and Laeven-Valencia (2018,
2020) database both provide larger samples (151+ episodes) that could be used for more rigorous
testing of full panel dynamics—identified as priority for subsequent research.

6. Methodology: PPLE Construction
6.1 Definition and computation
The Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE) of a policy p is defined as:
PPLE_p = (PLDI(X_with_p) − PLDI(X_baseline)) / cost_p
where: - X_with_p is the projected vector of macroeconomic dimensions assuming policy p is implemented - X_baseline is the counterfactual projected vector without policy p - cost_p is the policy’s
expected fiscal cost as a percentage of GDP per year
The numerator is in PLDI units (dimensionless). The denominator is in % GDP. PPLE therefore has

41

 units of “PLDI change per percentage point of GDP cost,” analogous to fiscal multiplier units but applied
to systemic risk rather than output.
Computation requires three inputs: 1. Baseline projection: a forecast of X(t+k) for k = 1, …, 24 months
without the policy 2. Counterfactual projection with policy: a forecast incorporating the policy’s expected effects on each dimension 3. Cost estimate: typically taken from official fiscal impact statements
(Treasury, PBO, ABS Government Finance Statistics)
6.2 Dimension-by-dimension policy effect modeling
For each dimension, we use response functions parameterized by point estimates with explicit uncertainty bounds drawn from the published economics literature.

6.4 Tail-PPLE for non-linear policies
A subset of policies exhibit non-linear PPLE: their effect on PLDI varies non-monotonically over time or
across stress conditions. Monetary financing is the canonical example. In the short term (1-3 years),
monetary financing of fiscal deficits appears strongly de-synchronizing: the C dimension stabilizes
as funding pressure eases, A may even decline as fiscal stress reduces. In the medium term (3-10
years), if inflation expectations unanchor, A breaches catastrophically and the policy becomes severely
synchronizing. Argentina, Turkey, Venezuela, Zimbabwe, and Weimar Germany all exhibit this pattern.
For such policies, we recommend evaluation by Tail-PPLE:
Tail-PPLE_p = E[PPLE_p | scenario in worst 25% of outcomes]
This is analogous to the Conditional Value at Risk concept in financial risk management. Tail-PPLE
captures the policy’s effect on dual breach probability conditional on the bad-tail outcomes that the
expected PPLE understates.
45

 6.5 Identification challenges
Three identification challenges deserve explicit discussion.
Challenge 1: Selection bias in policy timing — Policies are typically enacted in response to observed
pressure on specific dimensions. Naive PPLE estimation may attribute pre-existing dimensional pressure to the policy itself. We address through counterfactual baseline construction that explicitly models
the pre-policy trajectory.
Challenge 2: General equilibrium effects — Each policy affects multiple dimensions through general
equilibrium channels. Our partial-equilibrium response functions simplify these multiple channels into
single dimensional effects. A full GE PPLE estimation would require structural model implementation,
identified as priority for subsequent research.
Challenge 3: Time inconsistency — PPLE estimated at one point in time may not equal PPLE estimated
at another time, because the underlying dimensional configuration changes. We address by computing
PPLE conditional on the current macroeconomic state, and explicitly noting that PPLE should be reestimated as the configuration evolves.
Three-tier identification hierarchy adopted in this paper. The three sub-sections that follow address
the monetary-policy PPLE identification problem at three distinct levels of statistical rigour:
• §6.5a · Primary identification · Cross-country panel local projection on 17 advanced economies
(𝑛 = 553–1,190 country-quarters; peak 𝑡 = −3.08 on PLDI_pr at ℎ = 13). This is the framework’s headline empirical case for monetary-policy PPLE: a 17-country panel with countryclustered standard errors and harmonised high-frequency monetary policy shocks from five
published sources (Jarocinski-Karadi 2020, Braun-Miranda-Agrippino-Saha 2025, Altavilla et
al. 2019, Hambur-Haque 2023, Bolhuis-Das-Yao 2024). The substantial cross-country sample,
robust SE clustering, and multi-source HF identification together constitute the strongest causal
evidence for the framework’s central credit-cycle mechanism.
• §6.5b · Australia country case study · AUS-only LP analysis with Hambur-Haque (2023) shock
(𝑛 = 60 quarterly observations 2005-Q1 through 2019-Q4). This is the original AUS-only
single-country implementation that motivated the subsequent cross-country panel extension.
It is preserved as a country case study for Australia 2026 application context, with explicit
transparency on the small-sample limitation (HAC vs moving-block bootstrap CIs in §6.5b “Honest
summary”). The §6.5a panel evidence supersedes §6.5b as the primary identification claim.
• §6.5c · Robustness check · Indirect identification via Taylor-Rule gap (𝑃 𝑃 𝐿𝐸 ≈ −0.45 central
point estimate, 90% CI [−0.65, −0.25]). This is the indirect, structural-economic identification
of the monetary PPLE through the static Taylor-Rule benchmark gap, computed for the §8.3
Australian portfolio. It is preserved as robustness check rather than primary identification
because the elasticity calibration involves judgment that the direct HF-shock evidence in §6.5a /
§6.5b does not.
The three sub-sections are presented in descending order of statistical rigour to align the §1.2 contribution hierarchy with the §6 identification hierarchy.
6.5a Primary identification · Cross-country panel local projection on 17 advanced economies
The framework’s primary causal identification of monetary-policy PPLE is a Jordà (2005) localprojections analysis on a 17-country panel of harmonised high-frequency monetary policy shocks.

Panel construction. The panel uses five published high-frequency monetary policy shock series, harmonised under the Gü rkaynak-Sack-Swanson (GSS) tightening-positive sign convention. The five sources
span six monetary-policy entities, with the euro-area entity expanded to its twelve member countries
(DEU, FRA, ITA, ESP, NLD, PRT, IRL, FIN, AUT, BEL, GRC, LUX) under the single-ECB-shock structure:
• United States: Jarocinski and Karadi (2020) Fed-funds-futures-based shocks decomposed into
Monetary Policy (MP) and Central Bank Information (CBI) components via sign-restricted PCA
on FOMC-window interest-rate-derivative surprises, updated through 2024-Q1 by the original
authors.
• United Kingdom: Braun, Miranda-Agrippino, and Saha (2025) UK Monetary Policy Event-Study
Database (UKMPD) decomposing MPC- and press-conference-window asset-price surprises into
Target, Path, and QE factors over 1997 through 2026-Q1.
• Euro area: Jarocinski-Karadi methodology applied to Altavilla, Brugnolini, Gü rkaynak, Motto,
and Ragusa (2019) EA-MPD intraday OIS surprises, replicated across the 12 euro-area member
countries in the D3b panel.
• Australia: Hambur and Haque (2023) Action shock used in §6.5b, sign-flipped to align with the
GSS convention adopted for the panel (positive shock = tightening surprise).
• Canada and Japan: Bolhuis, Das, and Yao (2024) IMF WP 24/224 cross-country standardised
shock series (daily change in OIS rate around CB announcement). Bolhuis covers 21 advanced
economies under a single standardised methodology; we use it as the primary shock measure
for Canada and Japan (where country-specific richer series are not publicly available) and as a
methodology-mix robustness mirror for USA / GBR / Euro / AUS where richer series are also
used.

 6.5b Australia country case study · AUS-only LP with Hambur-Haque (2023) shock
The §6.5a primary identification uses a 17-country panel that includes Australia (Hambur-Haque 2023
shock, sign-flipped under GSS convention). This sub-section reports the AUS-only direct LP analysis,
which preceded the cross-country panel extension. The AUS-only LP is preserved as a country case
study for the Australia 2026 application context (§7–§10) and as an internal-consistency check on the
§6.5a panel result. The §6.5a panel evidence supersedes this AUS-only LP as the framework’s primary
causal identification claim; readers interested in cross-country generality should treat §6.5a as the
headline empirical case and read §6.5b as Australia-specific illustration.
We use the Hambur and Haque (2023) RBA Research Discussion Paper 2023-04 high-frequency monetary policy shock series for Australia. The published series decomposes RBA event-day yield-curve
surprises into three orthogonal components — Action (target-rate decision surprise), Path (forwardguidance surprise), and Premia (direct term-premium / risk-premium channel) — via principalcomponent analysis on the expected-rate and term-premium decomposition of yield-curve changes,
following the methodology of Kaminska, Mumtaz, and Š ustek (2021). The published baseline series
covers 199 monthly observations from 2001m4 to 2019m12. We aggregate monthly shocks to quarterly
via cumulative within-quarter sum (following Cloyne and Hü rtgen 2016) and merge with the Australian
slice of the pseudo-real-time PLDI panel.
Sign convention. Following the Hambur and Haque convention, a positive shock denotes an unexpected
easing (dovish surprise) — a downward yield-curve revision relative to market pricing. A positive β in
the impulse response of any outcome y to a positive shock therefore indicates that y rises following an
unexpected loosening of policy, which is the conventional credit-channel sign for credit growth, asset
prices, and inflation. This convention is the opposite of the Gü rkaynak-Sack-Swanson convention in
which positive MP shocks denote contractionary surprises; readers comparing IRFs to other monetarypolicy-shock literatures should account for the sign flip.
Estimation. We estimate Jordà (2005) local projections of the pseudo-real-time PLDI on the three shock
series, with 4 lags of both y and shock as controls and Newey-West HAC standard errors with truncation
lag h + 1. The specification is

years; all 90% HAC CIs include zero), followed by a delayed positive response peaking at h = 12 with
β = +0.027 (HAC 95% CI [+0.019, +0.034]; t = +6.61). The timing of this delayed response — 2.75 to
3.25 years post-shock — coincides with the typical credit-cycle peak lag documented in Schularick and
Taylor (2012) for cross-country panels of monetary-easing episodes, and with the BIS financial-cycle
peak frequency identified in Borio (2014, 2018).
Mechanism decomposition. Decomposing the response by the four PLDI dimensions reveals which
channels propagate the monetary shock:

49

 • Household-debt distance (d_a_pr): positive response peaking at h = 5 (β = +0.036, t = +1.73).
Consistent with the conventional credit channel — unexpected easing raises household debt
accumulation over a 1–2 year horizon.
• CPI distance (d_b_pr): negative response peaking at h = 15 (β = −0.055, t = −1.66). The negative
sign on a “dovish” Action shock is consistent with the information-effect interpretation — dovish
action surprises signal RBA private pessimism about inflation, lowering rather than raising
inflation expectations.
• Unemployment distance (d_c_pr): negative response (closer to NAIRU) peaking at h = 5 (β = −0.021,
t = −1.48). Labour-market channel: easing lowers unemployment distance over 1–2 years.
• Government-debt distance (d_h_pr): inert. Peak |β| = 0.005 (t = −1.04), no horizon achieves
statistical significance. Fiscal independence from monetary policy is preserved.
Three of the four PLDI dimensions activate under monetary shocks; the government-debt dimension
does not. This is consistent with the framework’s premise (§3.4, §6.5c indirect Taylor-Rule complement)
that PLDI captures monetary-fiscal coupling but not pure fiscal channels — monetary policy can move
dimensions A, B, and C, but the H dimension responds to fiscal rather than monetary instruments.
Reproduction of the Hambur–Haque “Yes and No” finding. Hambur and Haque (2023) document
that high-frequency monetary shocks transmit cleanly through financial variables (the “yes” of their
title) but exhibit information-effect contamination on real variables (the “no” — output, inflation,
unemployment exhibit perverse signs). Our LP estimates reproduce this asymmetry. The Action shock
yields a perverse positive coefficient on unemployment at h = 1 (β = +0.084, t = +4.21), inconsistent
with a pure expansionary effect but consistent with the information-effect interpretation that dovish
action signals private RBA pessimism about future labour-market conditions. By contrast, the Path
shock — which captures innovations in expected future rate paths rather than the current decision —
yields a clean negative coefficient on unemployment at h = 1 (β = −0.072, t = −2.71), the traditional MPtransmission sign. This pattern provides external validation that our LP pipeline correctly reproduces
a known property of the Hambur–Haque shock series.
Robustness (full tables in §A.6):
1. L = 2 lag-order reduction (relieves degrees-of-freedom pressure: 6 regressors vs. 10): peak at h =
12 reduces only to β = +0.022 (t = +4.18, n = 62). The IRF is not an over-fitting artifact of the L = 4
specification.
2. GFC-excluded subsample (removing 2008-Q1 through 2009-Q4 from the regression sample while
preserving these observations as lag controls): peak at h = 12 is β = +0.035 (t = +2.06, n = 52).
The point estimate strengthens, not weakens; the h = 11–13 spike is not driven by the extreme
+10.9 / −5.7 action shocks of 2008-Q4 / 2009-Q1.
3. Moving-block bootstrap (Brü ggemann, Jentsch, and Trenkler 2016 pair-block resampling on (Y,
X) rows, B = 2000 replicates, block length 4 quarters): 95% bootstrap CI at h = 12 is [−0.002,
+0.061] — approximately four times wider than the HAC interval, and including zero. The HAC
standard errors are downward-biased on the single-country n = 60 sample by roughly a factor of
four.
Honest summary. The point estimate is directionally robust across all three specifications: sign, magnitude (β ∈ [+0.022, +0.035] at the peak), and timing (peak at h = 11–13) all replicate. However, the small
single-country sample limits statistical precision. Under the moving-block bootstrap — the appropriate
inference standard for time-series regression at this sample size — 95% CIs at the h = 11–13 peak
include zero in the baseline specification. We therefore interpret the result as directional evidence
consistent with the credit-cycle hypothesis that easy monetary policy contributes to PLDI build-up
50

 over a 2.5–3.5 year horizon, with statistical strength insufficient to claim a sharp causal effect from this
Australia-only sample alone. Combined with the cross-country evidence in §8 (33-country panel, joint
AUC = 0.853, lift 8.4× at top-20% threshold) and the dimension-level mechanism documented here, the
LP results provide complementary directional support for the framework’s central claim that monetary
easing is a quantitatively important source of synchronization risk.
Relation to other identification methods. The AUS-only LP estimate is qualitatively consistent with the
indirect PPLE of −0.45 from §6.5c (Taylor-Rule gap robustness check): both indicate that monetary
easing systematically increases PLDI synchronization risk. The two estimates differ in units (PPLE is
in normalized risk-cost units; LP β is in PLDI-distance units), but they agree on sign, on dimensional
channel (A, B, and C activate; H does not), and on approximate magnitude relative to other policy
instruments in the §8.3 portfolio. The §6.5a cross-country panel extension of this AUS-only LP exercise
(using harmonised high-frequency shock series from Jarocinski-Karadi, UKMPD, Altavilla et al., Bolhuis
et al., and the same Hambur-Haque source used here) substantially tightens statistical precision: the
panel n > 1,000 country-quarters with country-clustered standard errors achieves peak |𝑡| = 3.7
versus the AUS-only HAC peak 𝑡 = 6.6 that the MBB bootstrap reveals as downward-biased on the n =
60 sample.

6.5c Robustness check · Indirect identification via Taylor-Rule gap
As a complementary structural-economic robustness check on the §6.5a / §6.5b direct LP estimates, we
report the indirect monetary-policy PPLE recovered from the Taylor-Rule benchmark gap. This indirect
approach was the original identification of the monetary PPLE in the SSRN-locked version (abstract
ID 6742863, 2026-05-10); subsequent work moved direct HF-shock LP identification to the primary
position (§6.5a). The two approaches agree on sign and dimensional channel; the indirect estimate
is preserved here because (i) the elasticity calibration provides explicit policy-portfolio mapping for
§8.3, (ii) the structural-economic interpretation is more transparent for policy audiences, and (iii) the
indirect-and-direct convergence is itself substantive evidence.
The PPLE estimate for “RBA accommodative stance vs Taylor Rule” deserves separate methodological
note from the discrete-policy portfolio entries in §8.3, because monetary stance is not a discrete policy
with a single fiscal cost. We compute it as the implicit fiscal subsidy of holding cash rate below the
Taylor Rule benchmark, multiplied by the elasticity bounds in §6.2.
Procedure: 1. Compute Taylor Rule benchmark: r* ≈ 5.5-6.0% 2. Actual cash rate: 4.35% 3. Gap:
115-165bp accommodative 4. Apply monetary tightening elasticities in reverse to identify the implicit
dimensional effects 5. Express as implicit % GDP cost via macro stress reduction equivalent
The resulting PPLE point estimate of −0.45 reflects systematic bias in current monetary stance toward
suppressing A and B pressures while consuming H buffer (sustained mortgage debt accumulation) and
C buffer (sustained inflation expectations risk). The 90% interval [−0.65, −0.25] reflects uncertainty in
Taylor benchmark, elasticities, and “implicit cost” calibration.
This estimate is the largest single negative PPLE in the Australian portfolio. If approximately correct,
monetary policy itself is the principal source of synchronization risk, dominating fiscal cross-subsidies
in magnitude. We treat this as the most important and most uncertain estimate in the §8.3 portfolio;
51

 the §6.5a panel LP evidence and the §6.5b AUS-only LP evidence both reach the same qualitative
conclusion (monetary easing systematically increases PLDI synchronization risk) via methodologicallyindependent direct causal identification, providing convergent validation of the indirect Taylor-Rule
estimate.

H (Household debt as % GDP): BIS Total Credit Statistics, 1977-Q1 to 2025-Q3. Cross-validated against

7.3 Australia historical PLDI: key observations
1977-1980 · Stagflation aftermath: PLDI 0.40-0.80, reflecting elevated inflation (8-12%) and rising
unemployment.
1980-1989 · Disinflation and Hawke-Keating reforms: PLDI gradually improves from 0.80 to 1.50.
1989-1992 · “Recession we had to have”: PLDI collapses from approximately 1.30 to 0.11 in 1990-Q4.
Dual breach of A (CPI 6.9%) and B (unemployment 8.4%). Convergence in C and H within 24 months.
1996-2007 · The “Great Moderation” Australian variant: PLDI rises to peak values around 1.97 (2005Q4). Resources boom, fiscal consolidation, low inflation. However, household debt rose continuously
from 60% to 95% of GDP.
2008-2010 · Global Financial Crisis aftermath: Australia’s PLDI fell to 1.56 in 2008-Q4, in warning zone
but well above Talon Threshold. The household debt dimension was the binding constraint, but A, B,
and C provided substantial buffer. Australia avoided dual breach.
2010-2019 · Slow deterioration: PLDI declines from 1.69 to 1.28. Household debt rose from 105% to
121% of GDP. Cumulative erosion of buffers.
2020 · COVID shock: PLDI fell to 0.65 in 2020-Q4 (under the corrected two-sided A formula; the legacy
single-sided reading was 0.93, reclassified per §8.1). Unusual configuration: A in deflation, B partially
breached, C deteriorated rapidly, H held stable by extraordinary policy support.
2021-2023 · Inflation surge and Hidden Phase Locking: PLDI fell to 0.44 in 2022-Q4—deeper than
1991—but received minimal attention. A breached, B at extreme low, C deteriorating, H stable. Avoided
crisis through (1) RBA aggressive tightening, (2) resources boom, (3) labour market tightness.
2024-2026 · Current state: PLDI recovered to 1.32 (2025-Q4) before declining to 1.16 (2026-Q1). A
distance 0.70, B distance 1.80, C distance 1.73, H distance 0.815. A and H are both within 1.0 distance
of breach.

7’.4 Canada cross-subsidy policy inventory: 2024-2026
Canada’s 2024-2026 active policy portfolio spans federal monetary, simultaneous fiscal expansion +
fiscal consolidation tensions, housing macroprudential, and provincial sub-federal additions. Unlike
the Australian portfolio (§7.4) where 11 of 14 policies are continuations of Labor-government legacies
plus monetary stance, the Canadian portfolio is structurally split by a mid-period regime change: the
Trudeau Liberal minority government to Mar 2025, followed by Mark Carney’s Liberal-led government
from Mar 2025 onward, with the latter actively reversing three Trudeau-era Defuser-candidate fiscalconsolidation measures under combined trade-war and electoral pressure. We enumerate 14 active or
recently-active policies satisfying the §6 PPLE evaluation criteria — four federal monetary / macroprudential, six federal fiscal (split 3 Trudeau-legacy + 3 Carney-era), one regulatory-only macroprudential
package, and three provincial / sub-federal Defuser-direction measures.
Policy convention for the three Carney reversals: per §6.1 PPLE-attribution rules, a policy that was
implemented and then reversed is evaluated for PPLE as if fully implemented at central elasticity, with
59

 the sign flipped to reflect the foregone Defuser effect. This convention treats the reversal as the policy
action of interest; the original implementation period (typically 3-15 months for the three reversed
policies) is treated as a small countervailing offset that is absorbed into the bootstrap CI rather than
separately modelled. Applied uniformly to: carbon tax repeal Apr 2025, capital gains hike cancellation
Mar 2025, DST rescission Jun 2025. The fuel excise suspension (Apr 2026 onwards) is a forward-looking
active policy and is modelled as such, not under the reversal convention.

Notes on regime structure:
1. Trudeau Liberal → Carney Liberal transition (Mar 2025): The fiscal-policy regime change at Mar
2025 is essentially intra-party but produced an immediate active policy reversal of three Trudeauera fiscal-consolidation measures (carbon tax, capital gains hike, DST). Under §6.5 identification

2. Carney reversal context — Trump tariff pressure: The DST rescission (Jun 2025) and partial framing
of the capital gains hike cancellation (Mar 2025) reflect the Trump administration’s 2025-Q1

we evaluate at the reversed-policy convention without attempting to partition exogenous-vsendogenous causation.
3. NATO 2% defence (#6) is the single largest Fuse-direction line by raw fiscal cost in the inventory.
The Carney government’s Mar 2026 acceleration commits Canada to reach 2.4% of GDP on defence
by FY 2025-26, 8 years ahead of the previous 2032 schedule. The +1% GDP incremental annual
cost is a direct C-channel charge but is partially offset by B-channel ALMP-style effects of defence
procurement employment (estimated −0.20 pp unemployment per % GDP, central elasticity from
OECD Employment Outlook 2024 ALMP table).
4. Provincial housing-cooling Defusers (BC SVT/APTT) differ structurally from federal Defusers
because they raise provincial revenue rather than impose a federal fiscal cost. Their PPLE is
computed via the §6.2 foreign-buyer transfer tax row (share-scaling rule, v0.10.8) with assumed
Vancouver-MSA foreign-buyer share ≥ 10%. The 2026-01 SVT 3-percentage-point hike is the
marginal new policy; the APTT 20% baseline has been in effect since 2018 and is reported here
for completeness because its cumulative-impact contribution to the 2024-2026 Canada H-channel
stress remains material.
5. OSFI MQR removal + LTI portfolio cap (#9) is the only net-ambiguous policy in the inventory by
direction. The Nov-2024 removal of the Minimum Qualifying Rate for uninsured mortgages is a
Fuse-direction easing of macroprudential controls; the Q1-2025 introduction of a Loan-to-Income
(LTI) portfolio cap (15% of new originations >4.5× income) is a Defuser-direction tightening.
OSFI’s stated intention (per Nov 2024 RAR letter) is that the LTI cap dominates the MQR removal
in net portfolio terms, but empirical evidence remains thin pending the OSFI 2025 Annual Risk
Report.
Note on policies excluded from the inventory: - 2024 budget specific line items (e.g., productivity tax
credits, sectoral SR&ED expansions): aggregated into Trudeau COVID fiscal legacy line because they are
individually small and methodologically not distinguishable at the framework granularity. - BoC repo and
balance-sheet runoff : implicit in the BoC easing cycle line, not separately tabulated. - Provincial energy
rebates and consumer price interventions (Ontario, Quebec, Alberta): too geographically fragmented
62

 and small individually to materially affect national PLDI. - Trade-war tariff retaliation packages (2025
onwards): separate from the cross-subsidy policy inventory framework because they are trade-policy
instruments, not fiscal-stress instruments per §6.2; impact on A-channel CPI is captured indirectly
through observed CPI passthrough.
7.5 Tool space measurement
Monetary tool space: Nominal 425bp from current 4.35% to ~0% effective lower bound. Effective tool
space substantially less (150-250bp) given inflation constraint.
Fiscal tool space: Distance from current 34.4% net debt to 60% threshold = 25.6 percentage points. At
current consumption rate (1.6-1.8% GDP/year per §7.4), exhausted in approximately 14-16 years; at
crisis-rate, 2.5-5 years.

1. Australia 2026-Q1 PLDI = 1.16 unchanged, because A = 4.6% is on the high-inflation side and

dual breach by extraordinary fiscal-monetary policy support and rapid recovery of inflation. The

65

These exceptions are informative. Both cases involved circumstances where the dual breach was largely
confined to specific channels—sovereign and banking in Norway 1988; fiscal and labour in Brazil
2015—without strong cross-dimensional transmission. The 7% non-convergence rate suggests that
the Dual Breach Principle is a strong but not deterministic regularity; specific institutional conditions
can constrain the propagation mechanism.
Statistical inference under the expanded sample:
The 93.3% support rate at the warning-zone convergence criterion is statistically distinguishable from
a null hypothesis of 50% random convergence (one-sided exact binomial test against H₀: π = 0.50 yields
p = 4.34 × 10⁻⁷ ≪ 0.001). The same support rate is distinguishable from the 80% threshold stipulated
in H1, though only marginally: the one-sided exact binomial test against H₀: π = 0.80 yields p = 0.044,
which rejects H₀ at the conventional 5% level but only narrowly, and would not reject under either
two-sided framing (p ≈ 0.088) or Bonferroni multiple-comparison correction for the two parallel tests
reported below (α = 0.025 post-correction). We report the exact p-value transparently rather than the
looser “p < 0.05” formulation because the proximity to the 0.05 cutoff is itself informative for assessing
the strength of evidence supporting H1.
The full-breach convergence rate of 76.7% is distinguishable from 50% (one-sided exact binomial test
against H₀: π = 0.50 yields p = 2.61 × 10⁻³) but is statistically indistinguishable from 80% (one-sided
test against H₀: π = 0.80 yields p = 0.761, far above any conventional significance level). The framework
therefore supports the warning-zone convergence claim materially more robustly than the full-breach
convergence claim, with the warning-zone result itself supported at only marginal exact significance
against the 80% threshold.
All four exact-test p-values reported above are computed using scipy.stats.binom (verified
independently against numerical pre-publication checks; see supplementary materials at
lean/T2_scipy_verification.py). Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals reported in Table
8.2 are computed via the Beta quantile function (scipy.stats.beta.ppf); the corresponding formal
statements are in Appendix A.5.
The 30-case analysis substantially strengthens but does not definitively prove the Dual Breach Principle.

 9. Historical Comparison
The empirical results in Section 8 motivate close comparison to historical analogues. We focus on
four cases that bracket the range of possible outcomes for Australia: the GIIPS crisis (synchronized
fast-onset), Japan 1990s (asynchronous slow-onset), Volcker 1979-82 (counterfactual policy success),
and Keating 1989-91 (Australian domestic precedent).
9.1 GIIPS 2010-2012: synchronized crisis
The Greek, Irish, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish (GIIPS) sovereign debt crisis of 2010-2012 is the
most relevant recent precedent for synchronized multi-dimensional macroeconomic stress in advanced
economies.
Ireland 2008-2012: Pre-crisis Ireland exhibited several features in common with Australia 2026: high
household debt (peaking at 130% of GDP in 2010), heavy banking sector reliance on housing loans,
current account deficit financed by foreign capital inflows, and low public debt (24% of GDP in 2007).
The crisis sequence:
• 2007-Q4: H breached as housing prices began declining
• 2008-Q4: H + C dual breach following bank rescue announcements; C jumped from 24% to 44%
of GDP within 12 months
• 2009-2010: B converged to crisis level (unemployment from 4.5% to 14%)
• 2009-2011: A entered deflationary breach (CPI YoY -2.4% to -1.5%)
• 2010-Q4: Full four-dimensional crisis; PLDI estimated at 0.18
The Irish trajectory exhibits the Dual Breach Principle in textbook form: H + C breached together in
2008-Q4, and the remaining two dimensions (B and A) converged within 24 months.
Spain 2009-2013: Spain entered the crisis with a different configuration—lower household debt
(87% of GDP at peak) but higher youth unemployment vulnerability and a more pronounced housing
construction boom. Spain illustrates that the dual breach configuration is not unique—different starting
configurations can lead to similar synchronized outcomes through different sequences.
Australia 2026 vs GIIPS pre-crisis comparison: Australia 2026 has notable similarities (high household
debt, housing sector exposure) and notable differences (currency sovereignty, AAA rating, floating
exchange rate, resource exports). The differences likely lengthen Australia’s transition window relative
to Ireland or Spain at comparable PLDI levels, but do not reverse the directional risk.
9.2 Japan 1990s-2020s: asynchronous gradual crisis
Japan’s three-decade post-bubble experience provides the most important counter-case to the Dual
Breach Principle as it applies to fast-onset crisis. Japan 1990 features:
• 1989-1990: H breached as asset prices began declining (commercial real estate down 40-60%,
equity down 60%)
• 1990-Q4: Single-dimension breach in H, but A, B, and C were not in breach
• No dual breach in the 24 months following
The Japanese outcome was not synchronized fast-onset crisis but rather decades of gradual deterioration.
Japan demonstrates that without dual breach, the Dual Breach Principle does not apply.
Australia 2026 vs Japan 1990 comparison: Japan 1990 had an extremely strong starting configuration
(low debt across all measures, low unemployment, low inflation). Australia 2026 starts from a weaker
77

 configuration (household debt at 113.7% vs Japan’s 73%, federal debt at 34% vs Japan’s 12%, inflation
at 4.6% vs Japan’s 3.1%, unemployment at 4.3% vs Japan’s 2.1%).
This observation deserves emphasis: Australia 2026 enters a potential stress period with weaker
starting buffers than Japan 1990.
9.3 Volcker Federal Reserve 1979-1982: counterfactual policy success
The Volcker Federal Reserve’s response to US inflation in 1979-1982 provides the canonical example of
policy preventing synchronized crisis through accepting concentrated short-term pain.
Pre-Volcker conditions (1979-Q3): - A: CPI 12% (well above threshold) - B: Unemployment 5.9% (rising)
- C: Federal debt manageable (~32% of GDP) - H: Household debt at the historical norm (~50% of GDP)
The dual breach risk was concentrated in A + B. Volcker’s approach: aggressive tightening to break
inflation expectations, accepting B costs as the price of preventing further A deterioration.
Volcker’s policy actions: - October 1979: Federal funds rate raised from 11.25% to 15.5% - 1980-1981:
Rate further raised to peak of 20% - Result: Unemployment rose from 5.9% to 10.8% peak in 1982-Q4 Inflation: From 14.8% peak to 3.2% by 1983
Outcome: A + B dual breach was avoided despite the recession. The subsequent period (1983-2007)
became known as the Great Moderation.
Lesson for Australia 2026: The Volcker example demonstrates that Sequenced Demolition is possible
and historically successful. The political and institutional conditions for Volcker’s approach were
specific.
9.4 Keating 1989-1991: Australia’s domestic precedent
Australia experienced its own Volcker-style episode in 1989-1991. The dual breach risk was concentrated in A approaching threshold and B deteriorating. The Reserve Bank of Australia undertook
aggressive tightening:
• Cash rate raised from approximately 10% in early 1988 to 17.5% by end-1989
• Maintained at restrictive levels through 1990
Outcome: - B fully breached (unemployment to 11.0% in 1992) - A returned to target band by 1991 - C
and H did not converge to crisis—both remained well-buffered - Australia experienced “the recession
we had to have,” but avoided dual breach
The post-Keating decade (1992-2007) then featured 30 years of recession-free growth.
9.5 Where Australia 2026 fits
Australia 2026’s path distribution under the framework is best characterized qualitatively rather
than with numerical probabilities. The 30-case historical sample is too small to support quantitative
probability calibration. We characterize four possible paths in qualitative terms:
1. Slow synchronization path: gradual erosion of dimensional buffers over 5-10 years, with eventual
dual breach in the late part of this window if policy direction is unchanged. We characterize this
as the framework’s central scenario based on extrapolation of current PPLE trajectory and the
absence of structural circuit-breakers in the current policy mix.

78

 2. Fast synchronization path: an external shock (China-related export shock, regional banking event,
sustained energy price spike) triggers dual breach within 2-3 years. This path requires both
elevated current vulnerability (which is supported by current PLDI readings) and a triggering
event (which is path-dependent on factors outside the framework).
3. Sequenced demolition path: political conditions shift sufficiently to support Volcker-Keating style
aggressive tightening, breaking inflation expectations and rebuilding policy capacity at the cost of
substantial short-term unemployment. Section 12 argues this path requires political conditions
not currently in evidence.
4. Soft landing path: mainstream institutional forecasts hold and underlying conditions improve
faster than current PPLE consumes buffer. This requires either (i) underlying economic improvement (China demand recovery, energy price decline, productivity surge), or (ii) policy adjustment
toward de-synchronizing measures absent from the current portfolio.
We do not assign numerical probabilities to these paths. Each path’s probability depends on factors—external shocks, policy adjustments, structural changes—whose joint distribution is not credibly estimable
from the available data. The framework’s claim is more modest: paths 1-3 collectively warrant substantially more probability weight than they receive in current institutional forecasts, and path 4 (soft
landing) warrants substantially less.

11. Ex-post Validation of PPLE-Based Policy Classification
11.1 Motivation and selection criteria
The framework’s central operational claim — that PPLE provides a quantitative classification of whether
a given policy is positive or negative for the macroeconomy — has rested in earlier sections on three
sources: the §6 mechanism specification, the §8.3 Australia 2026 forward-looking forecast (n = 1,
prospective), and the §9 narrative historical comparison (no quantitative ex-ante prediction). This is a
methodologically incomplete foundation: a reviewer asking “show me historical policy decisions where
your framework said the right thing before the outcome was known” cannot be answered without an
explicit ex-post validation track record.
This section closes that gap. We assemble a 10-case set of historical policy events satisfying five
selection criteria: (i) a specific implementation date with a clear policy event; (ii) ABCH data observable
at both t0-ε baseline and t0+24m endpoint; (iii) the t0+24m horizon already resolved (excludes the
§8.3 prospective Australia case); (iv) the framework’s ex-ante PPLE prediction unambiguous on at least
one dimension; (v) mixed political directions across the case set to avoid framework being read as
politically biased. The selected cases span 1979-2025, four monetary policy events, four fiscal policy
events, two emerging-market shock therapy events, and four political coalitions (left, right, technocrat,
populist).
The 10 cases are: (1) Truss UK 2022-09 mini-budget; (2) Volcker Fed 1979-82 disinflation; (3) Keating
Australia 1988-91 tightening; (4) Rudd Australia 2009 GFC stimulus; (5) Greek austerity 2010-12
Troika MOU; (6) Abenomics Japan 2013 QQE; (7) Biden ARP 2021 USD 1.9T; (8) Trump TCJA 2017 +
tariffs 2018-19; (9) Erdogan Turkey 2021-23 heterodox monetary; (10) Milei Argentina 2023-25 shock
therapy.
11.2 Methodology
For each case, the workflow is:
Step A: define policy event (country, date t0, type, magnitude, §6.2 channel mapping).
Step B: compute t0-ε baseline ABCH and Calibration A PLDI + PLDI_pr using only information available
before the policy implementation.
Step C: derive an ex-ante PPLE prediction per channel using §6.2 dimension-by-dimension policy effect
modeling and §6.5 / §6.5c elasticity ranges. The prediction has three components: signed direction per
channel, magnitude range per channel, and identification of the predicted-dominant policy-induced
channel.
87

 Step D: retrieve the observed ABCH at t0+24m endpoint and compute the observed ΔPLDI. Then construct a peer-country counterfactual by computing the same Δ on 6-8 advanced-economy or emergingmarket peers depending on the case context, and report the peer-adjusted excess (the country’s Δ
minus the peer-average Δ). The peer-adjusted excess is the framework’s signal of policy-attributable
effect net of contemporaneous global shocks.
Step E: score the prediction on three criteria, each scoring 0, 0.5 (partial), or 1. (i) Direction: did
the predicted-dominant policy-induced channel move in the predicted direction on the peer-adjusted
reading? (ii) Magnitude: was the predicted magnitude within ±50% of the peer-adjusted observed
magnitude? (iii) Channel attribution: did the predicted-dominant policy-induced channel turn out to
be the most-affected ABCH dimension in the peer-adjusted reading? A case is classified as “consistent
with framework prediction” if its total score reaches ≥ 2 of 3.
Step F: document caveats and confounders, including external shocks during the 24m window that contaminate the outcome, counterfactual identification challenges, and policy-implementation deviations
from the announced policy.
Full per-case methodology, peer-adjusted tables, and replication-grade computation details are reported
in the per-case audit documents outputs/ex_post_case0X_*.md for X ∈ {1, …, 10}.
11.3 Case 1 · Truss UK mini-budget (2022-09-23 announcement; partial reversal 2022-10-17)
The Kwarteng mini-budget proposed £45bn (≈ 0.7% of GDP/year over 5 years) of unfunded tax cuts,
immediately triggering a sterling crisis and 30-year gilt yield spike. The framework’s ex-ante PPLE
prediction was C-channel negative via direct gov-debt accumulation (+3 to +4 pp ΔC at 24m from Truss
policy alone). UK observed ΔC at 2024-Q3 was +4.5 pp absolute (peer-adjusted excess +4.3 pp vs the
average of {DEU, FRA, ITA, ESP, USA}). The peer-adjusted ΔC peer-excess is at the upper end of the
framework’s prediction; the channel-attribution match is the dominant policy-induced channel; the
direction is correct. Score: 3/3 consistent. The case scores notably even though most of the announced
policy was politically reversed within 24 days — this is the framework correctly classifying the policy
direction even when implementation was incomplete.
11.4 Case 2 · Volcker Fed disinflation (1979-10 onwards, 48m horizon)
Fed switches to reserves targeting on 1979-10-06; Fed funds rate from ~11% to 20% peak. Framework’s
ex-ante PPLE prediction at 48m: A-channel aggressive disinflation as intended primary effect (predicted
ΔA −3 to −6 pp); B-channel sacrifice cost (predicted ΔB +2 to +4 pp). USA observed (annual, 1978 →
1983): ΔA = −3.36 pp; peer-adjusted excess −3.05 pp (parallel UK Thatcher tightening is the comparable

magnitude, and intended attribution. Score: 3/3 consistent. The 48m horizon is necessary; the 24m
reading (1981) captures only the transitional phase with A still elevated and B rising. This case is the
framework’s strongest “policy as intended” empirical record in the 10-case set.

Discovered methodology limitations (write-up of negative findings):
1. PLDI_pr fails on abrupt regime transitions in either direction. Country-specific pseudo-real-time
rolling-σ methodology absorbs hyperinflation (Erdogan: TUR 2021-23) or abrupt disinflation
(Keating: AUS 1988-92) as the country’s “new normal” and produces wrong-direction aggregate
readings. Calibration A (fixed thresholds) correctly classifies both cases as deep crisis throughout. Policy implication: users deploying PLDI_pr should restrict use to stable-regime advanced
economies; for emerging markets, hyperinflation contexts, or large policy regime transitions,
Calibration A is the appropriate variant.
2. Aggregate-PLDI direction is the wrong framing for ex-post PPLE validation. The 24m window’s
signal is typically dominated by external shocks (energy prices, COVID, war, supply chains).
Channel-specific peer-adjusted scoring isolates the policy-attributable signal and is the correct
framing for PPLE validation. Paper §X-style validation should consistently report peer-adjusted
channel-specific readings rather than aggregate-PLDI direction.
3. Calibration A saturates at the d-floor for severe regimes. When two or more channels are already
at the breach-threshold floor (d_X = 0.01), Cal A PLDI can no longer differentiate “moderate crisis”
from “catastrophic crisis”. In the Turkey case, Cal A PLDI stays at 0.18-0.20 throughout, correctly
classifying as crisis but not distinguishing the worsening severity. This is a structural feature,
not a bug: the framework provides a binary “in crisis” classifier on Cal A; severity requires the
underlying channel-specific d-vector reading rather than the aggregate PLDI.

11.15 Open methodological questions for future research
Three methodological gaps surfaced by the 10-case validation merit future-research extension:
(i) Synthetic-control counterfactual upgrade: peer-country comparison is a simple counterfactual;
a synthetic control method (Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller 2010 Journal of the American
Statistical Association) could provide a more rigorous counterfactual at higher computational
cost. Re-running the 10-case set under synthetic control is a future refinement.
(ii) Longer horizons for monetary policy cases: the Volcker and Keating cases were scored at 48m horizon because monetary disinflation cycles span longer than 24m. For policies with longer transmission lags (structural reform, institutional change), even 48m may understate the framework’s true
ex-post performance. Extending to 96m or 120m horizons is a refinement for slow-mechanism
cases.
(iii) PPLE elasticity cross-validation: the 10 cases collectively imply specific elasticity ranges across
the §6 channels. A cross-validation exercise would compare the implied elasticities to the §6.5
/ §6.5c estimated ranges and report calibration drift. This is a methodological refinement that
closes the loop between ex-ante calibration and ex-post implied calibration.
The 10-case ex-post validation does not exhaust the universe of testable policy events. Geographic
gaps include the absence of African and Asian-EM cases (only Turkey + Argentina represent EM);
101

 historical gaps include the pre-1979 era where data availability is more limited. The Canada Phase
3 extension in §11.13 (5 additional sub-cases at advanced-economy quarterly frequency) partially
addresses the cross-country extension priority but does not address EM-coverage or pre-1979 history
gaps. Future extension should prioritise EM-coverage expansion and historical-data improvement to
scale the validation track record beyond the current 15-case combined set (§11.4-§11.12 plus §11.13ae).
The framework’s claim — that PPLE-based quantitative policy classification can ex-ante distinguish
positive-for-economy from negative-for-economy policies across political coalition and economic regime
— is empirically supported by 10/10 cases in the §11.4-§11.12 reference set + 4/5 cases in the §11.13
