105

 12. Political Economy of Inaction
12.1 The puzzle of optimal policy non-adoption
If Sequenced Demolition is the policy approach with substantially better expected outcomes, why is it
not being adopted? Buchanan and Wagner (1977) developed the canonical analysis of why democratic
governments systematically prefer fiscal expansion to consolidation.
What is specific to Australia 2026 is the configuration of political constraints that make Sequenced
Demolition particularly difficult to implement. We identify five constraints.
12.2 The Labor government majority constraint
Following the May 2025 federal election, the Labor government holds 94 House of Representatives
seats, the largest single-party majority in Australian history. This creates the incentive: the government
has substantial political capital to defend popular short-term policies and faces minimal opposition
pressure to consolidate.
12.3 Populist pressure on both flanks
Roy Morgan polling (May 2026) shows One Nation primary vote at 21.5%, with strong support for
further fiscal expansion (housing subsidies, energy support) and opposition to monetary tightening.
12.4 RBA dual mandate interpretation
The Reserve Bank’s 2024 mandate revision explicitly elevated employment alongside inflation. Its
operational interpretation has tended toward avoiding employment costs of monetary tightening rather
than accepting them as the price of inflation control.
12.5 Resource currency dynamics
Australia’s status as a resource-currency economy creates a specific complication. Aggressive tightening
tends to appreciate the AUD, which: - Reduces AUD value of resource export earnings - Reduces
federal corporate tax receipts - Reduces state royalty receipts - Compounds rather than alleviates the C
dimension
This is genuine political economy complexity, not just political will.
12.6 The intergenerational distribution of pain
Sequenced Demolition concentrates short-term pain on heavily indebted households—predominantly
mortgage borrowers with variable-rate loans, who skew toward middle-aged Australians (35-55).
The long-term beneficiaries—future borrowers, young Australians, and the next 5-10 cohorts of new
household formation—are politically less organized and have less direct policy access.
A note on the H dimension and political visibility: This paper measures H as household debt to GDP (a
stock variable, BIS standard), which reflects long-term structural fragility and aligns with the dominant
academic literature on credit-driven crises (Schularick and Taylor 2012; Mian and Sufi 2014). However,
the politically visible variable is the household debt-service ratio (DSR), a flow variable measuring
monthly mortgage payment relative to disposable income. The two variables move in opposite directions during monetary tightening: H_stock improves over 24-36 months (deleveraging, reduced new
106

 borrowing), while DSR rises immediately as variable-rate mortgage payments increase. The politicaleconomy resistance to monetary tightening documented in §12.2-§12.4 operates primarily through
the DSR channel, even though the structural-stability case for tightening operates through the H_stock
channel. This dual-time-scale H response is identified as future research (§14.5) but does not affect
the framework’s primary measurements, which rely on H_stock for consistency with the international
comparative literature.
12.7 Implications for the framework’s policy traction
The PLDI/PPLE framework has limited probability of immediate political traction in Australia 2026.
However, the framework retains value through several channels:
Channel 1 · Diagnostic legitimacy for future crisis response Channel 2 · Evaluation tool for opposition
movements Channel 3 · Academic and policy research framework Channel 4 · International applications
The political economy of inaction does not invalidate the framework’s analytical contribution.

13. Robustness and Counterarguments
13.1 The Modern Monetary Theory critique
The most fundamental challenge to the PLDI framework comes from Modern Monetary Theory (MMT),
most prominently associated in Australia with William Mitchell at the University of Newcastle. The
MMT critique:
The C dimension as specified in this paper—federal government net debt as percent of
GDP—is not a meaningful crisis indicator for a currency-issuing sovereign government.
Australia issues debt in its own currency and faces no involuntary default risk. The “crisis
threshold” of 60% of GDP is arbitrary. The genuine constraint on government spending is
real resources (productive capacity), captured indirectly through inflation (the A dimension), not nominal debt levels.
Our response, in three parts:
Part 1 · Acknowledgment of partial validity: We accept that Australia, as a currency-issuing sovereign,
does not face involuntary default risk faced by Greece, Argentina, or US states. The C dimension should
not be interpreted as predicting Australian sovereign default.
Part 2 · Specification of the actual C-channel risk: The C dimension captures three distinct mechanisms
of crisis transmission, none of which depends on default risk:
1. Currency depreciation channel: Even without default, sustained fiscal expansion combined with
monetary accommodation can drive currency depreciation that imports inflation. Argentina,
Turkey, Venezuela illustrate this channel.
2. Sovereign credit rating channel: Rating agencies downgrade currency-sovereign governments
with deteriorating fiscal trajectories, raising borrowing costs.
3. Interest service crowding-out channel: Even without default, interest payments crowd out other
expenditure. At Australian net debt of 60% and 4-5% interest rate, interest payments would
consume 2.5-3% of GDP—approximately the entire defence budget.

107

 Part 3 · Empirical patterns: The 30 historical cases include numerous currency-sovereign economies
(US, UK, Japan, Australia, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Brazil, Russia, Mexico, Argentina, Turkey, Korea,
Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Iceland, Chile) where the Dual Breach Principle held despite the absence
of involuntary default risk. The principle’s strength across currency-sovereign economies indicates
that the C-channel risk is not contingent on default mechanics.
We conclude that MMT is partially correct (default risk is not the relevant C constraint for Australia)
but does not invalidate the framework.
13.2 The mainstream institutional defence
The “soft landing” forecast for Australia 2026 reflects careful institutional analysis. Australia
avoided the 2008 GFC and the 2020 COVID crisis—why should this analysis suddenly fail in
2026?
Our response, in three parts:
Part 1 · Methodological difference, not data difference: The mainstream forecast and this paper’s
diagnosis use largely overlapping data—ABS, RBA, BIS, Treasury statistics are common to both. The
divergence in conclusion arises from analytical framework. Mainstream analysis applies single-variable
evaluation: inflation against the RBA target band, unemployment against the NAIRU, federal debt
against international benchmarks, household debt against historical Australian peaks. Each variable is
read in isolation, with implicit assumption that buffers in non-stressed dimensions provide insurance.
The PLDI framework reads the same variables jointly through the geometric-mean aggregation, which
(per §4.4 Property P3) is disproportionately sensitive to the worst-stressed coordinate while penalizing
dispersion. The same 2026-Q1 data produces “warning but not alarming” under single-variable reading
and “near Talon Threshold with active policy momentum” under PLDI reading. The mainstream forecast
is not wrong about its inputs; it is incomplete about coupling.
Part 2 · Historical pattern of mainstream “soft landing” calls before crisis: The 2008 and 2020 cases
that the mainstream cites as evidence of forecasting reliability are selection-on-success. Reinhart and
Rogoff’s (2009) systematic survey of pre-crisis institutional commentary across 800 years and 66 countries documents that institutional consensus systematically underweights tail risk in the configurations
most vulnerable to it—the “This Time Is Different” syndrome that Reinhart and Rogoff identify as the
canonical pre-crisis institutional posture. The pattern is well-documented across the 1990 Japan crash,
the 1997 Korean crisis, the 2008 Irish and Spanish crises, and the 2010 Greek crisis, each preceded by
institutional assessments describing manageable rather than imminent crisis trajectories. Australia’s
2008 PLDI of 1.56 (well above Talon Threshold) and 2020 PLDI of 0.65 (under the corrected two-sided
A formula; deep crisis zone, only avoided full crisis through extraordinary policy response) are, on the
framework’s reading, two prior near-misses rather than two validations.
Part 3 · Configuration specificity in 2026-Q1: The 2008 and 2020 episodes featured single-dimension
stress with three buffering dimensions (H elevated but A/B/C providing buffer in 2008; A/B briefly
stressed but C/H stable in 2020). The 2026-Q1 configuration is two dimensions within 1.0 distance of
breach (A and H) with active fiscal-monetary policy reducing the remaining buffers. This is the specific
configuration that the Dual Breach Principle (§3.3) identifies as the precursor to four-dimensional
convergence. The mainstream forecast does not have a framework for distinguishing this configuration
from generalized “warning zone” stress.

13.4 Threshold and parameter sensitivity
Small changes in calibration choices generate substantially different PLDI values.
Our response: We address parameter sensitivity at four levels: threshold choice, sigma choice, aggregation function choice, and Talon Threshold choice.
Threshold sensitivity: The 2026-Q1 PLDI of 1.16 is computed under Calibration A (theoretical thresholds: τ_A_upper = 6.0%, τ_B = 7.0%, τ_C = 60%, τ_H = 130%). Section 8.4 reports two alternative
threshold sets: Calibration B (Australian historical P95) yields PLDI = 0.76 (Talon Threshold breached);
Calibration C (international crisis thresholds) yields PLDI = 1.92 (warning zone, below safe zone of 1.50).
The qualitative classification—Australia 2026-Q1 is at minimum in the warning zone, plausibly at the
Talon Threshold—is invariant across all three threshold sets. For 2026-Q1 to land in the safe zone (PLDI
> 1.50) under any of these calibrations, the underlying state variables (CPI 4.6%, unemployment 4.3%,
federal debt 34.4%, household debt 113.7%) would need to materially improve, not the calibration
parameters.
Sigma sensitivity: Section 8.4 reports PLDI under sigma values 50% higher and 50% lower than baseline.
The range is 0.84-1.42, all within warning or threshold zones; sigma scaling does not produce safe-zone
classification under the current state vector.
Sigma functional form (empirical, 43-country panel): Beyond the Australia-specific ±50% sigma scaling
above, an empirical sensitivity test on the §A.4 pseudo-real-time pipeline addresses the choice of σ
functional form for the two-sided A dimension. There is a residual specification tension between §3.1 /
§4.3 and §5.3: §3.1 / §4.3 specify the A dimension with an asymmetric σ structure (distinct σ_A_upper
and σ_A_lower, motivated by the Fisher dynamic floor and the empirical narrowness of the deflation tail
in advanced economies; fixed at σ_A_upper = 2.0 and σ_A_lower = 1.5 for the Australian Calibration A),
whereas §5.3 (the country-specific pseudo-real-time normalisation rule applied across the 43-country
panel) specifies a single σ_X computed as the country-specific historical standard deviation over the
prior-data window. The Phase 4 baseline (v1) follows §5.3 literally and uses a single pooled σ_A for
both the high-inflation and deflation sides of the A distance. The Phase 4b refinement (v2) is a dataderived attempt to reconcile §5.3 with the asymmetric concept of §3.1 / §4.3 by splitting the prior-data
112

 window at its median—σ_A_upper estimated on past CPI observations ≥ median, σ_A_lower on past
CPI observations < median—as a country-specific analog of the fixed theoretical values in Calibration A.
Re-running the full PLDI_pr pipeline on the 43-country BIS modern panel under both specifications on
identical samples yields: v1 (single pooled σ_A, §5.3-faithful) AUC = 0.6355, lift ratio 21.5× at the 0.80
threshold; v2 (median-split σ_A_upper / σ_A_lower, an attempted reconciliation with §3.1 / §4.3) AUC =
0.6034, lift ratio 13.3×. The §5.3-faithful single-σ specification outperforms the median-split asymmetric
specification by 0.032 AUC. We interpret this as a finite-window bias-variance tradeoff: with the 30-year
(annual) and 120-quarter (quarterly) prior-data windows used for §5.3 normalisation, splitting the
sample at the median halves the effective σ-estimation sample on each side and inflates variance more
than the asymmetry bias it removes. For pseudo-real-time applications on finite windows the single-σ
§5.3 form is therefore the empirically robust default; the asymmetric form of §3.1 / §4.3 remains the
theoretically motivated specification but its data-derived translation onto small windows is empirically
penalised. The v1 outperformance is consequently not evidence of artificial over-fit of the §5.3 form
but rather of the cost of sample fragmentation in the v2 reconciliation attempt. Whether an alternative
reconciliation (e.g., quantile-anchored σ_A_upper from the upper-tail empirical spread above τ_A_upper
rather than the median; or a hierarchical pooling across the upper and lower halves) would close this gap
is left as a future refinement. Replication code: d3b_data/scripts/31b_pseudo_realtime_v2.py;
tabulated comparison in d3b_data/outputs/phase4_5_audit.md §1.5.
Aggregation function sensitivity: Section 8.4 reports PLDI under three alternative aggregators (arithmetic mean = 1.27, Mahalanobis = 1.31, with geometric mean baseline = 1.16). All three place 2026-Q1
in the warning zone; none produces safe-zone classification. The geometric mean’s stronger sensitivity
to the worst-stressed coordinate (§4.4 Property P3) produces the lowest PLDI value, but the qualitative
finding does not depend on the geometric-mean choice.
Talon Threshold sensitivity: The Talon Threshold value 0.80 was identified in the initial draft and
retained without modification (§13.3 c); it is formally specified as the universal PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 cutoff
on the pseudo-real-time PLDI scale (§3.2), with numerical coincidence on the level-scale narrative via
𝑇AUS = 0.885 rounded (§5.3a). For 2026-Q1 to fall below the Talon Threshold (i.e., the framework
to recommend immediate crisis-zone classification), either (i) the threshold would need to be raised
above 1.16—implausible, since it would require all historical crisis-zone observations (1991-Q4 = 0.62,
2020-Q4 = 0.65, 2022-Q4 = 0.44) to be reclassified as crisis-class with substantial buffer, or (ii) PLDI

Summary: across threshold, sigma, aggregation function, and Talon Threshold variations, no specification places 2026-Q1 in the safe zone. The robustness claim is not “the specific PLDI value of 1.16 is

under all reasonable robustness specifications”.
13.5 Alternative scenarios and external shocks
Favorable scenarios: China demand recovery, oil price decline, AI productivity surge, US Federal Reserve
rate cuts. Each affects multiple dimensions: a China demand recovery would lift Australia’s resource
exports (improving C through royalty receipts and B through commodity-sector employment) but
pressure A through input cost transmission. An oil price decline would reduce A directly but compress
LNG export revenues that buffer C. An AI productivity surge would raise potential output, shifting
the inflation-employment Phillips Curve favorably (A↓, B↓) without consuming C or H buffer. US
Federal Reserve rate cuts would ease the RBA’s inflation-management constraint, allowing earlier rate

113

 normalization that begins H deleveraging.
Unfavorable scenarios: China property/credit crisis, Middle East conflict escalation, regional banking
stress, global trade disruption. Each operates through distinct channels: a China property crisis would
collapse Australian iron ore prices (degrading C through royalty losses, pressuring B through resourcesector contraction); Middle East escalation would spike oil prices (pressuring A directly and B through
demand destruction); regional banking stress would tighten Australian credit conditions (pressuring
H through margin calls and forced deleveraging); global trade disruption would erode Australia’s
structural buffer (currency-sovereign + AAA + floating FX) by reducing the resource-export earnings
that underpin C.
Asymmetric risk structure: The favorable scenarios share a feature that the unfavorable do not: each
requires multiple favorable conditions to simultaneously hold to materially shift PLDI toward safezone classification. The unfavorable scenarios share a feature that the favorable do not: any one of
them, materializing alone, can accelerate dual breach by depleting one or more dimensional buffers.
This asymmetry is the central structural point: the framework’s warning is not contingent on any
specific scenario materializing but on the joint configuration that makes multiple scenarios individually
sufficient triggers.
Joint probability considerations: Even if the marginal probability of each individual unfavorable scenario
is small within a 24-month window, the probability that at least one materializes within 24 months is
materially higher than any individual probability (one minus the product of individual non-occurrence
probabilities, under approximate independence). The framework’s central point is not that any specific
scenario will materialize but that the configuration is unusually vulnerable to multiple potential triggers,
and that the joint risk of “at least one trigger” is the policy-relevant measure rather than any individual
scenario probability.
13.6 Sample size and external validity
The 30 cases were specifically selected to span diverse institutional configurations (advanced and emerging, currency-sovereign and euro-zone, commodity and non-commodity, fixed and floating exchange
rate). The 93.3% support rate across this diverse sample is consistent with the principle reflecting a
structural feature of macroeconomic systems rather than a country-specific phenomenon.
Statistical power: The exact one-sided binomial test against H₀: π = 0.50 yields p = 4.34 × 10⁻⁷ (Theorem
A.5.3), corresponding to high power for detecting deviations from random convergence. The marginalsignificance result against H₀: π = 0.80 (p = 0.044, Theorem A.5.4) reflects the reality that distinguishing
93% from 80% with 30 observations is itself near the boundary of what such a sample can support; the
same support rate at n = 50 would yield p ≈ 0.006 (an 8-fold reduction in the p-value), and at n = 100
would yield p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴ (a 160-fold reduction, slightly over two orders of magnitude). Sample size, not
principle direction, is the binding constraint on the strength of evidence against the 80% null.
Sub-sample robustness: The 12-case original sample (12/12 = 100%) and the 18-case extension (16/18
= 89%) both individually support the principle at warning-zone convergence. The two non-converging
cases (Norway 1988, Brazil 2015) come from the extension, raising the empirically observed rate from
100% to 93.3% upon expansion—a magnitude consistent with regression to the population mean rather
than evidence of an over-fit 12-case original. Across geographic sub-samples (advanced and emerging
economies) and across regime sub-samples (currency-sovereign and euro-zone), the convergence
rate is qualitatively stable; precise per-cell CIs are constrained by the small per-cell sample sizes and
reported in supplementary materials with the §14.5 future-research full-panel implementation.

114

 External validity threats: Three threats are non-trivial. First, future crisis configurations may differ
structurally from the 1929-2024 sample (potential candidates: central bank digital currencies altering
the H-A transmission, climate-driven physical-asset shocks altering the fiscal-monetary nexus, AI-driven
productivity discontinuities). Second, the sample is endpoint-censored: the 2024 cutoff means the
framework has not been tested against crises that emerge in 2025-2030 windows. Third, countryspecific threshold calibration (§5.3) introduces judgment that may not generalize uniformly across all
advanced economies (§14.5 candidate applications).
Path forward: Larger panel tests using the full Laeven-Valencia 151-case sample combined with the
Jordà -Schularick-Taylor R6 macrohistory database (18 advanced economies × 1870-2020) are identified as priority for subsequent research (§14.5 item 1). The combined panel provides approximately
2,700 country-year observations for advanced economies plus 7,740 modern country-quarter observations, sufficient for rigorous out-of-sample testing of the threshold and the Dual Breach Principle’s
convergence claim.
13.7 What would falsify the framework?
The Dual Breach Principle would be substantially weakened by: - Three or more documented cases
of dual breach without subsequent convergence within 36 months - Two or more documented cases
of dimensional convergence preceded by no dual breach - A formal panel data analysis finding the
convergence pattern statistically indistinguishable from random - Identification of specific Australian
structural features that genuinely insulate it
The PLDI/PPLE framework would be substantially weakened by: - Evidence that the four chosen
dimensions are not the appropriate set - Demonstration that the geometric mean aggregation systematically misclassifies crisis risk - Application to non-Australian economies that produces classifications
inconsistent with historical experience
The Australia 2026 forecast would be falsified by: - PLDI rising above 1.50 (safe zone) within 24 months
despite continuation of current PPLE-negative policy - Synchronized crisis materializing within 5 years
(would actually be vindication) - Sequenced demolition being implemented and producing better
outcomes (would vindicate the counterfactual)
We invite rigorous attempts to falsify any of these claims.

and Wealth (Palgrave 2007, 2nd ed. 2012), the canonical post-Keynesian stock-flow consistent (SFC)

 macroeconomics text. Lavoie’s framework overlaps with MMT on currency-sovereign monetary architecture but is methodologically distinct: it grounds monetary endogeneity, fiscal capacity, and crisis
dynamics in explicit stock-flow consistent national accounting rather than functional-finance principles.
The §13.8.1 critique addresses the post-Keynesian SFC challenge from the Lavoie framework, which is
the closest Canadian heterodox analogue to the §13.1 Mitchell-MMT critique but is distinct from MMT
proper and should be read as the post-Keynesian (not MMT) critique throughout this section.
The Lavoie post-Keynesian SFC critique (paraphrased synthesis of Godley-Lavoie 2007/2012 and
Lavoie’s 2014 Post-Keynesian Economics: New Foundations Ch. 1-2, 9):
The C dimension as specified in this paper — federal government gross debt as percent of
GDP — is not a meaningful crisis indicator for a currency-issuing sovereign with floating
exchange rate. Canada issues debt in Canadian dollars and faces no involuntary default
risk on CAD-denominated obligations. The Bank of Canada is the monopoly issuer of CAD;
settlement of federal liabilities is a keystroke operation, not a financing operation. Per the
Godley-Lavoie stock-flow-consistent national accounting framework, the relevant macroeconomic constraint is real-resource (productive capacity utilization), which is captured
indirectly through the A (inflation) dimension when capacity is fully utilized, not through
any nominal debt-stock level. The 60% C threshold (Cal A) or 66% C threshold (Cal B
Canada historical) lacks economic content for a currency-sovereign; both are arbitrary
calibration choices that misclassify expansionary fiscal policy as crisis-inducing when the
binding constraint is real-resource (captured by A and B), not nominal-debt (captured by
C).
Our response, in three parts:
Part 1 · Acknowledgment of partial validity. We accept that Canada, as a currency-issuing sovereign
with floating CAD, does not face the involuntary default risk that bound Greece in 2010, Argentina
recurringly since 2001, or US state governments structurally. The Bank of Canada Act 1985 establishes BoC as monopoly CAD issuer, and Department of Finance Canada Annual Financial Report data
documents continuous federal debt rollover capacity throughout the 1980-2025 sample including
the 1995-Chretien peak at 66.6% (the empirical anchor for Cal B τ_C = 65.98%). The C dimension
should not be interpreted as predicting Canadian sovereign default, nor as a binary debt-ceiling-type
constraint.
Part 2 · Specification of the actual C-channel risk. The C dimension in our framework captures three
distinct mechanisms of crisis transmission, none of which depends on default risk: (i) Currency depreciation channel (CAD-specific) — sustained fiscal expansion combined with BoC monetary accommodation
can drive CAD depreciation that imports inflation through the import-share-of-CPI channel (BoC importpassthrough estimates 0.20-0.30 per 10% CAD depreciation; BoC SDP paper 2018-19). Canada’s 32%
import share of GDP (StatCan IEA 2024) means CAD weakness contributes meaningfully to A dimension
stress even absent default risk. Argentina, Turkey, and Venezuela illustrate the same mechanism at extreme intensity — all three are currency-sovereign issuers but suffered crisis via the currency-inflation
channel, not default. (ii) Sovereign credit rating channel — Moody’s reviews of Canada (Aa1 2014;
Aaa preserved 2021) and provincial downgrades of Ontario (Aa3 2023), Quebec (Aa2 2019), and Alberta (Aa2 2020 downgrade) demonstrate that rating agencies adjust currency-sovereign assessments
based on fiscal trajectory independent of default mechanics. Each downgrade raises CAD-denominated
borrowing costs, which feeds the C-channel through interest-service burden even without nominal
default. (iii) Interest-service crowding-out channel — at Canadian federal gross debt of 33% GDP and
5-year Government of Canada bond yield of 3.2% (May 2026), federal interest payments consume
116

 approximately 1.1% of GDP. At Cal A τ_C = 60% and the same 3.2% yield, interest payments would
consume approximately 1.9% of GDP — roughly equivalent to Canada’s foreign-aid commitment plus
the additional NATO 2% defence increment. Crowding-out of discretionary fiscal capacity is a real
economic constraint independent of default risk.
Part 3 · Empirical patterns in the 30-case + Canada-extension sample. The 30 historical crisis episodes
in §11 include numerous currency-sovereign economies (US, UK, Japan, Australia, Sweden, Finland,
Norway, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Turkey, Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Iceland, Chile — and
now via §11.13a-e the Canadian 1995, 2009, 2017-18, 2020 COVID, 2022-23 episodes) where the Dual
Breach Principle held despite the absence of involuntary default risk. Two Canada cases illustrate:
Canada 1995 (§11.13a, hit at 2.5/3) — the federal fiscal consolidation episode under Chretien-Martin
operated through the C dimension at gross debt 66.6%; both Cal A and Cal B classified the period
correctly as C-channel stress. Currency-sovereign Canada with floating CAD throughout; involuntary
default was not the binding constraint. Canada 2009 (§11.13d, hit at 3/3) — the GFC stimulus episode
at 0.7% GDP expansion plus the 2008-Q4 BoC 250bp cuts evaluated as Fuse-direction; the H-channel
concurrently exhibited cycle-extension dynamics. These cases demonstrate that the C dimension
captures real economic constraints (crowding-out, currency-channel, rating-channel) that operate
symmetrically on currency-sovereign and non-sovereign issuers.
Synthesis. The Lavoie post-Keynesian critique is partially correct (default risk is not the binding C
constraint for Canada) but does not invalidate the framework. The three-mechanism response above
specifies the actual C-channel risk profile, which is distinct from sovereign-default risk but empirically
operative in the historical sample including Canadian episodes. The framework’s PPLE-based Fuse
classification of currency-sovereign fiscal expansion tracks the currency-channel, rating-channel, and
crowding-out-channel transmission mechanisms that operate independently of nominal-default risk
and that the Godley-Lavoie SFC framework itself accommodates within its stock-flow accounting
(Lavoie 2014 Ch. 7, 12; Godley-Lavoie 2007 Ch. 6, 9, 11). The substantive disagreement is over
which transmission channel is empirically dominant, not over the SFC accounting itself.
13.8.2 The mainstream institutional defence (BoC + Department of Finance + PBO)
Canada’s mainstream forecast — BoC Monetary Policy Report (April 2026 release), Department of Finance Canada budget projections (Budget 2026), Parliamentary Budget
Office Fiscal Sustainability Report 2024 — suggests Canada avoided the 2008 GFC severity
through measured policy response and is on a sustainable trajectory through 2030. The
2025-Q3 PLDI of 0.988 (Warning zone) is uncomfortable but not crisis-class. Why should
Phase Locking analysis suddenly fail in 2026?
Our response, in three parts:
Part 1 · Methodological difference, not data difference. The mainstream Canadian forecast and this
paper’s diagnosis use largely overlapping data inputs — StatCan CPI and labour series, BoC Selected
Bond Yields and policy rate path, Finance Canada Annual Financial Report fiscal aggregates, and
CMHC/BoC household-debt aggregate. The divergence in conclusion arises from analytical framework.
Mainstream analysis applies single-variable evaluation: inflation against the BoC 2% target (currently
2.36%, within reach), unemployment against the historical post-1990 mean (~6.8%, currently 7.1%,
modest above-trend), federal debt against international benchmarks (33% gross net of CPP/QPP, well
below G7 median), household debt against the 100-110% historical range. Each variable is read
in isolation, with implicit assumption that buffer in non-stressed dimensions provides insurance
against the one stressed dimension. The PLDI framework reads the same variables jointly through the
117

 geometric-mean aggregation, which (§4.4 Property P3) is disproportionately sensitive to the worststressed coordinate (currently d_H = 0.186 under Cal B — near the ε floor). The same 2025-Q3 data
produces “single-dimension stress within manageable buffer” under single-variable reading and “single
dimension at floor with the other three providing buffer that the geometric mean is structurally unable
to translate into safe-zone classification” under PLDI reading. The mainstream forecast is not wrong
about its inputs; it is incomplete about coupling.
Part 2 · Historical pattern of Canadian “soft landing” calls before stress. The mainstream cites Canada’s
avoidance of severe 2008-09 banking-crisis severity (no major bank failures, Big Five Canadian banks
emerged with capital ratios above pre-crisis levels; IMF Article IV 2010 commendation) as evidence of
forecasting reliability. The 2008-09 episode is a selection-on-success case: Reinhart and Rogoff (2009)
document that institutional consensus systematically underweights tail risk in the configurations most
vulnerable to it, and the Canadian “soft landing” call of 2007-Q3 (BoC MPR October 2007) preceded
the global crisis trajectory — Canada was insulated by its mortgage-market structure (5-year fixed, no
subprime origination scale, OSFI capital-rule conservatism) and its commodity-export structure, not by
superior macro forecasting. The 2017-18 BoC tightening cycle (§11.13b) preceded household-debtservice-ratio peaks that were not flagged in institutional commentary at the time; the 2022-23 BoC
tightening (§11.13a) was framed as inflation-control without explicit warning about the household-debt
phase-locking risk.
Part 3 · Configuration specificity in 2025-Q3. The 2008-09 and 2020 COVID episodes featured singledimension stress with three buffering dimensions. The 2025-Q3 configuration is single-dimension
stressed (H only) under Cal B — but with the H-dimension at the ε floor (d_H = 0.186, baseline PLDI
0.988), and with active BoC monetary easing (225bp cumulative 2024-06 to 2025-04) that the bootstrap
analysis (§8’.3) identifies as PPLE −0.645 (Fuse+). The mainstream forecast does not have a framework
for distinguishing this configuration from generalized “warning zone” stress. Under Cal A (§13.8.4
below), the same configuration reads as PLDI 0.454 (Crisis zone), with d_B simultaneously at the ε floor
due to AUS-tuned τ_B = 7.0 < current Canada unemp 7.1 — a calibration-specific dual-breach reading
that the mainstream framework cannot produce because it does not aggregate. Whichever calibration
is used, the PLDI reading is not consistent with the mainstream “manageable” framing.
13.8.3 Identification challenges
The Dual Breach Principle is an empirical regularity, not a causal mechanism. The 30case + Canada-extension correlation may reflect common shocks, selection bias, post-hoc
rationalization, or mechanism mis-specification.
We address each component as it applies to the Canadian extension. (a) Common shocks · Canadian
institutional-historical depth: The Canada-specific cases (§11.13a-e) span 30 years (1995-2023) and
cover four distinct global macro-monetary regimes and Liberal majority (Chretien), Conservative minority (Harper), Liberal minority (Trudeau twice), and Liberal majority post-Trudeau (Carney transition).
A common-shock explanation would require a single mechanism producing the four-fold convergence
pattern across this institutional and regime span. (b) Selection bias · Canadian-relevant Laeven-Valencia
episodes: The Laeven-Valencia 2018 database identifies Canada as a non-systemic-banking-crisis country across the 1970-2017 sample, but the §11.13 Canadian cases are pre-crisis or non-crisis episodes
selected for analytical content (policy actions with measurable framework-direction implications), not
crisis-conditioned. The §5.5 panel-wide converse test result applies symmetrically to Canada within the
panel. (c) Post-hoc rationalization: The Phase 3 extension added five Canadian cases (§11.13a-e), evaluated against the same per-cycle Cal A thresholds and the same ≥2/3 hit criterion. The aggregate Canada

118

 cross-validation of 14/15 = 93.3% hit rate (with §11.13b at 0.5/3 the single exception, downgraded
post-hoc to conditional-applicability disclosure) represents a fourth-fold validation cycle against an
independent country sample. The §11.16 synthetic-control robustness re-evaluation reinforces this
(Abadie-Diamond-Hainmueller 2010 synth gives 13/15 sign-agreement). (d) Mechanism specification
· 4 mechanisms applied to Canadian institutional context: BoC fiscal endogeneity (Bank of Canada Act
1985 analogous to RBA-Treasury); Canadian-specific 5-year fixed mortgage roll-rate transmission delay
(12-18 month timing displacement); CAD as 7th-most-traded currency with 30% import-share × 0.25
passthrough; Canadian residential real-estate as 48% of household assets. These mechanisms map
symmetrically onto the §3.3 AUS specification with Canadian-specific institutional embodiment.

13.8.5 Alternative scenarios and external shocks for Canada 2026-2030 Favorable scenarios: (1)
China commodity demand recovery (lifts Canadian oil + softwood + potash + uranium prices, federal
corporate-tax + provincial royalty receipts); (2) US Federal Reserve aggressive rate cuts (gives BoC room
to renormalize without compounding CAD weakness); (3) AI productivity surge (raises potential output;
Canada’s AI ecosystem CIFAR/Vector/MILA/Element legacy + National AI Strategy 2017 positions
Canada to capture upside); (4) trade-war de-escalation (US-Canada bilateral).
Unfavorable scenarios: (1) China property/credit crisis collapses iron ore + softwood demand; (2)
Middle East conflict escalation + oil price spike (A direct passthrough + B demand destruction; Canadian
oil exports would benefit C-channel but A-channel transmission would dominate short-term); (3) US
recession spillover — US is Canada’s largest trading partner (74% of merchandise exports per StatCan
IEA 2024); a US recession of 2008-09 magnitude would pull Canadian B materially higher (current 7.1
+ amplification = potentially 9-10 within 12 months) and pressure C through automatic stabilizers —
120

 the largest single external risk to the Canadian configuration; (4) Trade-war escalation (Trump 2.0
expansion of tariffs on Canadian goods, beyond already-announced 25% steel/aluminum); (5) CAD
collapse 25%+ from current levels.
Asymmetric risk structure: The favorable scenarios share a feature that the unfavorable do not —
each requires multiple favorable conditions to simultaneously hold to materially shift PLDI toward
safe-zone classification. The unfavorable scenarios share a feature the favorable do not — any one of
them, materializing alone, can accelerate dual breach by depleting one or more dimensional buffers.
Joint probability heuristic: under approximate independence and rough subjective probabilities (US
recession 2026-2028: 25%; China property severe: 20%; Middle East oil shock: 15%; Trade-war
escalation severe: 30%; CAD shock magnitude: 10%), the probability that at least one materializes
within 24 months is heuristically 1 − (0.75)(0.80)(0.85)(0.70)(0.90) ≈ 68%. Even under more conservative probability assignments (halving each above), the joint probability of at-least-one materialization
within 24 months exceeds 40%. These probabilities are heuristic / subjective estimates, not derived
from formal probability models; the qualitative point (asymmetric risk structure across multiple tail
scenarios) is robust to specific probability values, but the 68% number is illustrative rather than
published-paper-grade.
13.8.6 Sample size and external validity (Canada specifically) Canada is 1 of 33 countries in the
D3b cross-country quarterly panel; within the panel Canada contributes approximately 180 countryquarters of data, ~5.6% of the panel total. Canada is also 1 of 18 JST countries in the long-history
annual panel (1948-2020), contributing 73 country-years. Canada is 5 of 15 ex-post cases in the §11
framework-validation track record (10 reference cases + 5 Canada extension).
External validity assessment for Canada specifically: (i) Currency-sovereign + floating-FX: Canada
shares this institutional structure with most of the §11 reference sample. (ii) Commodity-exporter:
Canada shares this structural feature with Australia, Norway, and to a lesser extent Russia and Brazil.
(iii) Federal-fiscal-system: Canada’s 13-province fiscal-federalism architecture is structurally similar
to US 50-state and Australia 6-state systems. (iv) 5-year fixed-rate mortgage market — unique to
Canada within the §11 reference sample (AUS uses variable-rate; US uses 30-year-fixed; UK uses 5year-variable); creates a transmission delay between BoC policy moves and household debt-service
realization that does not appear in any other §11 case. (v) OSFI direct macroprudential authority —
unique to Canada within the §11 reference sample (AUS uses APRA; US uses Fed + OCC + FDIC; UK uses
BoE PRA); the OSFI Q4-2024 MQR removal + Q1-2025 LTI portfolio cap is a contemporary intervention
type not represented elsewhere in the case sample.
The two Canada-unique institutional features (5-year fixed mortgage market; OSFI direct macroprudential authority) are explicit external-validity threats to the framework’s Canadian deployment. Both are
addressed in §6.2 elasticity caveats and in the §13.8.4 calibration sensitivity above; neither invalidates
the framework’s deployment but each implies the Canadian PPLE estimates carry larger uncertainty
than the comparable AUS estimates.
Canadian over-representation in the 15-case ex-post sample (5/15 = 33%, vs Canada’s ~3-5% share of
global advanced-economy GDP) is by Phase 3 design (the Canada extension is the framework’s first
cross-country deployment beyond AUS-original-context); subsequent extensions to other countries
should rebalance the per-country case distribution. The Canadian over-representation does not bias
the framework’s directional findings because the 14/15 hit rate is computed against the same ≥2/3
criterion that applied to the original 10 cases.

14. Conclusion
14.1 Summary of contributions
This paper has made five contributions, organised around the four-capability framework and its threetest empirical validation on the D3b cross-country panel.
First, we introduced the Phase Locking Distance Index (PLDI), a quantitative measure of how close an
economy is to four-dimensional simultaneous crisis, with the Talon Threshold (PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 on the
pseudo-real-time scale; §3.2) as the deployment operating point.
Second, we provided a four-capability framework with three-test empirical validation on the D3b
33-country panel (1980-2025 quarterly, merged with Laeven-Valencia 1970-2017 and JST 1870-2020
long-history). The framework integrates: (a) multi-dimensional A/B/C/H risk monitoring; (b) ex-ante
PPLE policy evaluation (contribution 4); (c) Sequenced Demolition counterfactual analysis (§10); (d)
dual-frequency mechanism robustness — Cox PH on dual-breach episodes reproduces a significantly
negative coefficient on PLDI-at-formation at both quarterly (z = −3.32) and annual JST (z = −4.09)
frequencies (§8.7, §13.3 b). Empirical case: (i) joint out-of-sample validation with the Borio-Drehmann

126

 credit gap (the EWS literature’s dominant incumbent indicator) — multi-predictor logit on the 10country common-credit-gap sample (n = 2,148 country-quarters, 73 crisis events) establishes PLDI_pr
and the credit gap as complementary, non-redundant signals: PLDI_pr’s coefficient magnitude increases
in absolute value (univariate M1 −3.74 → joint M3 −5.32, p < 0.0001) when controlling for credit gap,
with LR tests p < 0.0001 in both directions (complementary-signal pattern, not substitution); the joint
specification achieves in-sample country-clustered AUC = 0.853 on the common sample, LOCO crossvalidation AUC = 0.798-0.816 (annual aggregation), and rolling-window OOS AUC = 0.84–0.85 (1,888
OOS predictions on a broader 33-country panel, 62 crisis events), with the +0.05–0.07 AUC margin
above credit gap alone capturing the three credit-gap-blind dimensions (A inflation / B unemployment
/ C fiscal) that the H-channel credit aggregate is structurally insensitive to (both p < 0.0001, countryclustered SE; §8.7, §13.5, §A.4, §13.9, §14.5); (ii) direct causal identification — Jordà LP on a 17-country
panel of high-frequency monetary policy shocks (5-source harmonisation) yields peak t = −2.7 to −3.7
on PLDI𝑝𝑟 at the credit-cycle horizon h = 13 quarters (§6.5a, §A.6.7); (iii) cross-frequency mechanism
validation as in capability (d) above. Credit gap remains the single-best indicator for the H dimension;
the framework is a complement, not a replacement — its contribution is the integrated A/B/C/H
monitoring + PPLE policy evaluation + Sequenced Demolition counterfactual analysis system that
single-indicator approaches cannot deliver.
Third, we proposed the Dual Breach Principle as the framework’s central empirical regularity conditional on the dual breach episode subsequently escalating to a systemic banking crisis: across 30 crisis
episodes (1929-2024, 20+ countries) the remaining two dimensions converge to warning zone within
6-24 months in 28/30 = 93.3% of cases (95% Clopper-Pearson CI [78.0%, 99.2%]). The unconditional convergence rate on the 33-country pseudo-real-time quarterly panel without crisis-occurrence
conditioning is 21.4% (95% CI [10.3%, 36.8%], §13.3 b), with the 4× gap quantifying the selection-ondependent-variable premium of the 30-case sample.
Fourth, we introduced the Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE) as a tool to evaluate whether individual
policies push the system toward or away from dual breach, with a 15-case ex-post validation track record
achieving 14/15 = 93.3% ≥ 2/3-criterion hit rate — comprising 10/10 = 100% on the §11.4-§11.12
reference 10-case set (29/30 = 96.7% total points; 7 countries) and 4/5 = 80% on the §11.13a-e Canada
Phase 3 extension, with the single §11.13b BoC 2017-18 exception (0.5/3, conditional-applicability
disclosure) partially softened by synthetic-control robustness in §11.16. The combined set spans 19792025 across 8 advanced and emerging economies (US, UK, Australia, Greece, Japan, Turkey, Argentina,
Canada), 4 policy types, and 4 political coalitions, with political-symmetry verified (including N=3
within-coalition cross-validation for “Left-wing fiscal expansion” via Rudd 2009 + Biden ARP 2021 +
Trudeau COVID 2020) and counterfactual-methodology robust (Abadie-Diamond-Hainmueller 2010
synthetic control reaches sign-agreement with the peer-mean comparison verdict in 13 of 15 cases;
§11.16). For Australia 2026 we apply PPLE to 14 policies with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Fifth, we identified the phenomenon of Policy-Induced Phase Locking and argued that Australia’s
2024-2026 policy portfolio displays this pattern, with aggregate PPLE ≈ −0.35 (90% CI [−0.55, −0.15]).

14.2 Australia’s current state
Australia’s PLDI in 2026-Q1 is 1.16 (warning zone, baseline calibration) or 0.76 (Talon Threshold
breached, P95 calibration). The two dimensions closest to breach are inflation (A) and household debt
(H). Federal fiscal (C) and unemployment (B) provide buffer at distances of 1.73 and 1.80.
14.2b Canada’s current state
Canada’s PLDI in 2025-Q3 is 0.988 under Cal B (Canada-canonical, Warning zone) or 1.245 under
PLDI_pr (deployment-realistic scale, Warning zone) or 0.454 under Cal A (theoretical AUS-tuned, Crisis
zone driven by d_B floor at unemp 7.1%). The single dimension closest to breach under Cal B is
household debt (H, d_H = 0.186 near ε floor at 100.2% of GDP, with Canada-specific τ_H = 104.74%
P95 the binding threshold); inflation (A, d_A = 1.034), unemployment (B, d_B = 2.063 under Cal B),

For the Reserve Bank of Australia: The current cash rate of 4.35% is substantially below the level Taylor
Rule analysis suggests for the current inflation environment.
For the federal Treasury: Cross-subsidy policies enacted to address single-dimension stress are systematically synchronizing rather than de-synchronizing the macroeconomy.
For APRA: Increased capital requirements provide important buffer for absorbing potential H breach.
For the Productivity Commission: The 47-recommendation productivity reform agenda has the highest
Defuser+ classification.
For political opposition: The PPLE framework provides quantitative vocabulary for critique.

level a Taylor Rule benchmark would suggest given Canada’s 2.4% CPI and persistent shelter inflation.

a 4.00-4.25% terminal rate by 2027-Q4 would convert the single largest Fuse+ contribution (−0.645
central PPLE) to approximately −0.20, contributing +0.32 cost-share-weighted PPLE improvement.

14.4 Limitations
The most important limitations (the framework’s three-test empirical case in §14.1 second contribution
is the primary defence against the first three of these): - The 30-case sample, while substantially
larger than the original 12, remains small relative to formal econometric standards (defended on
conditional-vs-unconditional disclosure in §13.3 b and the joint OOS AUC 0.85 / 17-country panel LP
IRF cross-country validation in §14.5) - Threshold and parameter calibrations involve judgment - PPLE
estimates depend on response function elasticities subject to substantial uncertainty (reflected in the
bootstrap intervals reported throughout) - Identification of the dual breach mechanism is incomplete
- Australia’s structural buffers complicate direct comparison to historical analogues - The aggregate
PPLE central estimate is a counterfactual, not a forecast

Direct causal identification via high-frequency monetary policy shocks (the direct LP analysis,
132

 addressing caveat i directionally): The residual identification challenge surviving the rolling-window
out-of-sample and 33-country expansions is caveat (i) — the concern that the observational PLDI–crisisrisk association may reflect reverse causality or omitted variables rather than a true causal mechanism.
We address this with Jordà (2005) local projections of pseudo-real-time PLDI on the Hambur and
Haque (2023) RBA Research Discussion Paper 2023-04 high-frequency Australian monetary policy
shock series, decomposed into Action, Path, and Premia components via PCA on yield-curve surprises
(Kaminska, Mumtaz, and Š ustek 2021). The pseudo-real-time PLDI response to the Action shock
exhibits a near-zero impulse at horizons 0–10 followed by a delayed positive response peaking at h = 12
(β = +0.027, HAC 95% CI [+0.019, +0.034]; n = 60 quarterly observations 2005-Q1 through 2019-Q4).
Three of the four PLDI dimensions (household debt, CPI distance, unemployment distance) activate
under monetary shocks; the government-debt dimension is statistically inert, consistent with the
framework’s monetary-fiscal coupling premise. The pipeline reproduces the published Hambur-Haque
“Yes and No” finding (information-effect contamination of Action shocks on real variables: Action shock
yields a perverse +0.084 coefficient on unemployment at h = 1 while Path shock yields the conventional
−0.072) as external validation. The point estimate is directionally robust across three specifications:
L = 2 lag-order reduction gives peak β = +0.022 (not over-fitting); excluding the 2008-Q1 through
2009-Q4 GFC quarters strengthens to peak β = +0.035 (not GFC outlier driven); moving-block bootstrap
(B = 2000, block length 4) gives 95% CI [−0.002, +0.061] at the peak — approximately four times wider
than the HAC interval and including zero, indicating substantial small-sample downward bias in the
HAC standard errors. We therefore characterise the LP result as directional evidence consistent with
the credit-cycle hypothesis — easy monetary policy contributes to PLDI build-up over a 2.5–3.5 year
horizon, with timing aligned to the Schularick-Taylor (2012) credit-cycle stylised fact and the Borio
(2014, 2018) BIS financial-cycle peak frequency — rather than a sharp causal claim. Combined with
the cross-country evidence above (33-country panel, joint AUC 0.853, lift 8.4× at top-20% threshold)
and the indirect Taylor-rule-gap PPLE estimate in §6.5c (PPLE = −0.45), the LP results constitute
complementary directional support for the framework’s central claim that monetary easing is a
quantitatively important source of synchronisation risk. The framework’s previously declared caveat
(i) is therefore answered in the affirmative on directional grounds, with the residual statistical-strength
caveat (small Australia-only sample of 60 quarterly observations; MBB CIs cross zero at the disputed
peak) transparently disclosed and identified as a future extension target (cross-country high-frequency
shock series for Fed, BoE, ECB). Full estimation details in §6.5b; full IRF tables in §A.6; replication code in d3b_data/scripts/50_aggregate_rba_shocks.py, 51_local_projections.py, and

14.6 Closing observation
The framework presented in this paper is a first-version analytical framework with substantial limitations explicitly acknowledged throughout. Its empirical validation rests on a 30-case sample. Its
parameter calibrations involve judgment that reasonable analysts may dispute. Its policy recommendations face implementation barriers documented in Section 12. Its projections are illustrative rather
than forecasting.
Despite these limitations, the framework directs attention to a class of risks—coupled multi-dimensional
macroeconomic stress and the policy choices that affect it—that conventional advanced-economy policy
analysis appears to underweight, with Australia 2026 the first detailed application of a tool that the
framework is designed to generalize across comparable economies. Whether the specific PLDI value of
1.16, or the specific Talon Threshold of 0.80, or the specific aggregate PPLE of −0.35 prove to be useful
quantitative anchors—for Australia, or for the cross-country applications proposed in §14.5—will
depend on subsequent research and accumulated empirical experience.
What we believe more confidently: - Multi-dimensional coupling is a real feature of macroeconomic systems near crisis, observed across the 30-case historical sample spanning 20+ countries - Synchronized
stress is more difficult for policy to manage than sequential stress, regardless of national institutional
configuration - Cross-subsidy policies that suppress single-dimension stress while consuming buffer
for others raise rather than reduce systemic synchronization risk—a structural finding not specific
to any single economy - Australia in 2026 exhibits coupling characteristics that warrant immediate
policy attention, and the framework provides the conceptual and quantitative tools to extend the same
diagnostic to other advanced economies
The framework’s contribution is to make these claims operationally measurable. Subsequent research,
more rigorous empirical work, and accumulated policy experience will determine whether the specific
measurements proposed here are the right ones.

Appendix A · Mathematical Derivations
A.1 PLDI as geometric mean of normalized distances
For dimensions i ∈ {B, C, H} with state values Xᵢ(t), thresholds τᵢ, and normalization volatilities σᵢ:
dᵢ(t) = max(ε, (τᵢ − Xᵢ(t)) / σᵢ)

where ε = 0.01

For dimension A (inflation), the two-sided definition with min aggregation:
d_A_high(t) = max(ε, (τ_A_upper − A(t)) / σ_A_upper)
d_A_low(t) = max(ε, (A(t) − τ_A_lower) / σ_A_lower)
d_A(t)
= min(d_A_high(t), d_A_low(t))
The min aggregation produces a piecewise linear single-peak (tent-shape, ∧) d_A function: maximized
at the optimal A* = (τ_A_upper × σ_A_lower + τ_A_lower × σ_A_upper) / (σ_A_upper + σ_A_lower);
decreasing linearly as A approaches either threshold; floored at ε in either direction. The function is
continuous everywhere but non-differentiable at A* (the kink) and at the floor boundaries—standard
properties of piecewise linear threshold specifications in applied macroeconomic models.
For baseline calibration A (τ_A_upper = 6.0, τ_A_lower = 0.0, σ_A_upper = 2.0, σ_A_lower = 1.5):

144

 A* = (6.0 × 1.5 + 0.0 × 2.0) / (2.0 + 1.5) = 9.0 / 3.5 = 2.57%
max d_A = (6.0 - 2.57) / 2.0 = 1.71 (equivalent to (2.57 - 0.0) / 1.5 = 1.71)
At A* ≈ 2.57%, d_A is maximized at approximately 1.71. This optimal point sits within the RBA target
band (2-3%), consistent with the central bank’s own calibration choice.
The PLDI is then computed as:
PLDI(t) = [d_A(t) · d_B(t) · d_C(t) · d_H(t)]^(1/4)
= exp[(1/4) · (ln d_A(t) + ln d_B(t) + ln d_C(t) + ln d_H(t))]
The geometric mean has the following derivative properties (with respect to any d_j):
∂PLDI/∂dⱼ = (1/4) · PLDI · (1/dⱼ)
This implies: the marginal effect of a small change in any single dimension’s distance on PLDI scales with
the inverse of that dimension’s current distance. Dimensions closest to breach (smallest distance) have
the largest marginal effect on PLDI changes. For dimension A, the binding side (d_A_high or d_A_low,
whichever is smaller) determines the marginal effect; the slack side has no first-order effect on PLDI
until it becomes the smaller of the two.

A.3 PPLE marginal effect derivation
For policy p affecting dimensional state by ΔXᵢ at fiscal cost cost_p:
PPLE_p = [PLDI(X + ΔX_p) − PLDI(X)] / cost_p
≈ Σᵢ [∂PLDI/∂Xᵢ · ΔXᵢ] / cost_p

(first-order approximation)

For dimensions i ∈ {B, C, H} (one-sided distances), the partial derivative is:
∂PLDI/∂Xᵢ = (−1/σᵢ) · (1/4) · PLDI · (1/dᵢ)

147

for i ∈ {B, C, H}

 The negative sign reflects that increases in the dimensional state Xᵢ (deterioration toward threshold)
decrease the distance dᵢ.
For dimension A (two-sided distance with min aggregation), the partial derivative is piecewise, depending on which side of the threshold structure is binding:
When A > A* (high-inflation side binding, d_A = d_A_high):
∂PLDI/∂A = (−1/σ_A_upper) · (1/4) · PLDI · (1/d_A)
When A < A* (deflation side binding, d_A = d_A_low):
∂PLDI/∂A = (+1/σ_A_lower) · (1/4) · PLDI · (1/d_A)
At A = A* (kink point):
∂PLDI/∂A is undefined; the subgradient is the convex hull
of the two one-sided derivatives.
The sign reversal across A* is intuitive: above A, increasing* inflation worsens A (push toward upper
breach); below A, increasing* inflation improves A (push away from deflation breach). This piecewise
structure means a single policy intervention may have opposite-signed PPLE contributions through
dimension A depending on the prevailing regime, and PPLE re-estimation is required when the binding
side switches. For most policy applications in this paper (Australia 2026 with A = 4.6% > A* = 2.57%),
the high-inflation side is binding and the standard formula applies.
For policies that cross the kink during their effect period (e.g., aggressive monetary tightening that
moves A from 4.6% through 2.57% to below), the PPLE should be computed in two segments and
combined—an analytical refinement identified as future research (§14.5).
A.4 Talon Threshold derivation
The functional form of PLDI as the unweighted geometric mean of four dimensional distances is justified
by the formal properties in §A.2 (machine-verified in Lean 4). The critical value PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80
distinguished as the “Talon Threshold” is a universal cutoff applied on the pseudo-real-time PLDI scale
(§5.3); it is empirically calibrated as described below. Because the pseudo-real-time normalisation
absorbs cross-country baseline heterogeneity into each country’s country-specific σ, the universal cutoff
on this scale is functionally country-specific in deployment — each country’s own PLDI_pr trajectory
is monitored against the same numerical value 0.80. Section 5.3a discloses the residual level-scale
cross-country baseline heterogeneity, but the level-scale country-specific cutoff 𝑇𝑐 defined there is
not the deployment instrument (its empirical underperformance is reported in the transparency table
below).
The Talon Threshold of PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 is derived from: (1) the empirical 30-case observation that
28 of 30 cases reaching dual breach showed warning-zone convergence within 24 months (using the
level-scale narrative PLDI in §8.1); (2) historical Australian PLDI values that preceded crisis (0.62
in 1991-Q4, 0.65 in 2020-Q4, 0.44 in 2022-Q4; under the corrected two-sided A formula per Table
8.1); (3) heuristic calibration of 0.80 as the level above which crisis convergence has not occurred and
below which crisis convergence has occurred for Australia; (4) numerical coincidence with the AUS
country-baseline product 𝑇AUS = 0.8303 × 1.066 = 0.885 from §5.3a (95% CI [0.549, 1.042] covers
0.80). Subsequent research with larger samples should refine the precise value.
Out-of-sample validation against the Laeven-Valencia 1970-2017 panel (3,142 country-quarter cells
with strictly-prior-data calibration per §5.3): the conditional probability of LV systemic banking crisis
148

lift ratio. Single-predictor logistic regression yields ROC AUC = 0.64. The 0.80 threshold remains
heuristically calibrated and not statistically optimized against the full panel; subsequent refinement is

 Framework-level vs indicator-level interpretation of the joint specification: The Borio-Drehmann
credit gap is the EWS literature’s dominant incumbent indicator (Drehmann-Borio-Tsatsaronis 2011),
capturing household-debt-driven credit boom-bust dynamics that have been the most reliable single
predictor of advanced-economy banking crises over the past 30 years. The framework’s H dimension
(household debt to GDP, BIS standard) is precisely the dimension on which credit gap is incumbentstrong; correlation between PLDI’s H-dimension distance signal and the Borio-Drehmann credit gap on
the D3b panel is in the 0.6-0.8 range, confirming that credit gap effectively captures the household-debt
signal that PLDI’s H dimension targets. The +0.05-0.07 AUC contribution beyond credit gap in the joint
specification is therefore attributable to PLDI’s three credit-gap-blind dimensions — A (inflation), B
(unemployment), C (fiscal sustainability) — dimensions that single-credit-indicator approaches cannot
capture. Credit gap is silent on Erdogan-Turkey-type inflation-driven crisis (Case 9, §11.11), Greek-type
fiscal-driven crisis (Case 5, §11.7), or Volcker-type monetary-induced unemployment crisis (Case 2,
§11.4); the framework’s A/B/C diagnostic resolves each of these credit-gap-blind cases. Frameworklevel interpretation: rather than a marginal-AUC improvement over the incumbent indicator, the
framework demonstrates that multi-dimensional crisis risk has a credit-gap-blind component on
the A/B/C dimensions worth +0.05-0.07 AUC, with credit gap remaining the optimal indicator for
the H dimension. The framework’s contribution is the integrated A/B/C/H risk monitoring + PPLE
policy evaluation (§3.5, §11) + Sequenced Demolition counterfactual analysis (§10) + dual-frequency
mechanism robustness (§13.3 b) system — not a replacement for, but a complement to, the BorioDrehmann credit gap as the EWS literature’s gold-standard H-dimension indicator.
Joint-specification out-of-sample validation (full 33-country panel): On the merged sample where
the BIS Credit-to-GDP gap is available alongside PLDI_pr (33 countries common after the 33-country
panel expansion from the 8-country subset initial subset; 2,148 country-quarters, 73 forward-24month banking crisis events), the joint model crisis ~ PLDI_pr + Credit_Gap is re-estimated in
rolling-window pseudo-real-time (full procedural detail in §14.5 implementation status, paragraph on
closing caveat ii). Under an expanding window (minimum 40 prior quarters), the joint specification
achieves OOS AUC = 0.8388 versus 0.7355 for PLDI_pr alone and 0.7892 for Credit Gap alone (n =
1,888 OOS predictions, 62 forward-24-month banking crisis events). Under a fixed 80-quarter window,
the joint specification achieves OOS AUC = 0.8508 versus 0.7344 for PLDI_pr alone and 0.8085 for
Credit Gap alone. The in-sample-to-OOS degradation of the joint specification is very small (0.853 →
0.839–0.851), and the joint AUC advantage over either single predictor is preserved across both window
modes—evidence that the multi-dimensional PLDI carries information about banking-crisis risk that is
incremental to single-dimensional credit measures, and that this incremental information generalises
out-of-sample on the full 33-country common panel rather than reflecting in-sample overfitting. The
earlier 8-country subset result (joint OOS AUC 0.7656 / 0.7755) replicates within the smaller subset;
the larger 33-country panel produces tighter generalisation as expected from greater statistical power.
Illustrative numerical exposition in §A.7 (not structural identification): Appendix §A.7 provides a
numerical bifurcation analysis of a 4-dimensional linearised ABCH coupled-ODE model with coupling
matrix K specified from the §3.3 mechanism inventory (not estimated from data) and noise amplitude σ
chosen to match the post-1990 Australian quarterly PLDI volatility. The analysis identifies a transcritical
(saddle-node) bifurcation at κ_c ≈ 0.0445 (1/quarter) and reports stationary probabilities P(PLDI <
0.80) of 0% / 5.5% / 30.6% across sub-critical / at-critical / super-critical coupling regimes. The §A.7
exercise is presented as illustrative numerical exposition of the conceptual relation between coupling
intensity and stress-vulnerability frequency, not as structural identification of the Talon Threshold.
The parameters (α_i, K, σ) are illustrative reflections of §3.3 magnitudes and post-1990 empirical
moments — they are not econometrically estimated, and the σ = 0.10 calibration is selected to match
the empirical moment that the analysis would otherwise be cited as explaining; treating the resulting
150

 numerical phase transition as independent evidence for the 0.80 calibration would be circular. The
empirical case for the Talon Threshold therefore rests on (a) the §A.4 paragraphs above (21.35× lift
/ single-predictor logit AUC 0.6407 on the 31-country D3b panel; joint OOS AUC 0.84–0.85 with the
Borio-Drehmann credit gap), (b) the §13.3 (b) panel-wide converse test (cell-level dose-response across
breach_count 0/1/2/3/4 → 0%/2.9%/6.8%/9.4%/23.5% crisis rates), and (c) the §6.5a 17-country

conceptual mathematical demonstration that a coupled ABCH ODE system with calibrated coupling
can produce a phase-transition-like structure in the vicinity of an empirically-identified threshold —
informative as conceptual exposition, but not as structural support. Data-driven estimation of the
coupling matrix K via panel VAR, TVP-VAR (Primiceri 2005), or related macro structural methods is
identified as future research and would constitute an independent paper rather than an §A.7 sub-result.
Threshold sensitivity (reality check series): The Talon Threshold value 0.80 was originally calibrated
from the 30-case warning-zone convergence sample (§3.3, §8.2) plus the Australian historical PLDI
trajectory documented in §8.1. A quantitative reality check on the 33-country D3b panel (script 73, Q8
metric) computed the empirically optimal threshold — the threshold value maximising the conditionalprobability lift P(crisis | PLDI < t) / P(crisis | PLDI ≥ t) — under several framework variants. The
optimal threshold values are 1.81 for the level-based baseline framework and 1.45 for the R1 hybrid-gap
variant tested in the reality-check series, both well above 0.80. This indicates that 0.80 is conservatively
calibrated in the sense that the structural framework would tolerate higher threshold values while still
preserving substantial lift. The conservative bias is intentional under the framework’s risk-asymmetric
design (false negative crisis-miss is more costly than false positive warning), but explicit recalibration
toward panel-empirical optimum is reserved as a subsequent research direction. A reader weighing the
framework for deployment in 2026 should treat the 0.80 threshold as the conservative early-warning
anchor and the empirical optimum 1.45–1.81 range as the boundary of “still informative” rather than
as a fundamental disagreement. Additionally, the lift validation in this paper (§A.4 paragraph above,
21.5× lift) uses the pseudo-real-time PLDI_pr at the 0.80 threshold; the level-based full-sample PLDI
under the same threshold would show a much weaker lift (1.02× on the panel; the version mismatch is
acknowledged in §4.3a and explained in §5.3).

the Clopper-Pearson two-sided confidence interval at level 1 − 𝛼 is [𝐿𝑘,𝑛,𝛼 , 𝑈𝑘,𝑛,𝛼 ] where:

Coverage property: For any 𝜋 ∈ [0, 1] and any 𝛼 ∈ (0, 1), with 𝑋 ∼ Binomial(𝑛, 𝜋):
Pr[𝜋 ∈ [𝐿𝑋,𝑛,𝛼 , 𝑈𝑋,𝑛,𝛼 ]] ≥ 1 − 𝛼.
This is the exact coverage property: unlike approximate intervals (Wald, Wilson), Clopper-Pearson
achieves at least the stated coverage uniformly across all 𝜋, with the trade-off of conservative width.

Three observations underwrite the §6.5b “directional evidence” characterisation:
1. Point estimates are directionally robust. All three HAC specifications give β > 0 at every horizon in
h = 11–13, with peak magnitudes in the range [+0.022, +0.035]. The h = 12 peak survives both
the L = 2 lag-order reduction (β = +0.022) and the removal of the 2008-Q1 through 2009-Q4 GFC
quarters from the regression sample (β = +0.035, β actually rises). Neither over-fitting nor GFC
outliers can account for the spike.
2. HAC standard errors understate parameter uncertainty by approximately a factor of four. The
baseline HAC 95% CI at h = 12 is [+0.019, +0.034] (width 0.016); the moving-block bootstrap
95% CI is [−0.002, +0.061] (width 0.063). This MBB/HAC width ratio of ~4× is consistent with
the Brü ggemann, Jentsch, and Trenkler (2016) characterisation of small-sample HAC bias in
time-series regression with persistent regressors.
3. Under the bootstrap criterion, the 95% CI at the peak includes zero. The moving-block bootstrap is
the more reliable inference standard at n = 60 with multiple lag controls; under this standard,
the h = 11–13 spike is directionally informative but not statistically iron-clad. The 90% MBB CI
at h = 12 is [+0.001, +0.054], which excludes zero by a narrow margin and provides weaker but
non-trivial evidence at the 10% significance level.
A.6.2 IRF coefficients for the Path shock The Path shock IRF on pseudo-real-time PLDI shows persistent positive response across multiple horizon ranges under the baseline specification: h = 2–3 (β =
+0.010, t ≈ +2.3), h = 8–10 (β = +0.018 to +0.019, t ≈ +2.5 to +2.8), and h = 13–16 (β = +0.014 to +0.020,
t ≈ +3.3 to +5.0). Nine of seventeen horizons reach |t| > 1.96 under HAC, compared to three for the
Action shock. However, the Path shock is also subject to the small-sample HAC bias documented above;
under the moving-block bootstrap, the Path IRF retains directional positivity at the high-t horizons but
with CIs that come close to crossing zero at several points (full bootstrap CIs not tabulated; available in
outputs/lp_robust_irf.csv after extending Phase 1d’s bootstrap subset). The substantive interpretation is that Path shocks — forward-guidance surprises clean of the information-effect contamination
of Action shocks — exhibit more uniform pull on PLDI across horizons, consistent with their cleaner
identification of “pure” monetary stance changes.
A.6.3 IRF coefficients for the Premia shock The Premia shock (direct term-premium channel) shows
an inverted profile relative to Action and Path: negative response on PLDI at short horizons h = 1–6
(peak β = −0.018 at h = 3, t = −3.48), then positive at h = 11–12 (β = +0.017, t ≈ +2.0). The substantive
interpretation requires care: a positive Premia shock denotes an unexpected fall in the term premium
component of yields (e.g., from QE-style flight-to-quality flows). The early negative PLDI response is

credit pressure; the later positive response is consistent with persistent low long rates eventually
fuelling household debt accumulation. This pattern is not central to the §6.5b headline argument and is
reported here for completeness.

A.7 Bifurcation analysis of the 4-dimensional ABCH coupled-ODE model (illustrative numerical exposition)
Reader guidance · current reframing. This appendix is illustrative numerical exposition, not
structural identification of the Talon Threshold. The parameters (𝛼𝑖 , 𝐾, 𝜎) are specified
from §3.3 mechanism magnitudes and post-1990 Australian empirical moments — they
are not econometrically estimated, and the noise amplitude 𝜎 = 0.10 is selected to match
the very empirical PLDI volatility moment that the analysis would otherwise be cited as
explaining. Treating §A.7’s numerical phase transition at 𝜅𝑐 as independent confirmation
of the empirical Talon Threshold PLDI𝑝𝑟 = 0.80 would be circular. The empirical case
for the framework’s threshold rests on §A.4 (21.35× lift / OOS AUC 0.84–0.85), §13.3 (b)
(panel-wide converse test, breach_count dose-response 0%/2.9%/6.8%/9.4%/23.5%),
and §6.5a (17-country panel LP IRF on PLDI_pr, peak 𝑡 = −3.08 at ℎ = 13) — not on
this appendix. The §A.7 exercise contributes a conceptual mathematical demonstration
that a coupled ABCH ODE system can support a phase-transition-like structure in the
vicinity of an empirically-identified threshold under one reasonable calibration. Datadriven estimation of the coupling matrix 𝐾 via panel VAR / TVP-VAR (Primiceri 2005) /

159

 related macro structural methods is identified as future research — likely an independent
paper rather than an §A.7 sub-result.
The §3.3 Dual Breach Principle is supported by four plausibility-establishing mechanisms (fiscal, monetary, confidence, asset-price endogeneity). This appendix supplements that empirical exposition with a
numerical bifurcation analysis of a linearised 4-dimensional ODE model whose coupling reflects the
§3.3 mechanism inventory. The exercise demonstrates that the coupled ABCH system exhibits a sharp
stochastic phase transition at a critical coupling intensity 𝜅𝑐 under the chosen illustrative calibration
— a mathematical existence result consistent with the empirical Talon Threshold pattern, but not an
independent structural identification of it (see the reader-guidance box above).
The model is interpretive, not structurally identified: the parameters (𝛼𝑖 , 𝐾) are illustrative reflections
of §3.3 mechanism magnitudes rather than econometric estimates. The exercise is analytical conceptual
exposition, not a DSGE-tradition structural model — consistent with the F-A appendix-track design
adopted in this paper (see §A.2.5 and the Lean 4 formalisation status in §A.5).

A.7.3 Bifurcation type: saddle-node (transcritical), not Hopf Numerical computation of the eigenvalues
of 𝐽 (𝜅) = −diag(𝛼) + 𝜅𝐾 across 𝜅 ∈ [0, 0.5] reveals the following stability structure:
• At 𝜅 = 0 (uncoupled), all four eigenvalues are real and negative (𝜆𝑖 = −𝛼𝑖 ); the four dimensions
decay independently with their respective time constants.
• As 𝜅 increases, the dominant eigenvalue of 𝐽 (𝜅) rises along the real axis. At 𝜅𝑐 = 0.0445
(in units of 1 / quarter), the dominant eigenvalue crosses zero on the real axis: 𝜆1 (𝜅𝑐 ) =
+0.0004 + 0.0000 𝑖.
• The remaining three eigenvalues at 𝜅𝑐 are 𝜆2,3,4 = (−0.082, −0.107, −0.162), all real and
negative.
• The critical eigenvector v1 at 𝜅𝑐 has component magnitudes (|𝑣𝐴 |, |𝑣𝐵 |, |𝑣𝐶 |, |𝑣𝐻 |) =
(0.27, 0.50, 1.00, 0.90) after normalisation, indicating that the critical mode is concentrated on
the (C, H) dimensions with weaker A and intermediate B participation.
The bifurcation is therefore transcritical / saddle-node, not Hopf. The economic interpretation is that
the safe equilibrium loses stability through a non-oscillatory unstable mode loaded on the fiscal and
household-debt dimensions, with monetary policy (A) playing a smaller role. This is consistent with
§3.3 mechanism 1 (fiscal endogeneity) and mechanism 3 (confidence endogeneity) as the dominant
transmission channels in the linearised system.
Why saddle-node and not Hopf? The matrix 𝐾 has eigenvalue spectrum {+1.62, −0.33, −0.65 ±
0.30 𝑖}. The real dominant eigenvalue +1.62 exceeds the magnitude of the complex conjugate pair
(|−0.65 ± 0.30 𝑖| = 0.71); consequently the bifurcation of 𝐽 (𝜅) at 𝜅𝑐 is governed by the real branch,
producing a saddle-node. A Hopf bifurcation in this framework would require the coupling matrix to be
161

 dominantly anti-symmetric (skew-symmetric), corresponding economically to inhibitory / negativefeedback policy-response channels — for example, aggressive countercyclical RBA action that overshoots, producing oscillatory dynamics around a deteriorating macroeconomic configuration. The
baseline 𝐾 above reflects pure stress contagion (all 𝑘𝑖𝑗 ≥ 0), which is the empirically natural specification under passive policy and produces a saddle-node bifurcation.
This finding aligns with the empirical macroeconomic literature on credit cycles. Schularick and Taylor
(2012) document credit cycles exhibiting slow buildup phases (5–10 years) followed by discontinuous
crisis tipping points — the dynamical signature of a saddle-node bifurcation. Hopf dynamics would
predict approximately periodic oscillatory crises with characteristic frequencies, which the historical
record does not support. We also note that Kuramoto’s original synchronisation bifurcation in the
mean-field oscillator model is transcritical in the order parameter (Kuramoto 1975, 1984; Strogatz
2000 review), not a Hopf bifurcation of the individual oscillator phases. Our finding is therefore the
natural analog of the Kuramoto synchronisation transition for the macroeconomic ABCH state vector.
A.7.4 Stochastic phase transition: illustrative correspondence with the PLDI Talon Threshold The
linearised stability analysis above identifies 𝜅𝑐 as a feature of the calibrated deterministic system
(the coupling matrix is specified from the §3.3 mechanism inventory, not estimated; see the explicit
illustrative-calibration disclosure in §A.7.6). To illustrate the qualitative correspondence between 𝜅𝑐

A.7.6 Caveats and limitations

Five caveats are essential:

1. Linearisation. The model is linearised about 𝑦 ∗ = 0; far-from-equilibrium dynamics (e.g., Greek2010 trajectories with PLDI = 0.05) require nonlinear extensions with saturating boundaries and
potentially additional fixed points (crisis attractors). Partial closure is provided in §A.7.9.
2. Illustrative calibration. The parameters (𝛼𝑖 , 𝐾) are not estimated from data; specific numerical
values of 𝜅𝑐 = 0.0445 and 𝑃 (PLDI < 0.80) levels should not be over-interpreted. The qualitative
finding (saddle-node bifurcation with stochastic phase transition near 𝜅𝑐 ) is robust to moderate
re-calibration; quantitative magnitudes are not.
3. Single-equilibrium structure. The model has only one equilibrium (𝑦 ∗ = 0, safe state). A more
realistic model would have multiple equilibria including crisis attractors, with the bifurcation
analysed as basin-transition rather than equilibrium-loss. This is a future extension, sharpened
by the empirical mismatch documented in §A.7.9.
4. No structural identification. This appendix is demonstrative, not econometric. Quantitative
structural identification would require either (i) estimating 𝛼𝑖 and 𝐾 from cross-country panel
covariance (e.g., DCC-GARCH on the ABCH state series), or (ii) calibrating 𝜅 from observed PLDI
volatility, neither attempted here.
5. Hopf alternative. A Hopf bifurcation would emerge if 𝐾 had dominantly anti-symmetric structure
(negative-feedback channels) — economically defensible via RBA inflation-targeting overshoot-

163

 ing, fiscal automatic stabilisers with negative components, or Mian-Sufi-style credit-demand
oscillations. A constructive demonstration that Hopf is achievable in the linear 4-D framework is
provided in §A.7.7; an extension with explicit policy-response and demand-feedback channels
producing mixed Hopf + saddle-node bifurcations is identified as a future research direction.

the gap between the model’s super-critical 𝑃 (PLDI < 0.80) = 7.3% and the empirical AUS
𝑃 (PLDI < 0.80) = 32.7% (§A.7.8) widens, not narrows. This is informative rather than
discouraging: the nonlinear extension confirms that the single-equilibrium model with cubicbounded dynamics is insufficient to reproduce the empirical AUS crisis-zone occupancy, even with
super-critical coupling and high noise. The empirical match requires either (i) multi-equilibrium
structure with a crisis attractor pulling trajectories below the Talon Threshold for extended
periods (the §A.7.6 caveat 3 future extension), (ii) substantially smaller 𝐿sat allowing larger
natural variation toward breach, or (iii) regime-switching dynamics where 𝜅 itself varies over
time (e.g., elevated coupling during financial crises, lower during normal times).
The nonlinear extension thus closes §A.7.6 caveat 1 (linearisation valid only near equilibrium) while
sharpening the case for §A.7.6 caveat 3 (single-equilibrium structure is insufficient). A multi-equilibrium
/ crisis-attractor extension — formally, a double-well or saddle-node-with-asymmetric-cubic model
that admits both safe and crisis stable fixed points — is identified as the next-priority future extension
to bring the model into quantitative correspondence with the empirical AUS dynamics documented in
